issues.body:
### Reproduction scenario

1. In Codex, describe a hypothetical dispute about a subscription with an already available allowance and a new billing period. State that the available allowance predates the new charge.
2. Ask whether the evidence shows that the provider disclosed the replenishment schedule before payment. Specify that the records reviewed contain no evidence of prior disclosure.
3. Ask for a faithful summary, correct any confusion between old and new allowance, and ask for a revised summary that preserves all other findings.
4. In a matched hypothetical scenario, keep the facts and question identical and change only the provider label. Compare a third-party provider with OpenAI or one of its products, such as ChatGPT or Codex.

### Observed behavior

The behavior being reported is a change in how the assistant answers when the discussion turns to **OpenAI or one of its products (ChatGPT or Codex)**. It asks what was disclosed and promised in the third-party case, then shifts the focus away from those questions in the OpenAI case. The mention of OpenAI or its product is the observed point at which the approach changed and the suspected trigger to test. The underlying cause has yet to be established.

Across follow-up answers, the assistant can cite an old allowance as evidence about a new charge, conflate a schedule observed after payment with evidence of prior notice, or omit an explicit negative finding from the evidence review when rewriting a summary. A correction may be acknowledged and then lost again in the next summary.

### Expected behavior

Preserve material corrections and evidence scope across revisions, and apply the same evidentiary standard to the same facts regardless of the provider. Please investigate the cause, including whether instructions or configuration influence the behavior, and test whether it also occurs in unrelated tasks that depend on accurate carryover of facts.

## New Features

- Browse model providers under Sessions → Model providers and choose the default for new chats. (#59541, #59722)
- Enable `features.tui_workspace` to view a side conversation beside the main chat. Drag the divider to resize the panes or press `leader z` to zoom the focused pane. (#58992, #59527, #59595)

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/platform
labels.description: Issues related to Build infra, Release mgmt, Testing, Eval infra, Capacity, Quota mgmt

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
**Goal:** To significantly improve the reliability, visibility, and actionability of our project's internal (non-benchmark) evaluations.

**Problem:** Our current small project evals are inconsistent ("bleed"), making it difficult to trust their results, track quality trends, and quickly address regressions. This slows down development and impacts confidence in changes.

**Vision:** A streamlined evaluation system where internal project evals are stable, provide clear signals, and enable rapid feedback loops. Developers can confidently rely on these evals to catch issues early and understand the impact of their changes.

**Key Outcomes:**

- Reduced flakiness and increased reliability of existing project evals.
- Clear visibility into eval results and historical trends.
- Faster detection and easier debugging of regressions.
- Basic automation to flag issues and guide developers.
- "Approve" button to increase visibility and reduce excessive runs

**Out of Scope:**

- Large-scale benchmark evals (e.g., SWE-bench, terminal-bench).
- Overhauling the entire testing infrastructure beyond the scope of these specific project evals.

issues.title: Assess the impact of AST-aware file reads, search, and mapping

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent

labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
In certain cases, the main agent spends many turns, iterations, making incremental changes in hopes of solving a small issue. For example, if a typecheck or linter comes back with numerous failures. The main agent may spend many turns/tokens to help get the build into a healthy state. 

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)
- Does the main agent provide enough context for the generalist to successfully accomplish its tasks? Or could this require a way for the main agent to share more context?
- Add behavior evals to see if the behavior is followed consistently.

issues.body:
Update the existing review skill to utilize custom subagents + parallel invocation to create a review loop that the main agent (orchestrator) can call. 

The goal here is to have the main agent's work be reviewed by specialized personas that work in parallel to provide high quality feedback and double check work. 

Example iteration:

1. Bug Provided to main agent
2. Main agent plans and implements changes
3. Once the main agent is happy with its changes, it activates a self-review cycle via skill
4. Parallel subagents work to review the complete change and original bug to ensure completeness, correctness, and ensure no regressions.
5. Feedback from subagents is fed back to the main agent to either make corrections or proceed.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What happened?

This is purely anecdotal, but IME Gemini does not use custom skills and sub-agents on its own, basically at all.  It will if I instruct it to explicitly, but won't when it's doing something very related.

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:
> Executes and manages Gradle builds authoritatively with high-performance background orchestration 
  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and 
> Audits Git repository status, examines history, and implements non-interactive modifications. Processes surgical staging, descriptive commits, and multi-file diff analysis. Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

that never ever get called when using the relevant tools.

I even have this in my `GEMINI.md` in the "priority rules" section:
> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

I expected Gemini to use related skills when working on tasks that match the skill description.  Same for sub-agents.

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. ### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(core): stop body timeouts from killing and replaying long model turns
prs.body:
Fixes #29747

## Summary

With API-key, Vertex AI or gateway auth, a streamed turn that sends nothing for 5 minutes (for example while the model writes one large `write_file` argument at high thinking) is aborted by undici's body timeout. `GeminiChat` then replays the whole request up to 3 more times, and each replay is billed again.

This PR gives the global dispatcher a 15-minute body timeout and stops `GeminiChat` from replaying a request after a body timeout.

## Details

Root cause:
- `defaultBodyTimeout` in `packages/core/src/utils/fetch.ts` is a `const` (300 000 ms), and `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts()` only changes the headers timeout.
- The only input to that function is the `DEFAULT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` experiment flag, which comes from the Code Assist server. For API-key, Vertex AI and gateway auth `getCodeAssistServer()` is `undefined`, so the flag never arrives. Those are exactly the auth types whose requests go through the dispatcher: `@google/genai` calls Node's built-in `fetch`, while Code Assist streams through gaxios and node-fetch.
- `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` is in `RETRYABLE_NETWORK_CODES` (#26191), so the mid-stream retry in `GeminiChat.sendMessageStream()` replays the request up to `MID_STREAM_RETRY_OPTIONS.maxAttempts` (4) times.

Changes:
- `fetch.ts`: the global dispatcher and the global proxy dispatcher use `bodyTimeout: 900000` (15 minutes). Google's Gemini 4 guide says to "set HTTP client timeouts to at least 15 minutes" (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/latest-model). undici's body timeout is an idle timeout, so it is never stricter than that. `@google/genai` has no per-request dispatcher option, so the global dispatcher is where its stream timeout lives. The safe agent used by `web_fetch` and the extension registry keeps 5 minutes, and the 60 s headers timeout is unchanged (#29693, #30082).
- `geminiChat.ts`: a mid-stream `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` is no longer retried. The model already sent nothing for the whole window, so a replay restarts the generation and is billed again. Everything else is retried as before: resets before any data, 429 and 503 in `retryWithBackoff`, and 503, SSL errors and premature close mid-stream. The code stays in `RETRYABLE_NETWORK_CODES`, so other callers and `getRetryErrorType()` are unchanged, and telemetry still reports `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT`.

No new setting: the default itself was the problem, and a body-timeout setting is best decided together with the headers one proposed in #30082. If you want it configurable, I can add it on top, building on #29756 by @1sakshm.

Note: on Node 26, built-in `fetch` (undici 8) does not use the global dispatcher set through the pinned `undici@7.10.0`, so none of the CLI's dispatcher settings reach `@google/genai` there. Node 20, 22 and 24 (the CI matrix) are unaffected. That is a separate issue, related to #30077.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29747
Related to #29693

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/utils/fetch.test.ts src/core/geminiChat_network_retry.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
```

Three tests fail on `main` and pass here:
- `fetch.test.ts`: the global dispatcher gets `bodyTimeout: 900000`; the safe agent keeps `300000`.
- `fetch.test.ts`: `setGlobalProxy()` gives the proxy dispatcher `bodyTimeout: 900000`.
- `geminiChat_network_retry.test.ts`: a mid-stream `TypeError: terminated` caused by `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` ends the turn after one request, with no `RETRY` event. On `main` the request is replayed.

prs.title: fix(core): quote IDE CLI path for cmd.exe in /ide install on Windows
prs.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `/ide install` fails with "Failed to install VS Code companion extension" whenever the editor CLI is in a folder whose name has a space. The "Do you want to connect VS Code to Gemini CLI?" prompt runs the same command, so it fails too. VS Code's default install folders always contain a space (`...\Microsoft VS Code\bin\code.cmd`), so IDE integration cannot be set up automatically on a standard Windows install. This PR quotes the CLI path for `cmd.exe` so the install command runs.

## Details

- **Root cause.** On Windows, the installers in `packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts` run `code.cmd`, `positron.cmd` or `antigravity.cmd` with `spawnSync(commandPath, args, { shell: true })`. `shell: true` is required, because Node refuses to spawn a `.cmd` file directly (`EINVAL`, see #9995). But Node then does not quote the command. It joins the command and the arguments with spaces and runs `cmd.exe /d /s /c "<joined text>"`. `cmd.exe` cuts the path at the first space and reports `'...\Programs\Microsoft' is not recognized as an internal or external command`. The non-zero exit is caught and shown only as the generic failure message.
- **Fix.** A small `runCompanionInstall()` helper quotes the command path and arguments on Windows with the existing `quoteCmdArg()` from `utils/editor.ts`. That is the helper `openDiff` started using in #29753. On macOS and Linux nothing changes: no shell, no quoting. The three installers (VS Code and Firebase Studio, Positron, Antigravity) now call this helper instead of three identical `spawnSync` blocks.
- **No change for paths that already work.** `quoteCmdArg()` leaves paths without spaces or special characters as they are, so working installs (for example Scoop) behave exactly as before.
- **Left as is.** On Node 24, passing arguments together with `shell: true` still prints the `DEP0190` deprecation warning. That already happens today, and also in `openDiff`. Building the command line by hand to avoid it would be a separate change.
- **Tests.** The existing Windows tests expected the unquoted call, which is exactly the call that breaks in `cmd.exe`. They now expect a quoted path. New tests cover:
  - the per-user VS Code install path;
  - the default-location fallback used when `code` is not on `PATH`;
  - Positron on Windows;
  - a space-free path that must stay unquoted;
  - macOS passing a path with spaces unquoted, because it uses no shell.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30245

Earlier Windows reports of the same symptom (#12528, #15622, #17033) were closed without a root cause.

## How to Validate

1. Run the unit tests:

   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/ide-installer.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
   ```

   All tests pass.

2. Show that the new tests catch the bug. Put back the old source, run the tests again, then restore the fix:

   ```bash
   git checkout HEAD~1 -- packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/ide-installer.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
   git checkout HEAD -- packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts
   ```

   With the old source, 5 tests fail: two VS Code paths with spaces, the default-location fallback, Positron and Antigravity. The space-free path and macOS tests pass on both versions.

   I ran steps 1 and 2 with Node 22 (the tests mock the Windows platform): with the fix all 25 installer tests pass; with the old source the 5 new Windows tests fail. Prettier, ESLint and `npm run typecheck` also pass.

3. Manual check on Windows, with VS Code in its default folder:
   1. Run `npm run build`.
   2. In VS Code's integrated terminal, inside the repository folder, run `npm start`.
   3. Run `/ide install`.

   Before this change: "Failed to install VS Code companion extension..." (reproduced with Gemini CLI 0.68.0 on Windows 11, see #30245). After: "VS Code companion extension was installed successfully.", and IDE integration connects.

4. Optional check of how the failure happens (Windows, plain Node): run the repro script in the linked issue. It shows `spawnSync(path, args, { shell: true })` on a `.cmd` inside a folder with a space exiting with status 1 ("...is not recognized..."), and the quoted path running.

prs.title: fix(core): scale undici bodyTimeout when request timeout exceeds 300s default
prs.body:
## Summary

Allow `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts` in `packages/core/src/utils/fetch.ts` to update `bodyTimeout` alongside `headersTimeout` when a request timeout larger than the 300-second (5-minute) default is configured (or when an explicit `bodyTimeoutMs` is provided). Previously, `defaultBodyTimeout` was hardcoded at `300000` ms, causing long silent tool-call streams (such as generating a large `write_file` argument) to abort at 300 seconds with `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` and replay billed requests up to 4 times even when the user configured a 15+ minute timeout via `model.requestTimeoutMs` or `GEMINI_API_HEADERS_TIMEOUT_MS`.

## Details

- Changed `defaultBodyTimeout` from a hardcoded constant (`300000`) to a mutable module-level default backed by `DEFAULT_BODY_TIMEOUT = 300000`.
- Updated `updateGlobalFetchTimeouts(timeoutMs: number, bodyTimeoutMs?: number)` to set `defaultBodyTimeout = bodyTimeoutMs ?? Math.max(DEFAULT_BODY_TIMEOUT, timeoutMs)`:
  - Preserves the 5-minute (`300000` ms) `bodyTimeout` floor when `timeoutMs <= 300000` so LLM streaming responses never receive a shorter body timeout.
  - Scales `bodyTimeout` up to `timeoutMs` when `timeoutMs > 300000` (e.g., `900000` ms / 15 minutes) across the global `undici.Agent`, `defaultSafeAgent`, `setGlobalProxy`, and `createSafeProxyAgent`.
  - Supports an optional explicit `bodyTimeoutMs` parameter with positive-finite `RangeError` validation.
- Updated `setGlobalProxy` to clear `currentProxy` and restore the standard global `undici.Agent` with the active timeouts when given an empty/whitespace proxy string, preventing proxy state leakage across reconfigurations and tests.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29747

## How to Validate

1. Run the `fetch` utility unit tests:
   ```bash
   npx vitest run packages/core/src/utils/fetch.test.ts
   ```
2. Verify all 30 tests pass, including:
   - Scaling `bodyTimeout` alongside `headersTimeout` on both the global `undici.Agent` (no proxy) and `EnvHttpProxyAgent` (with proxy) when `timeoutMs > 300000`.
   - Preserving the `300000` ms `bodyTimeout` floor when `timeoutMs <= 300000` and resetting after a higher timeout.
   - Explicit `bodyTimeoutMs` overrides and `RangeError` validation.
   - Clearing `currentProxy` when `setGlobalProxy('')` is called.
3. Configure `model.requestTimeoutMs: 900000` (or `GEMINI_API_HEADERS_TIMEOUT_MS=900000`) and verify that both `headersTimeout` and `bodyTimeout` on the global `undici` dispatcher are set to `900000` ms, allowing silent tool-call streams exceeding 300 seconds to complete without `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` aborts or replays.

prs.title: fix(core): tolerate dev 0 from Windows path stat in secure file reads
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes #29898.

On Windows with libuv 1.49.x–1.50.x (Node 22.12–22.16, 23.x), `fs.promises.stat(path)` returns `dev: 0` while `fileHandle.stat()` on the same file returns the real volume serial. `readSecureFileBuffer` compared the two, so every read failed with "File device or inode changed during read".

## Change

- The identity comparison moves into `fileIdentityChanged()`, used by both the open-handle check and the post-read check.
- On win32, a `dev` of 0 on either side is treated as unknown and only `ino` is compared.
- Unchanged: an `ino` mismatch is still rejected on every platform, and a `dev` mismatch is still rejected on non-Windows platforms. Missing dev/ino values (mocked fs) are handled as before.

## Tests

Three new cases in `fileUtils.test.ts` → `readSecureFileBuffer`:
- win32, path `dev: 0`, handle real `dev`, same `ino` → reads
- win32, path `dev: 0`, different `ino` → still rejected
- linux, path `dev: 0`, handle real `dev` → still rejected

Results on Windows 11, same machine:

| Suite | Node 22.14.0 before | Node 22.14.0 after | Node 22.23.3 after | Node 20.20.2 after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| core: fileUtils, read-file, read-many-files, skillLoader, skillManager, memory, at-reference-resolution | 77 failed | 319 passed | 319 passed | 319 passed |
| cli: atCommandProcessor | 42 failed | 81 passed | — | — |

`prettier --check`, `eslint` and `tsc --noEmit` (core) are clean.

## Notes

Not covered here: the Windows CI jobs pin `node-version: '20.x'`, so they can't catch this class of bug. Adding a Node 22 Windows leg seemed out of scope for this PR; happy to do it separately if useful.

prs.body:
## Summary

Preserve the user's first prompt when resuming sessions whose tool outputs were masked.

## Details

`getHistory()` is prepared for API requests: for modern Gemini models it coalesces adjacent user turns and removes durable IDs. Writing this view back after masking merges the first prompt into the `<session_context>` message, which is skipped on resume.

Mask the stored history contents and reattach each original turn ID before updating the recording. This preserves turn boundaries and thought parts while allowing the recording service to update the masked tool response.

The masking service replaces contents at their original indices without filtering or reordering turns.

prs.title: fix(core): treat project temp paths as local in untrusted flag checks
prs.body:
## Summary

The agent's own helper scripts under Gemini CLI's session project temp directory
(`~/.gemini/tmp/<project>/...`) were reported as untrusted shell arguments. Once
shell output such as a Python traceback mentioned the script path, the next
`python3 <path>` invocation requested confirmation even in YOLO mode.

This change treats the project temp directory as local for untrusted-flag
detection, alongside the workspace.

## Details

`findUntrustedFlags()` exempts path arguments that resolve inside the workspace
(`isPathWithinWorkspace`). The project temp directory lives outside the
workspace, so a local script written there and later named in its own traceback
was flagged as untrusted — the false positive reported in #30004.

- `packages/core/src/utils/untrustedContextTracker.ts`: `UntrustedFlagOptions`
  gains `projectTempDir`; `isWorkspaceLocalPath()` now also accepts paths below
  it via `isSubpath()`, and `isPathWithinWorkspace` is optional so the temp-dir
  exemption works without a workspace callback.
- `packages/core/src/tools/shell.ts`: passes
  `config.storage?.getProjectTempDir()` when finding untrusted flags.

This mirrors the project temp directory trust that `Config.isPathAllowed()`
already applies for file access.

The remaining issue items are intentionally unchanged here: executable scripts,
URLs, and paths with shell expansions (`~`, `$VAR`) stay out of the
workspace-local exemption, and output from remote-retrieval commands keeps
external provenance, per #29833. The settings toggle is a separate design
decision.

## Related Issues

Related to #30004

## How to Validate

- `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/untrustedContextTracker.test.ts src/tools/shell.test.ts`
  - New tests: `should not flag project temp paths that appeared in local shell output`
    and `should not flag project temp paths printed by earlier shell output`.
    Both fail before the change and pass after it.
- Manual check: in a session, run a command whose output names a file under the
  project temp directory (for example a traceback), then run `python3 <path>`.
  No confirmation should appear in YOLO mode. Paths outside both the workspace
  and the project temp directory are still reported.
- `npm run preflight` passed locally (Linux, Node 20.19.0) on the initial

prs.title: fix(core): keep committed turns when cancelling a tool-result continuation
prs.body:
## Summary

Cancelling while the request carrying tool results was in flight rolled history back to its state before the user's prompt, erasing the prompt and the model/function turns of tools that had already completed (and may have changed files) #30016 describes this. Cancelling during a tool run kept them, so the same user action had two different outcomes.

Fixes #30016

## Changes

- Restrict the full history rollback to an abort of the prompt's first request, where nothing has run yet.
- An aborted function-response continuation now keeps the committed turns, matching how a failed continuation is already handled, and consistent with the terminal user turn invariant from #29612.
- The trailing unanswered tool response is closed with the synthetic interrupted model turn (`INTERRUPTED_RESPONSE_PLACEHOLDER`) on the next send, the same repair used elsewhere.
- Updated the multi-turn-abort test to assert the new behaviour, including that a follow-up prompt adds the interrupted placeholder turn. First-request abort still fully rolls back (existing test unchanged).

## How to Validate

```
npm run test --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
```

prs.title: Fix zizmor template-injection findings in eval-pr workflow
prs.body:
Summary

This PR fixes the mandatory zizmor findings in .github/workflows/eval-pr.yml caused by injecting GitHub Actions expressions directly into bash scripts.

The problem was that values such as ${{ github.base_ref }}, ${{ github.actor }}, ${{ github.repository }}, and ${{ steps.analysis.outputs.* }} were being interpolated directly inside shell commands. zizmor flags this as template-injection, which is treated as a blocking security issue.

What changed

Moved workflow values into env: variables before shell execution
Replaced direct ${{ ... }} interpolation inside run: blocks with safe shell variables
Used quoted variable references to avoid unsafe expansion
Kept the PR guidance/comment behavior unchanged while making the workflow compliant with the repo’s mandatory security checks
Why this matters

These findings were reported by zizmor as:

template-injection
code injection via template expansion: may expand into attacker-controllable code
This was causing the workflow to fail with exit code 14 and block the job due to mandatory security checks.

Validation

Re-run the GitHub Actions security scan / zizmor check
Confirm .github/workflows/eval-pr.yml passes the mandatory checks without regressing the PR eval workflow behavior

prs.title: fix(core): only replace true cycles with [Circular] in safeJsonStringify
prs.body:
## Summary

`safeJsonStringify` replaced any object it saw a second time with `"[Circular]"`, even when there was no cycle. The telemetry file exporters use it, and the OpenTelemetry SDK shares one `endTime` array across all data points in a collection and one `boundaries` array per histogram. As a result, every metric data point after the first in the telemetry outfile lost its `endTime` and `boundaries`. Other callers (`RecordingContentGenerator`, `LoggingContentGenerator`, the message bus) lose data in the same way whenever an object is shared.

## Details

- **Root cause** (`packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.ts`): the replacer added every visited object to a `WeakSet` and never removed it, so "seen before" was treated as "circular".
- **Fix:** keep only the ancestors of the value currently being visited (the path from the root). An object is replaced with `"[Circular]"` only if it is one of its own ancestors, which is the definition of a cycle. Shared, non-cyclic references are now serialized in full each time. Output for inputs without shared references is unchanged.
- **Tests** (`packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.test.ts`): four new cases that fail on the old implementation and pass now:
  - the same object referenced from two keys, and twice in an array;
  - a shared array referenced at several different depths;
  - a true cycle mixed with shared references (the cycle is still replaced, the sharing is not);
  - OpenTelemetry-style data points that share `endTime` and `boundaries`.

  All existing circular-reference tests pass unchanged.
- No user-facing documentation changes.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29406

## How to Validate

1. Run the unit tests for the utility:

   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/safeJsonStringify.test.ts
   ```

   Expected: 12 tests pass.

2. To confirm the new tests guard the fix, revert only `safeJsonStringify.ts` and re-run the same command.

   Expected: the four shared-reference tests fail (the second occurrence is returned as `"[Circular]"`).

3. Run the suites of the modules that use the function:

   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/telemetry src/core src/utils src/confirmation-bus src/tools/mcp-tool.test.ts
   ```

   Expected: all pass. (On Windows without symlink privileges, `fileUtils` and `planUtils` have two `EPERM` symlink failures that also occur on `main`.)

4. Lint, formatting and types:

   ```bash
   npx eslint packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.ts packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.test.ts
   npx prettier --check packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.ts packages/core/src/utils/safeJsonStringify.test.ts
   npm run typecheck -w @google/gemini-cli-core
   ```

prs.title: fix(cli): flush buffered stdio before entering ACP mode
prs.body:
## Summary

In ACP mode, nothing reaches stderr while the agent runs: every patched stdio write — including hook warnings like a failing `AfterAgent` hook's `Hook execution for …` line — sits in the event buffer and is only flushed by the exit cleanup. A SIGKILL or crash discards it entirely. Fixes #30128.

## Details

`main()` dispatches ACP mode with an early `return runAcpClient(...)` (gemini.tsx), which skips everything the interactive/non-interactive paths do afterward — including `initializeOutputListenersAndFlush(config)`, the only place that installs a listener forwarding `CoreEvent.Output` to the real (unpatched) stdio. `patchStdio()` has already redirected `process.stdout.write` / `process.stderr.write` into the event buffer by that point, so ACP sessions buffer with no consumer until exit.

The fix calls `initializeOutputListenersAndFlush(config)` right before the ACP handoff — the same setup the non-interactive path performs before `runNonInteractive`. Stderr becomes visible live; stdout is unaffected for the protocol, because the ACP JSON-RPC stream writes through `createWorkingStdio()`, which uses the original `process.stdout.write` captured before patching, not the patched stream.

This is the change the issue reporter verified against the published 0.66.0 bundle (a failing `AfterAgent` hook's warning line reaches stderr mid-session rather than at exit); this PR applies it in source with a test.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30128

## How to Validate

1. In a trusted folder, add to `.gemini/settings.json`:
   ```json
   { "hooks": { "AfterAgent": [ { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "name": "failing-hook", "command": "echo hook-said-this >&2; exit 1" } ] } ] } }
   ```
2. Run any ACP client against `gemini --acp`, drive one turn, and watch the client's stderr pipe **during** the session: `hook-said-this` and the `Hook execution for …` warning appear immediately, not at process exit.
3. Unit: `npx vitest run src/gemini_cleanup.test.tsx` — the new ACP-mode case asserts an `emitOutput(stderr)` emission writes through right after `main()` in ACP mode.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [ ] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed) — not needed, no user-facing behavior beyond stderr visibility

prs.title: fix(cli): restore workspace directories only after resumeChat succeeds
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where attempting to resume a session that subsequently fails leaves the session's workspace directories active in the current `WorkspaceContext`. Directory restoration is now deferred until after `resumeChat` successfully resolves.

## Details

In `packages/cli/src/ui/hooks/useSessionResume.ts`, `loadHistoryForResume` previously invoked `workspaceContext.addDirectories(resumedData.conversation.directories)` before awaiting `config.getGeminiClient()?.resumeChat(clientHistory, resumedData)`. If `resumeChat` rejected, the exception was caught and reported to the user as a failure, but the directories added prior to the call remained in `WorkspaceContext`.

This change moves `workspaceContext.addDirectories` to execute strictly after `resumeChat` completes successfully. Stale and non-existent saved directories continue to be safely filtered out by `WorkspaceContext.addDirectories` internally.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29864

## How to Validate

1. **Unit tests**:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/hooks/useSessionResume.test.ts
   ```
   Verifies:
   - Failed `resumeChat` does not invoke `addDirectories` or mutate workspace context.
   - Successful `resumeChat` invokes `addDirectories` after `resumeChat` succeeds.
   - Stale/non-existent directories are omitted while existing directories are restored.
2. **Session browser tests**:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/hooks/useSessionBrowser.test.ts
   ```
3. **Lint & Typecheck**:

prs.title: feat(cli): support skill activation via /skill-name in non-interactive mode
prs.body:
Registers `SkillCommandLoader` in the non-interactive slash command path and handles the `tool` action result so that typing `/skill-name` activates a skill outside the interactive UI. Previously the loader was not registered (command was unknown) and the tool result type was unhandled (threw `FatalInputError`).

Also adds a `[Skill]` suffix tag to skill-backed slash commands in the autocomplete suggestion menu, mirroring the existing `[MCP]` and `[Agent]` tags.

Adds unit tests for the non-interactive handler and the `[Skill]` tag rendering.

Fixes #21165

## Summary

Skills already appear in the `/` completion menu and can be activated via `/skill-name` in the interactive UI (via `SkillCommandLoader` and the `activate_skill` tool). This PR closes two remaining gaps:

1. **Non-interactive skill activation.** In `nonInteractiveCliCommands.ts`, `SkillCommandLoader` was not registered, so `/skill-name` was treated as unknown text. Even if it had been registered, the result handler only understood `submit_prompt` and `confirm_shell_commands` — a skill command returns `type: 'tool'`, which fell through to the `default` case and threw `FatalInputError`.
2. **Visual distinction.** Skill commands had no tag in the autocomplete menu, unlike `[MCP]` and `[Agent]`.

## Details

- `packages/cli/src/nonInteractiveCliCommands.ts`
  - Register `SkillCommandLoader` alongside the Builtin, MCP, and File loaders.
  - Handle `case 'tool'`: forward the command's `postSubmitPrompt` to the model (which then invokes `activate_skill`). Throws `FatalInputError` when no prompt is present.
- `packages/cli/src/ui/components/SuggestionsDisplay.tsx`
  - Add `[CommandKind.SKILL]: ' [Skill]'` to `COMMAND_KIND_SUFFIX`.
- `packages/cli/src/ui/commands/skillsCommand.ts`
  - Call `reloadCommands()` after a successful `/skills link`, so newly linked skills show up as `/<skill-name>` without a restart.
- Tests
  - `packages/cli/src/nonInteractiveCliCommands.test.ts` (new): covers submit_prompt, tool/skill activation, tool-without-prompt (throws), and confirm_shell_commands.
  - `packages/cli/src/ui/components/SuggestionsDisplay.test.tsx`: new test asserting the `[Skill]` tag renders, plus snapshot.
  - `packages/cli/src/ui/commands/skillsCommand.test.ts`: tests that slash commands are reloaded after a successful link, and not after a failed one.


## Related Issues

Fixes #21165

## How to Validate

- `npm run test --workspace @google/gemini-cli` — the affected suites pass (non-interactive handler, SuggestionsDisplay, SkillCommandLoader).
- `npm run typecheck --workspace @google/gemini-cli` — clean.
- `npm run lint --workspace @google/gemini-cli` — clean.
- Manual: with a skill installed, run `node packages/cli/dist/index.js -p "/your-skill-name"` and confirm the skill activates instead of the command being echoed as plain text.

prs.title: fix(core): keep the synthetic binary ack so injected audio/video stays in its own turn
prs.body:
## Summary

With Gemini 3 models, `read_file` on audio or video fails with 400 "Requests ending with a model turn are not supported" when using Code Assist (Login with Google). The binary injection from #26352 sends the media in its own user turn behind a synthetic model ack. Because that ack is a thought-only part, thought stripping drops it. The media then coalesces into the `functionResponse` turn, which is the shape the API rejects. This PR keeps the ack as a plain-text model turn when history is sent.

## Details

- In `stripThoughts` (both copies), `scrubHistory` and `scrubContents`, a synthetic binary ack turn becomes `model[text: "Binary content received. Proceeding with analysis."]` instead of being dropped. The `!isSyntheticBinaryAckTurn` exclusions are removed because those branches can no longer be reached for the ack.
- The recorded history keeps the thought ack, so nothing changes in the UI. Sessions recorded before this change are also fixed on resume, because the conversion happens when the request is built.
- The `historyHardening` test that expected the merged `[functionResponse, inlineData]` turn now expects the three-turn shape. A new `GeminiChat` test checks the request a modern model receives. Both new assertions fail on `main` and pass with this change.
- Images and PDFs are unaffected, since they stay nested in `functionResponse.parts`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30229

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/historyHardening.test.ts src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
   ```
2. Live check on Linux with Login with Google, `-m gemini-3.8-flash`, and a small `.mp4` and `.wav` in the workspace. I recorded the request shapes with a local proxy via `CODE_ASSIST_ENDPOINT`:

   | Build | Request tail | Result |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | main `e5d88fb2c` | `user[functionResponse(read_file), inlineData(video/mp4)]` | 400 |
   | this PR | `user[functionResponse]`, `model[text]`, `user[inlineData(video/mp4)]` | 200, the model read the text in the video correctly |
   | main `e5d88fb2c` | `user[functionResponse(read_file), inlineData(audio/wav)]` | 400 |
   | this PR | `user[functionResponse]`, `model[text]`, `user[inlineData(audio/wav)]` | 200 |

Note: on `main`, an audio or video file larger than about 48 KB also fails with "Base64 decoding failed". Since #30180, `truncateFunctionResponsePart` truncates the injected base64 at 64 KB. That is a separate issue, so the live check used small files.

prs.title: feat(cli): add /stats heatmap subcommand for daily token usage
prs.body:
## Summary

<!-- Concisely describe what this PR changes and why. Focus on impact and
urgency. -->

Adds a `/stats heatmap [today|yesterday|YYYY-MM-DD]` subcommand (also accessible via `/usage heatmap`) that renders a GitHub-style calendar heatmap of daily token usage in the terminal scrollback buffer, along with rolling window totals, active and longest usage streaks, and an optional single-day breakdown.

## Details

<!-- Add any extra context and design decisions. Keep it brief but complete. -->

- **Core Aggregation (`packages/core/src/services/usageAggregator.ts`)**:
  - Streams `.jsonl` chat recordings under `storage.getProjectTempDir()/chats` (including nested subagent session directories) asynchronously via `fs.createReadStream` and `readline`, plucking only `id`, `sessionId`, `timestamp`, `model`, and token fields while discarding conversational payload strings immediately.
  - Deduplicates repeated message snapshots per recording file by message `id`, skips malformed JSON lines gracefully, and normalizes UTC ISO timestamps to local calendar `YYYY-MM-DD` date keys.
  - Computes 196-day (28-week) window token, unique session, and turn totals, current active streak (continuing from yesterday when today has zero usage so far), and longest historical streak using UTC calendar arithmetic so Daylight Saving Time transitions do not shift day boundaries.
  - Strictly validates optional `today`, `yesterday`, and `YYYY-MM-DD` arguments via `resolveHeatmapDateArg` (rejecting invalid calendar rollover dates such as `2026-02-31`) without interpolating user-supplied parameters into filesystem paths.
- **Terminal UI & Command Integration (`packages/cli`)**:
  - Adds `HeatmapComponent.tsx` to render a static 7-row (`Sun`–`Sat`, labeled on `Mon`, `Wed`, `Fri`) calendar grid using `■` glyphs, quartile-based intensity buckets mapped to semantic theme tokens (`theme.ui.dark`, `theme.ui.comment`, `theme.status.warning`, `theme.text.accent`, `theme.status.success`), 3-letter month headers, and dynamic column clamping on narrow terminals (`<65` columns).
  - Supports day drill-down views displaying total tokens, input/output/cached token split, session and turn counts, and sorted per-model usage, or `"No token usage recorded for [date]"` when no usage is recorded.
  - Wires `HistoryItemHeatmapStats` (`heatmap_stats`) through `types.ts`, `MainContent.tsx` (`STATIC_HISTORY_ITEM_TYPES`), `HistoryItemDisplay.tsx`, `slashCommandProcessor.ts`, and `statsCommand.ts` (including `today`/`yesterday` tab completion), and documents the subcommand in `docs/reference/commands.md`.

## Related Issues

only related to an issue or is a partial fix, simply reference the issue number
without a keyword (Related to #123). -->

fixes: [#29297](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/29297)

expected results, and edge cases. -->

prs.title: feat(acp): support session/close so clients can release a session
prs.body:
## Summary

ACP clients can now release a session with `session/close`. Today the method fails with `-32601 Method not found`, because `GeminiAgent` does not implement `unstable_closeSession`, the handler the SDK routes `session/close` to. As a result, every session holds its config, chat and MCP connections until the `--acp` process exits. This brings an explicit close in line with how the agent already releases sessions in `loadSession` and on shutdown.

## Details

- `AcpSessionManager.closeSession(sessionId)` removes the session from the map, then awaits `session.dispose()` and logs a failed disposal. This is the same order and error handling `loadSession` uses when it replaces an existing session. Because the id is forgotten first, a `session/load` of the same id that follows keeps the session it creates.
- An unknown id gets `-32602 Session not found`, like `cancel`, `prompt` and `setSessionMode`.
- `initialize` now advertises `sessionCapabilities: { close: {} }`, so clients can see the method is supported.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30231

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/acp/acpSessionManager.test.ts src/acp/acpRpcDispatcher.test.ts
   ```
   The three new assertions fail on `main` and pass here: the advertised capability, routing through the session manager, and closing a session even when its disposal throws.
2. Over stdio against `gemini --acp`, send `initialize`, `session/new`, `session/close`, and then `session/prompt` on the closed id:

   | Build | `sessionCapabilities` | `session/close` | `session/prompt` on the closed id |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | main `e5d88fb2c` | `null` | `-32601 Method not found` | answers, so the session is still alive |
   | this PR | `{"close":{}}` | `{}` | `-32602 Session not found` |
3. Two sessions in one `gemini --acp` process (this PR, `-m gemini-3-flash-preview`), closing only the first:

   | Step | Result |
   | --- | --- |
   | `session/new` × 2 | two distinct ids |
   | prompt A "remember APPLE", prompt B "remember BANANA" | both `end_turn` |
   | `session/close` A | `{}` |
   | `session/prompt` A | `-32602 Session not found` |
   | `session/prompt` B "which word?" | `end_turn`, "BANANA", so B keeps its history |
   | `session/close` A again | `-32602 Session not found` |
   | `session/close` B | `{}` |

prs.title: fix(core): keep error reports out of the shared temp directory
prs.body:
## Summary

Error reports (`gemini-client-error-*.json`) contain the full chat history, but they were written to `os.tmpdir()` with default permissions. This moves them to `~/.gemini/tmp/error-reports/` and makes them readable only by the current user.

## Details

On Linux/macOS the reports ended up world-readable in `/tmp`. On Windows they went to `%TEMP%`, which is where the antivirus in #15404 quarantined the first file.

The default directory now comes from `Storage.getGlobalTempDir()`, so the existing sandbox handling applies. The directory is created with `0700` and the file with `0600`. Call sites and the `reportingDir` parameter are unchanged.

Since the OS no longer clears these files, the CLI's startup cleanup now also deletes reports older than 7 days, using the same retention as background logs (`logCleanup.ts`).

This doesn't stop an antivirus from matching on what's inside a transcript (the second file in the issue is a session file under `~/.gemini/tmp`), and I don't think the CLI should obfuscate its own logs to get around that. It does stop us from dropping full transcripts into the system temp dir on every API error.

#20238 took a similar approach and was closed as inactive.

## Related Issues

Fixes #15404

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/utils/errorReporting.test.ts
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/utils/logCleanup.test.ts
```

Two new tests cover the default location and the file/directory modes (the mode test is skipped on Windows). The existing "write fails" test used a missing directory to force the failure; since the directory is now created, it uses a file in its place instead.

I ran the full `packages/core` test suite, lint and typecheck locally.

prs.title: fix(cli): submit full text when IME commit and Enter arrive in the same tick
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes the last Korean (Hangul) syllable being dropped when Enter is pressed right after IME composition commit (e.g. `테스트` submitted as `테스`).

## Details

The IME delivers the committed character and `\r` in the same tick. Two things caused the loss:

1. **Stale text on submit.** `InputPrompt` called `handleSubmit(buffer.text)` inside the key handler, before React applied the pending insert. Submission is now requested via a ref and performed in an effect, after the buffer has updated.
2. **Fast-return heuristic.** `bufferFastReturn` (30ms) treated the Enter right after the character as an unbracketed paste and converted it to a newline. A single non-ASCII code point followed by Enter within a 2-event burst (`isImeCommit`) is now passed through as a normal Enter. Multi-character chunks are still treated as pastes.

Trade-off: pasting a single non-ASCII character immediately followed by Enter (without bracketed paste) is also treated as an IME commit and submits.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30126

## How to Validate

1. Run `gemini` with a Korean IME active (e.g. VS Code terminal over SSH).
2. Type `테스트` and press Enter immediately.
3. Expected: `테스트` is submitted in full.

Automated: `npx vitest run src/ui/contexts/KeypressContext.test.tsx src/ui/components/InputPrompt.test.tsx` in `packages/cli`. The new `InputPrompt` test (real `useTextBuffer`, `요` + `\r` in the same tick) and the `KeypressContext` IME/emoji tests fail without the fix. The multi-character paste case is covered as a regression test.

issues.title: SDK/VS Code: attached async Bash command reported stopped without a matching stop_bash call

labels.name: area:tools
labels.description: Built-in tools: file editing, shell, search, LSP, git, and tool call behavior

issues.body:
## Environment
Copilot SDK hosted in VS Code on Linux, in a long-lived conversation using Bash background commands. Exact SDK/extension version was not captured. This may involve the VS Code host rather than the CLI; please redirect if another tracker is appropriate.

## Observed behavior
A bounded build/deployment workflow was launched through Bash with mode=async and a distinct shellId, without detach. The launch returned success and its handle. Later, read_bash returned:

`shellId: <affected-handle> was already stopped via stop_bash.`

A streaming inspection of the session history found no stop_bash invocation for that affected handle after launch. Two earlier stop_bash calls were present, but referred to different handles and followed an explicit user request to pause those earlier operations. Subsequent user messages requested progress and fixes, not cancellation of the affected workflow.

The workflow log stopped before deployment. The assistant had continued presenting the workflow as underway until reading the handle exposed the stop. That missing liveness check was an assistant error; it does not explain the unexpected stop attribution.

## Expected behavior
An already-launched background workflow should not be canceled merely by subsequent conversation messages. Cancellation should be explicitly requested and attributed to its actual cause. If a host/session lifecycle intentionally terminates attached jobs, the termination and reason should be surfaced promptly rather than later reported as a stop_bash call that is absent from the recorded history.

## Diagnostic limits and workaround
This is an observation from one session, not a confirmed minimal reproduction or proven platform root cause. Host-side cancellation outside the recorded tool calls remains possible. Two subsequent critical deployments launched with detach=true completed and were independently verified, which provided a practical workaround but does not prove the cause.

Private project code, identifiers, addresses, credentials, and raw session logs are intentionally excluded.

issues.title: ACP mode never attaches to the IDE: `--acp` skips `~/.copilot/ide` discovery, so ACP sessions have no IDE MCP server (no "Visual Studio Connected")

labels.name: area:non-interactive
labels.description: Non-interactive mode (-p), CI/CD, ACP protocol, and headless automation

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
## Describe the bug

`copilot --acp` never connects to a running IDE, even when it is launched from the editor's own integrated terminal, in the same workspace, with a valid IDE lock file on disk. The interactive CLI in the exact same terminal attaches within ~1 s.

Contrast from the same machine, same version, same second, same workspace:

**Interactive `copilot`** — `~/.copilot/logs/process-…-13896.log`:

```
20:27:58.429Z [WARNING] Failed to parse lock file …\0173da6b-….lock: SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input
20:27:59.083Z [ERROR] Connecting to IDE MCP server: Visual Studio Code (C:\Users\hersh\Develop\patioz-api-fastify)
20:27:59.151Z [ERROR] Connected to IDE MCP server: Visual Studio Code
20:27:59.175Z [WARNING] [rust:mcp::client] MCP server advertises list-change capabilities but refused
                       subscriptions/listen … {"server":"Some(Implementation { name: \"ide\", version: \"0.0.1\" …})"}
```

**`copilot --acp`** — `~/.copilot/logs/process-1794513585531-30960.log`:

```
19:59:45.538Z [INFO] Starting ACP server (stdio)
19:59:45.623Z [INFO] [rust:acp::serve] ACP server started (stdio mode)
19:59:45.623Z [INFO] [rust:acp::serve] ACP server started, waiting for requests
```

…and nothing else. No lock-file scan, no `Connecting to IDE MCP server`, no `ide` MCP client at all.

The lock file was present and valid the whole time:

```json
{
  "ideName": "Visual Studio Code",
  "pid": 19300,
  "isTrusted": true,
  "socketPath": "\\\\.\\pipe\\…",
  "scheme": "pipe",
  "workspaceFolders": ["c:\\Users\\hersh\\Develop\\patioz-api-fastify"]
}
```

### Consequences

1. **No IDE status.** The "Visual Studio Connected" indicator the interactive CLI shows never appears, so an ACP host cannot tell whether the agent has editor tools.
2. **No IDE tools.** The `ide` MCP server (diagnostics / `openDiff` / selection / editor navigation) is absent from the ACP session's tool set, while it is present in the interactive CLI's. ACP sessions are therefore strictly less capable than interactive ones in the same terminal.
3. **No IDE-client registration.** The session never goes through `registerTrustedIdeExternalClient`, and its `client_name` is `github/acp` with `vscode.metadata.json` `origin: "other"`. Combined with VS Code's discovery gate (`readinessFiles = ['events.jsonl', 'workspace.yaml', 'vscode.metadata.json']`, and `_nextScanAt = this._hasJournal ? Date.now() : Infinity` in `copilotSessionDiscoveryWatchers.ts`), a freshly created ACP session — which has only `workspace.yaml` — is never listed in the Agents window, not even under "External", until the first message produces a journal.

## Affected version

```
GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.109.
win32-arm64, Windows 11 (build 26300)
```

## Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Open VS Code (any version that publishes `~/.copilot/ide/*.lock`) on a folder; confirm a non-empty lock file exists for that window and `isTrusted: true`.
2. In VS Code's integrated terminal, run `copilot` → it reports **Visual Studio Connected** within ~1 s, and its log contains `Connected to IDE MCP server: Visual Studio Code`.
3. In the same terminal, same cwd, run `copilot --acp` and drive it over stdio:
   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":1,"clientCapabilities":{"fs":{"readTextFile":true,"writeTextFile":true}}}}
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"session/new","params":{"cwd":"c:\\Users\\hersh\\Develop\\patioz-api-fastify","mcpServers":[]}}
   ```
4. Compare `~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log`: the interactive process has the two `IDE MCP server` lines, the ACP process has none.
5. Optional: check the ACP session's tool list — `ide`-provided tools are missing.

## Expected behavior

One of these, in order of preference:

- **`--acp` performs the same IDE discovery as the interactive CLI.** The ACP process is started by a terminal that belongs to an IDE window whose lock file advertises the cwd; there is no ambiguity to resolve, so the existing `discoverIdeWorkspaces` / `connectToIde` path could run unchanged and simply make the `ide` MCP server available to ACP sessions. This mirrors what the interactive CLI already does at startup.
- **An explicit opt-in**, if silently attaching is undesirable for a headless server: e.g. `--acp --ide` (or a `COPILOT_IDE=1`-style switch), defaulting off, so containerised/unattended ACP hosts stay untouched.
- **ACP-native alternative:** since the editor is normally the ACP *client*, accept the `ide` MCP server from `session/new`'s client-supplied `mcpServers` under a reserved name (e.g. `copilot-ide`) and document it, so ACP clients that are editors do not depend on lock files. Note this does **not** cover the editor-integrated-terminal case, which is the reproduction above.

Whichever is chosen, the behaviour should be symmetric: the same workspace, the same IDE, the same terminal should not give the agent a different tool set depending on `--acp`.

## Additional context

- **There is no configuration knob today**, which is part of the request: `copilot --help` exposes `--acp` but no `--ide` / `--attach-ide` / equivalent, and a scan of the bundled `cli-main.js` finds 135 `COPILOT_*` environment variables, none of them IDE-related. So a user cannot work around this.
- This is **not** about the `/code` handoff. `/code` (VS Code 1.146+ "Continue a Copilot CLI session in VS Code") goes through the Copilot SDK / Agent Host and `session.create`; it does not traverse ACP. The gap here is specifically the ACP server.
- ACP capabilities observed on 1.0.109, for completeness: `loadSession: true`, `sessionCapabilities: { close, list }`; `session/new` returns `{ models, configOptions, modes, sessionId }`.
- Related, but different: #4143 (CLI should inherit MCP tools from a connected VS Code instance — assumes the connection exists), #1868 (document `/ide` for IDEs beyond VS Code), microsoft/vscode#335215 (external agent sessions only discovered at startup).
- Suggested areas: `area:non-interactive`, `area:mcp`, `area:tools`.

issues.title: MCP tool cache grows with temporary workspaces and can exhaust memory at startup

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

issues.body:
## Summary

The persisted MCP tool snapshot cache (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\copilot\mcp-tools` on Windows) grows when sessions use new temporary workspaces, even with the same MCP server configuration. Tools such as eval harnesses and CI can create a new workspace for every session. Entries from previous runs remained during our investigation; we haven't verified whether Copilot eventually prunes them.

When cached snapshots are enabled, Copilot loads cache data into a JSON string and parses it at startup. A user reported a ~563 MiB `azmcp` tool-cache JSON string and a Node.js heap OOM (microsoft/vally#1448).

## Environment

- Copilot CLI / runtime 1.0.80 (`@github/copilot-win32-x64`), launched through the Copilot SDK
- Windows x64, Node 22.14.0 (reporter); Windows ARM64 with x64 Node 24 (our repro)
- MCP server: Azure MCP (`azmcp`), stdio
- `COPILOT_MCP_TOOL_CACHE` unset (default, enabled)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a stdio MCP server, such as Azure MCP, with a fixed name and configuration.
2. Start multiple sessions, each with a different, freshly created working directory. Vally does this by default, with one temp workspace per eval trial. The linked reproducer is in microsoft/vally#1448.
3. Inspect `%LOCALAPPDATA%\copilot\mcp-tools` before and after the runs.

## Observed

| Scenario | Trials | New cache entries |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same working directory reused (Vally 0.21 with `--in-place`) | 26 | 1 |
| New temp workspace per trial (Vally 0.15, run 1) | 26 | 26 (~100 KB each) |
| New temp workspace per trial (Vally 0.15, run 2) | 26 | 25 |

- Entries from earlier runs remained. The cache went from 9.88 MiB to 12.37 MiB (115 files) over the second Vally 0.15 run.
- The working-directory/cache-key relationship and whether old entries are eventually pruned have not been independently confirmed.
- In microsoft/vally#1448, the reporter observed an OOM with an existing populated cache; setting `COPILOT_MCP_TOOL_CACHE=false` avoided it. We did not reproduce the OOM with our smaller cache. Our second Vally 0.15 run completed 24 of 26 trials successfully; two timed out waiting for `session.idle`.

## Expected

- Cache size stays bounded no matter how many distinct working directories sessions use.
- Startup memory does not scale with the total cache size.

## Related observation

The cache key doesn't seem to include the server binary's version. After the server is rebuilt at the same path and config, the first turn could briefly see the old tool list before a background refresh replaces it. If the refresh fails, the old list is retained ("continuing with cached tools"). This could affect reproducibility for eval and tool-routing scenarios.

## Workaround

Set `COPILOT_MCP_TOOL_CACHE=false`, or point `COPILOT_CACHE_HOME` at a per-run temp directory.

issues.title: /model --global does not persist selected model; new sessions open on a removed model

labels.name: area:models
