prs.title: fix(ios): avoid rerendering recent diagrams when the cache fills
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unnecessary diagram rendering when native chat requests a recent diagram again after the render cache reaches capacity.

## User Impact

User impact: recent diagrams can reuse their existing rendered images instead of losing the entire cache at once. Diagram appearance, grouped replies, sidebar animation, word fade, and existing memory limits are unchanged. No migration or user action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Evict only enough least-recently-used diagrams to satisfy the existing 32-entry and 12 MiB limits. Preserve the source/width/display-scale/theme key, actual bitmap + SVG + source byte accounting, oversized-result nonretention, memory-warning full clearing, and renderer safety guards.

This remains local to the existing Mermaid renderer: no shared cache framework, new manager, or dependency on another performance PR. The production change adds eight net lines; the two renderer regressions add 74 net test lines.

Contributor credit: Vyctor Brzezowski and Mike Nguyen.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/6b98dedd-1923-4f79-837e-5d48ac84b6c4)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/e01da31f-f6b3-4cbc-95a0-d33f1870d560)

## Evidence

- `git diff --check` passed; complete diff inspected and simplified.
- Independent Auto Review, OpenClaw engine with `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`, P0–P2: `scoped-clean`, no findings. Reviewed the complete local patch against base `0633f256350b5580a5bdbcd8a6a5782750de03d4`; diff SHA-256 `6af6a81d0e4c465924495ecdbac612b1f70073ee516f29cbb4a97b7baa306486`.
- Added two tests through the real native renderer/WebKit/snapshot/cache boundary: count-limit LRU retention, multiple byte-limit evictions, and oversized-result nonretention. They were authored, not run.
- **Draft proof gaps:** this implementation environment is Linux with no Swift, Xcode, SwiftFormat, or SwiftLint. Compilation, native lint/format, baseline-red/candidate-green results, mounted/device verification, and before/after video remain pending on the exact published head. Native test runtime and CI cost are unknown; the count case performs 33 successful renders and the byte case performs six, with canceled miss probes in addition. No measured speedup is claimed.

### Source-bound acceptance workload

The view requests rendering through `onChange(of: request, initial: true)` after width measurement, on request changes, and on explicit retry. Disappearance cancels a subscriber; a retained view keeps its own result. Scrolling alone is not evidence that a diagram rerendered.

1. Count case: 32 distinct synthetic `flowchart LR; A-->B` diagrams differentiated by comments, width 80 and display scale 1; touch the first, insert the 33rd, and verify only the untouched oldest misses. Check actual total bytes are below 12 MiB so this isolates the count limit.
2. Byte case: measure the real layout, render three approximately 3-MiB results, touch the first, and insert approximately 8 MiB. Validate actual returned byte costs: two old entries must leave, while the touched entry and new result fit. A successful approximately 14-MiB result must not be retained or purge those survivors.
3. Mounted proof: use completed synthetic Mermaid fences in native chat, cross capacity, and revisit recent requests through a confirmed remount. Count submissions, cache hits, native render starts, and snapshots separately. If navigation retains the view and submits no request, report that rather than calling it cache proof. Check rotation/theme changes, source toggle, expand, cancellation, and retry without changing grouped layout or animations.
4. Memory warning: in the isolated debug app, verify full cache/order clearing, zero byte bookkeeping, and idle document retirement; then verify successful fresh rendering. Preserve the existing active-render behavior.

Before measurements, use five interleaved baseline/candidate pairs on the same device and synthetic workload, separating cold and warm runs. Count render starts/snapshots first, confirm both limits, and record CPU, memory, latency median/p95, and scrolling/frame behavior. Recent surviving requests should not start new render jobs; visual behavior must remain unchanged. Performance results are pending, not inferred from this patch.

### Focused Mac verification

Use a task-owned checkout at the exact published head and a separate checkout at base `0633f256350b5580a5bdbcd8a6a5782750de03d4` with only this PR's test changes applied. Do not disturb another agent's branch or device. Select an available task-owned simulator and a fresh result-bundle label:

```bash
git rev-parse HEAD
git status -sb
xcodebuild -version
xcrun simctl list devices available
pnpm ios:gen
./scripts/format-swift.sh ios
./scripts/lint-swift.sh ios
/usr/bin/time -p xcodebuild \
  -project apps/ios/OpenClaw.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenClaw \
  -configuration Debug \
  -destination "platform=iOS Simulator,id=${SIMULATOR_ID:?}" \
  -parallel-testing-enabled NO \
  -resultBundlePath ".openclaw/tmp/mermaid-${PROOF_LABEL:?}.xcresult" \
  -only-testing:OpenClawTests/ChatMermaidRendererTests \
  -only-testing:OpenClawTests/ChatMermaidRenderModelTests \
  test
```

The existing project-generation hook prepares Mermaid assets and the test TLS resource. Record native test wall time and CI seconds when available. Fixture or build setup failure is not a product verdict. Run the mounted workload and capture before/after video on the same connected iPhone using the OpenClaw Debug scheme; no release or TestFlight upload is part of this PR.

The tab-identity cases fail with the earlier published detail owners (Review instead of Excalidraw), then pass with the fix; they also cover missing artwork, App replacement, ordinary Review restoration, and native host retirement.

The failing CI merge-tree base c74c7a977c060678604b01968547b45c4997cd7c was integrated for a faithful paired check: chat boot JS is −88 B, New Session boot JS is −179 B, startup is unchanged, and CSS is −4 B gzip / unchanged raw. prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unnecessary form reconstruction every second while a pending question's countdown runs in native chat.

## User Impact

The existing question UI, answers, secret masking, consent fields, accessibility labels, and submit/skip behavior stay the same. Only the countdown label needs periodic updates. This shared component serves iOS and macOS; native build and measured performance validation are still pending, so this PR must remain a draft.

## Why This Change Was Made

Move the one-second timeline from the whole question form to a countdown-only view. The existing expiry owner still transitions the card to its expired summary at the deadline. If the displayed countdown reaches zero first after a forward clock change, the leaf reports that crossing to the same owner; it does not invalidate the form on every tick. Foreground return also reconciles overdue cards through that owner before asynchronous refresh. Keyboard actions check the current time rather than a captured tick.

No cache, additional timer manager, configuration, schema, or animation changes. The production delta is +54/-36 lines; focused test changes are +60/-9 lines. The only added callback connects the countdown crossing to existing expiry settlement.

## Evidence

- Passed: `git diff --check`; exported patch reverse-application check.
- Fresh independent Auto Review, P0–P2: no findings on the updated three-file candidate against `0633f256350b5580a5bdbcd8a6a5782750de03d4`, with complete question/expiry-owner source supplied. Static review only, including the clock-crossing callback.
- Extended the expiry-owner regression to cover observable invalidation at and after the deadline, rejected submit/skip/number-key selection, cleared drafts, attention removal, task cleanup, retained summary, and idempotent settlement. Added a foreground regression requiring overdue drafts to expire before asynchronous refresh while future questions retain their selections.
- **Not run:** Swift compilation/tests, SwiftFormat/SwiftLint, iOS typography tests, mounted UI/keyboard/VoiceOver checks, before/after captures, or performance measurements. The implementation environment is Linux without Swift, Xcode, SwiftFormat, or SwiftLint. Test wall time and CI seconds are unavailable. No frame-rate, CPU, or latency improvement is claimed yet. Countdown crossing and foreground behavior still need mounted Mac/iOS validation.

**Exact-head Mac commands:**

```bash
swift test --package-path apps/shared/OpenClawKit \
  --scratch-path .openclaw/tmp/question-countdown-swift-build \
  --disable-index-store -Xswiftc -gline-tables-only --no-parallel \
  --filter 'ChatQuestionCardTests|ChatViewModelTests.*(question|foreground|secret)'
./scripts/lint-swift.sh ios
IOS_DEST='generic/platform=iOS Simulator' pnpm ios:build
pnpm ios:test OpenClawTypographyTests
```

**Mac acceptance rule, recorded before measurement:** use the same synthetic pending-question workload on the pinned base and candidate. After settling, 10 idle countdown ticks must cause zero evaluations of question sections, option rows, secret-consent controls, and the footer on the candidate, while the label keeps ticking and expiry still retires the form. Count the builders inside the baseline timeline, not just the outer card body. Run at least five interleaved base/candidate samples. Record evaluation counts, main-thread CPU, frame time/hitches, and input latency (median, p95, and spread); stop on any 20% regression and require a demonstrated reduction in work. Also verify foreground return past expiry, a forward-clock deadline crossing, submitting-at-expiry, keyboard actions, masked entry, and unchanged layout. Measurements, a reproducible mounted workload, and native evidence remain pending before ready/merge.

Fixes unnecessary code re-highlighting when the native chat cache fills and discards every previously highlighted block.

## User Impact

prs.title: fix(channels): answered recent history is re-quoted after tool-progress turns
prs.body:
Closes #197995

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Discord guild and Slack turns re-quote requests the agent already answered under "Recent chat history" when newer turns used tools or ran internal runtime exchanges.

## User Impact

User impact: busy Discord/Slack channels stop feeding the model duplicate copies of already-answered requests, so the recent-history block only carries messages the agent has not handled yet.

## Why This Change Was Made

The answered-row lookup read only two transcript rows per history candidate. Tool-progress text (the unphased "let me check…" text an Anthropic-shaped model writes before a tool call) and internal runtime exchanges also take rows, so they pushed older answered requests out of the read and those requests were quoted again.

The cheap two-per-candidate read stays first. Only when that read comes back full and still has not reached every candidate does it read once more with a fixed 200 extra rows. That is at most two reads, and the extra is absolute so one long tool turn or a full 100-message window is still covered (a per-candidate multiplier only moves the threshold).

## Evidence

**Regression tests (real SQLite transcript writers, not a mocked reader)** in `session-transcript-context.sqlite.test.ts`, four variants, all RED on `main` and GREEN here:
- internal runtime exchanges crowding the window
- one tool-progress row in each newer turn
- one 50-row tool turn (also RED under an 8×-per-candidate multiplier)
- internal exchanges in a full 100-candidate window (also RED under `max(limit, 200)`)

**Live A/B: built Gateway + the bundled Discord plugin against Crabline (QA Lab fake Discord), mock provider on the Anthropic wire** (`pnpm openclaw qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 --channel-driver crabline --channel discord`, `historyLimit: 50`). Flow: an answered commentary+exec request, four more commentary+exec rounds, one unaddressed bystander message, then a check turn. Inspected the first model request of the check turn:

- base `d24b84d43ea` (dist rebuilt): `history_count: 2`, quoting the **already-answered** request `SLACK-QA-COMMENTARY-FA43A1CA …` plus the bystander.
- head `4fc5d430dda` (dist rebuilt): `history_count: 1`, only `QA Bystander: unaddressed side discussion BYSTANDER-SIDE-NOTE-…`.

On the OpenAI Responses wire the pre-tool text is `phase: commentary` and is already excluded from the projection, so that route does not reproduce; the Anthropic shape (text + tool_use, `stopReason: toolUse`) does.

**Checks:** `check:changed` green on the final head (lint, dead-export scan, import cycles, guards); test-lines ratchet within allowance.

<details><summary>Relation to #198044</summary>

#198044 targets the same issue with an attempt-bounded growing loop, tested against a mocked reader. This PR differs in covering tool-progress rows and the full-window boundary explicitly against real transcript storage, and in the live Discord A/B above. Happy for maintainers to take whichever shape they prefer, or fold these tests into the other PR.
</details>

AI-assisted: built with Claude Code and reviewed with Codex (default pass clean; two max-effort rounds each raised a valid P2 — per-candidate multiplier and full-window repeat — both fixed with the variants above; the final round-2 fix was not re-reviewed by a third full round). I reviewed and understand the change.

prs.title: fix: prevent worker writes to trusted runtime storage
prs.body:
Stacked on #193823, targeting `codex/node-trusted-writable-ancestors` at `1632274c7895819d4054fa2364bbb0ff0666defb`.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes filesystem-isolated workers being able to overwrite trusted runtime files or replace peer scratch storage when writable paths overlap protected storage.

## User Impact

Unsafe workspace, model HOME, and scratch layouts are rejected before worker execution. Valid projects beneath broad read grants, including `/usr/src`, continue to run with confined workspace writes and existing descendant cleanup.

## Why This Change Was Made

Landlock grants within one ruleset are additive: a read-only runtime grant cannot cancel an overlapping writable grant. The existing filesystem-launch owner now checks all writable roots against protected runtime paths and captured trust files, and prevents them from encompassing captured execution HOME or the shared temporary root.

The checks protect canonical targets and replaceable pathname entries along the resolution chain. This includes original bundle, HOME, and shared-temporary-root paths, relative targets, intermediate aliases, repeated/trailing separators, and ordinary directories before `..`. Precise executable/library roots and the selected native helper storage remain protected without treating the entire broad `/usr` or `/proc` read grant as private storage. Scratch rejection retains the existing cleanup owner. The fix stays in the existing filesystem-launch owner, with no new public API or test-only production hooks; the added traversal is needed because canonical-target checks alone miss proven pathname redirection. Relative to the parent, production code grows by 77 lines and tests by 267 lines.

## Evidence

- Secretless task-owned UTM guest: Ubuntu 24.04 arm64, Linux 6.8.0-147, Landlock ABI 4, non-root UID 1001.
- Native before/after proof: the original implementation allowed a confined worker to replace a disposable Node executable, followed by unconfined host re-execution. The candidate rejects that layout before execution. The original also allowed peer-scratch replacement through a `/tmp` workspace; the candidate rejects it while preserving the peer.
- Native controls demonstrated replacement of captured CA pathnames through aliases and ordinary directories before `..`, while their canonical targets remained intact. Separate bundle/HOME/temp alias proofs demonstrated later trusted resolution changing while canonical storage stayed intact; the temp case used the real selector. The candidate rejects these layouts. A valid `/usr/src` project still runs, writes inside its workspace, and receives `EACCES` outside it.
- All 81 relevant tests passed: 31 grant regressions, 3 real filesystem-owner cases, and retained proof for 18 startup and 29 idle cases. The new regression file ran through `pnpm test ... --maxWorkers=1` in 2.25 seconds wall time. Negative cases were demonstrated red on the applicable unfixed implementation, including native helper storage, system executable directories, and original-root aliases. Hosted CI timing is pending.
- Production and node-host test type graphs, focused repository oxlint (zero warnings/errors), focused oxfmt, and `git diff --check` passed. Pinned-Bun lint parity was unavailable because the guest could not stage that artifact; the documented focused oxlint route passed.
- Fresh local autoreview covered the complete four-file snapshot against `1632274c7895819d4054fa2364bbb0ff0666defb`, including unchanged owner context, at P0–P3. Outcome: `scoped-clean`, complete, no remaining actionable findings. The reviewed tree was committed unchanged as `412ae587c5f4c9236c05e6339398c54fb1ef4714`. prs.title: fix(ui): agent-excluded skills inflate Needs setup
prs.body:
Closes #198026

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the Skills page counts skills excluded by the selected agent's allowlist as **Needs setup**, even when they have no missing prerequisites.

## User Impact

Users can distinguish **Excluded** skills from skills that actually need setup, using consistent counts, filtering, row badges, and details. A skill with missing prerequisites still needs setup even if the agent also excludes it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The inventory now shares one status classifier and adds a neutral Excluded filter. Disabled remains distinct, and existing ClawHub warnings, agent access rules, and the global enable toggle retain their behavior.

## Evidence

- The regression failed before the implementation: Needs setup was 3 where only 1 fixture had missing prerequisites. The final focused suites pass **63 tests** (26 inventory tests and 37 page/mutation tests; +34 net test lines).
- On the rebased commit, all 14 core-test typecheck shards, UI type checking, typed lint, formatting, i18n verification, controller checks, and line limits pass.
- Full `pnpm build` passes on `a86c6735` (644.477 s; WSL2 Ubuntu 26.04, Node 26.12.1, pnpm 12.15.0). Existing CSS/boot-JS size-budget warnings remain; this is not a budget-pass claim.
- `check:changed` remains nonzero solely because the script export scan reports `scripts/bench-ci-planner.mts: runPlannerFlow`. The identical Knip 6.40.0 command reproduces that finding on clean parent `4e8898bc`; production and full-tree export scans pass with zero entries. The branch includes upstream #198056, which removed the two earlier Talk export findings.
- On the final built commit, real agent switching (including an empty allowlist), both filters, exclusion reasons, and the unchanged enable toggle pass. The mixed missing-and-excluded fixture stays Needs setup. Navigation and the status control fit at 400/820/1280 px without horizontal overflow. Full repository tests and native Windows/macOS runs were not performed.

The production fixture uses a built Gateway, real CLI status reports, and Chromium without RPC stubs. Served assets were checked against the build on disk. Before the fix, an eligible `proof-excluded` skill with empty `missing` fields was shown under Needs setup. The before capture is from `db4b2edd6`; the six affected source files are unchanged in the rebased parent. The final build has these counts:

| Agent | Needs setup before | Needs setup after | Excluded after | CLI missing |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main allowlist | 56 | 36 | 20 | 36 |
| empty allowlist | 53 | 36 | 17 | 36 |

Before:

![Before: agent-excluded skills inflate Needs setup](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7f3bd629-739d-4490-bf19-e782f979ada4)

After:

![After: only missing prerequisites appear in Needs setup](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8b689a14-edb2-439d-800a-2a9b18d8d530)

prs.title: fix(qa-channel): match canonically equivalent message searches
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Channel message searches miss visually identical text when the message or attachment uses a different canonical Unicode form. For example, searching `CAFE\u0301` does not find a message containing `Café`, despite the existing case-insensitive search.

## User Impact

QA message search finds canonically equivalent message text, attachment filenames, alternative text, and transcripts. Message IDs, original text, attachment contents, account/conversation selectors, deletion filtering, and result limits retain their existing contracts. Accents remain significant: this does not introduce accent-insensitive or fuzzy matching.

## Why This Change Was Made

`searchQaBusMessages` is the single search owner behind QA Channel's HTTP search action and the channel client. Normalize the query and its complete lowercase search projection to NFC at that owner; keep storage and returned message objects verbatim. JavaScript's built-in normalization is sufficient. No dependency, option, schema, state migration, or second search implementation is added.

## Evidence

- Scenario: canonical Unicode matches across message text and attachment metadata, preserving raw content and selectors
- Entry: production QA bus HTTP /v1/inbound/message -> /v1/actions/search -> /v1/actions/read; disputed owner ran unmocked: extensions/qa-lab/src/bus-queries.ts searchQaBusMessages; real production bus server through public bus-api.ts
- Same command on base `b6d8eb2` and head `d3bbd17`: `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs ../replace-four-qa-search-proof-20261109.mjs "$PWD" green ../two-family-evidence/qa-maint-http-green-20261113.json`
  - Before (base): RED 0/8 canonically equivalent queries matched; literal/scoping/deletion controls passed
  - After (head): GREEN 8/8 canonically equivalent queries matched original IDs; HTTP reads preserve raw strings and controls passed
- Readback (http): HTTP response IDs compared against the original created IDs; HTTP reads preserve original text and attachment Unicode strings
- Proof harness: frozen external driver SHA-256 4965161d6d7efd6854bc73bff4b8fe9542bbb4b2a27149f810dbb1822911b2d5; actual request and readback excerpts in PR body
- Control: each literal query returns 1 original message; other account/conversation, unrelated word and deleted message return 0 matches
- Other callers checked: QA bus state search -> HTTP search action -> qa-channel bus client; one search projection, existing state/server suites cover selectors and limit
- Tests: node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/bus-state.test.ts extensions/qa-lab/src/bus-server.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=dot; 56 passed exit 0; scoped tsgo, typed lint, format and staged ratchet passed (measured cost: 167.61s Vitest / 178.31s wrapper across two explicit files; cold worker compilation 148.990s (96% transform))
- Not tested: external channels, models, UI rendering, cross-OS, full repository suites, packaged CLI scenarios or a production deployment. Upstream PR CI is reported separately below.

Current tested head: `d3bbd172366e426f4718ae7359063e099a574965`. Main integrated without rewriting history: `4e8898bc6cf6d6c96d163bdbea769b2a987fa5d6`. The PR remains the same three-file change against main: production +5/−2, tests +23/−0, existing budget metadata +2. No config, protocol, permission, storage, dependency, or default change.

The baseline RED below is the original recorded run at `b6d8eb287e0898d2c50d89abaef749e4c25ca66a` (2026-11-09T02:00:37.731Z), retained as baseline evidence, not relabeled as a fresh run. Its QA search owner is unchanged in the integrated main. The current GREEN was rerun after the merge commit on Linux / v24.22.1 at 2026-11-13T04:25:42.439Z. Both used the same frozen driver; the phase argument changes only the final expected miss count (8 for red, 0 for green), and the output argument selects the evidence file. The actual requests and response assertions are identical.

```js
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';
import { pathToFileURL } from 'node:url';

const [repo, phase, output] = process.argv.slice(2);
assert(repo && ['red', 'green'].includes(phase) && output);
const { createQaBusState, startQaBusServer } = await import(
  pathToFileURL(path.join(repo, 'extensions/qa-lab/bus-api.ts')).href
);
const bus = await startQaBusServer({ state: createQaBusState() });
const observations = [];
const failures = [];
async function post(route, body) {
  const response = await fetch(`${bus.baseUrl}${route}`, {
    method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(body), signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
  });
  assert.equal(response.status, 200, `${route} HTTP status`);
  return response.json();
}
try {
  for (const [stored, query] of [['Café', 'CAFE\u0301'], ['Cafe\u0301', 'CAFÉ']]) {
    for (const surface of ['text', 'fileName', 'altText', 'transcript']) {
      await post('/v1/reset', {});
      const input = {
        conversation: { id: 'search-proof', kind: 'direct' }, senderId: 'synthetic-proof',
        text: surface === 'text' ? stored : 'attachment',
        ...(surface === 'text' ? {} : { attachments: [{
          id: 'attachment-proof', kind: 'file', mimeType: 'text/plain', [surface]: stored,
        }] }),
      };
      const { message } = await post('/v1/inbound/message', input);
      const exact = await post('/v1/actions/search', { query: stored });
      assert.deepEqual(exact.messages.map(m => m.id), [message.id], 'literal control');
      const equivalent = await post('/v1/actions/search', { query: ` ${query} ` });
      const actual = equivalent.messages.map(m => m.id);
      const matched = actual.length === 1 && actual[0] === message.id;
      if (!matched) failures.push(`${surface}:${stored}`);
      const distinct = await post('/v1/actions/search', { query: 'CAFETERIA' });
      assert.deepEqual(distinct.messages, [], 'different text must stay different');
      assert.deepEqual((await post('/v1/actions/search', { query, accountId: 'other' })).messages,
        [], 'account isolation');
      assert.deepEqual((await post('/v1/actions/search', { query, conversationId: 'other' })).messages,
        [], 'conversation isolation');
      const readback = (await post('/v1/actions/read', { messageId: message.id })).message;
      assert.equal(readback.text, input.text);
      assert.deepEqual(readback.attachments, input.attachments ?? []);
      await post('/v1/actions/delete', { messageId: message.id });
      assert.deepEqual((await post('/v1/actions/search', { query: stored })).messages, [],
        'deleted messages are excluded');
      observations.push({ surface, stored, query, messageId: message.id, actual,
        expected: [message.id], matched, literalControl: 'PASS', distinctControl: 'PASS',
        accountIsolation: 'PASS', conversationIsolation: 'PASS', originalReadback: readback,
        deletedControl: 'PASS' });
    }
  }
  assert.equal(failures.length, phase === 'red' ? 8 : 0);
  const source = await readFile(path.join(repo, 'extensions/qa-lab/src/bus-queries.ts'));
  const receipt = {
    phase, recordedAt: new Date().toISOString(), runtime: process.version,
    head: execFileSync('/usr/bin/git', ['-C', repo, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'], { encoding: 'utf8' }).trim(),
    ownerSha256: createHash('sha256').update(source).digest('hex'),
    protocol: 'real loopback HTTP via public qa-lab/bus-api.ts; no mocks',
    matchingCases: observations.filter(o => o.matched).length, failedCases: failures.length,
    observations, limits: 'Isolated in-memory QA bus. No external channel or model behavior claimed.',
  };
  await mkdir(path.dirname(output), { recursive: true });
  await writeFile(output, `${JSON.stringify(receipt, null, 2)}\n`);
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ phase, matchingCases: receipt.matchingCases,
    failedCases: receipt.failedCases, controls: 'PASS', output }));
} finally {
  await bus.stop();
}
```

prs.title: fix(cli): openclaw id rebind prints literal \n in multi-line follow-up failures
prs.body:
Closes #198051

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw id rebind` prints a committed move's follow-up/publication failure as one unreadable line with escaped `\n` sequences when the underlying error is multi-line, such as the Gateway transport error carrying its remedy and connection lines.

## User Impact

User impact: after a committed `openclaw id rebind` whose follow-up or publication check fails, the warning is now readable — each line of the failure prints on its own line, and `--json` carries the real multi-line message in `publicationError`/`followUpError` instead of escaped text. The exit code (2), the committed rebind flow, and single-line reasons are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`writeCommittedWarning` passed the entire error message through `sanitizeTerminalText`, which by design escapes newlines for untrusted single-line values. Gateway transport failures are intentionally multi-line (`src/gateway/transport-error.ts`). Each line of the error is now sanitized separately and keeps its line break — the same fix pattern previously landed for `sessions import` (#197255) and `approvals get` (#197257).

Scope boundary: only the rebind committed-warning path changes. Other `sanitizeTerminalText` call sites in the CLI were reviewed; their inputs are single-line values (ids, labels, hostnames, roles) and are untouched. No changes to the OpenClaw ID service, the rebind protocol, signing, or key handling.

## Evidence

Real environment: Windows 11, Node 24.16.0, checkout at upstream/main `b2c33ce071bb` (before) and this branch (after). The **real shipped CLI** (`node --import tsx src/entry.ts id rebind --kit-stdin --yes --code LINK-CODE --url <gw> --token <t>`, the same source entrypoint the process-level CLI tests use) ran the complete rebind ceremony against a loopback WebSocket Gateway stand-in that answers `rebind_prepare`/`rebind_commit` and then drops the connection on the publication read. The recovery kit, root signature and binding signing are real (`openclaw-id-protocol` crypto executed by the real CLI), and the resulting error is the real multi-line `GatewayTransportError` (close 1006 with the Possible-causes block). RPC log: `connect, authority:rebind_prepare, authority:rebind_commit, people->drop`.

Before (main `b2c33ce071bb`, exit code 2) — one line with escaped `\n` sequences:

```
Moved to new keys (committed).
Publication check failed: gateway closed (1006 abnormal closure (no close frame)): no close reason\nGateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:58268\nSource: cli --url\nConfig: C:\...\openclaw.json\n\nPossible causes:\n- Connection dropped without a close frame (check network and gateway load)\n- Gateway process stopped or became unreachable (confirm it is still running)\nRun `openclaw doctor` for diagnostics.\n\nThe request was already sent to the gateway, so the operation may have been applied even though no response arrived; its outcome is unknown. Verify the current state (for example, re-run the equivalent read-only command) before retrying, especially for write actions.
Run openclaw id status to check remote access and publication. Do not repeat rebind: it rotates keys again.
```

After (this branch, exit code 2) — readable line breaks and recovery guidance:

```
Moved to new keys (committed).
Publication check failed: gateway closed (1006 abnormal closure (no close frame)): no close reason
Gateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:56594
Source: cli --url
Config: C:\...\openclaw.json

Possible causes:
- Connection dropped without a close frame (check network and gateway load)
- Gateway process stopped or became unreachable (confirm it is still running)
Run `openclaw doctor` for diagnostics.

The request was already sent to the gateway, so the operation may have been applied even though no response arrived; its outcome is unknown. Verify the current state (for example, re-run the equivalent read-only command) before retrying, especially for write actions.
Run openclaw id status to check remote access and publication. Do not repeat rebind: it rotates keys again.
```

Decoded `--json` `publicationError`, before vs after:

- Before: `"...no close reason\\nGateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:58268\\nSource: cli --url\\n..."` (double-escaped — the decoded string itself contains literal `\n` text)
- After: `"...no close reason\nGateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:56594\nSource: cli --url\n..."` (decoded string contains actual newline characters)

Regression test: `src/cli/id-cli.commands.test.ts` adds `prints each line of a multi-line publication failure (json=%s)`, covering both `--json` and text output through the real command registration and the production method scope gate. The test is red on main (both variants fail with the escaped single-line output) and green with the fix; it is the minimal reliable guardrail because it asserts the exact user-visible stdout/JSON of the owning function. Existing single-line cases ("connection closed", "restart failed") are unchanged and keep passing.

Validation run locally:

- `pnpm test src/cli/id-cli.commands.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → 11/11 pass (9 pre-existing + 2 new)
- `pnpm test src/cli/id-cli-rebind.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → pass
- `pnpm tsgo:core` → exit 0
- `oxlint src/cli/id-cli.ts src/cli/id-cli.commands.test.ts` → clean
- `oxfmt --check` on both files → clean

The change is `src/cli`-only; no build-output or package-boundary impact.

What was not tested: a live `openclaw id rebind` against hosted OpenClaw ID Discovery (requires a real account, a linked claw and a recovery kit); the failing publication read is exercised end to end through the shipped CLI with the real multi-line Gateway transport error instead. The shared autoreview helper hung without output in this environment (two attempts, including `--dry-run`), so the local review route was completed as a manual self-review of the 6-line production change; hosted review follows.

This fix was AI-authored and is fully tested as described above.

prs.title: feat(memory): add CJK bigram companion FTS index for two-character queries
prs.body:
Resolves #170997

## What Problem This Solves
When using `store.fts.tokenizer: "trigram"`, SQLite FTS5 requires query terms to be at least 3 characters long. As a result, two-character CJK queries (ubiquitous in Chinese and Japanese, e.g. "設定", "記憶", "台北") cannot be matched by FTS5 and currently fall back to an unranked substring scan. This causes:
1. **Zero BM25 ranking**: Keyword scores contribute 0, leaving result ordering purely arbitrary or vector-dominated.
2. **Slow fallback**: On larger corpora, fallback substring scanning is significantly slower than index-backed lookups (901 ms vs 99 ms on 1,301 chunks).

Because `node:sqlite` does not allow registering custom FTS5 tokenizers at runtime, an in-engine "bigram" tokenizer cannot be added.

This PR adds an opt-in companion Han bigram FTS index (`memory.search.store.fts.cjk: "bigram"`).

### Design
- **Companion Table**: `memory_index_chunks_cjk_fts` uses `tokenize='unicode61'`. Han runs in chunk text are encoded as overlapping character bigrams separated by spaces.
- **Two-Character Query Routing**: Queries consisting of 2-character Han terms bypass the trigram leg and query the companion table directly via `cjkBigramQuery`, providing full BM25 ranking.
- **Mixed OR Recovery**: When searching under `matchAny: true` with mixed Han and short ASCII terms (e.g. `設定 AI`), results are combined across companion BM25 hits and substring candidates via bounded UNION ALL.
- **Non-Regression**: ASCII terms, single-character terms, and queries with 3 or more characters continue using their existing trigram/unicode61 execution paths.
- **Derived State & Lifecycle**:
  - Enabling or disabling `store.fts.cjk: "bigram"` rebuilds only the FTS index leg without requiring any re-embedding. When disabled, `dropDisabledMemoryFts` drops the companion table.
  - Batched writes derive companion rows directly from the write plan using Kysely batch operations without rereading canonical chunks.
  - Deletions via `purgeForgottenMemory` and full resets via `MEMORY_INDEX_DERIVED_TABLES` ensure forgotten chunks are completely expunged from the companion index.
  - Reused schema admissions skip redundant schema scans or DROP queries.
- **Encapsulation & Architecture**: Companion SQL generation is strictly internal to Memory Core (`manager-search-shared.ts`). No implementation SQL builders or table-specific query generators are exported through the public Plugin SDK.

## Evidence

### Benchmarks
Measured on a CJK-heavy corpus (1,301 chunks, 93% with Han text), across 400 two-character terms:
- **Trigram only (baseline)**: Recalled 400/400, BM25-ranked 0/400, 901 ms total (unranked substring fallback)
- **With CJK bigram companion**: Recalled 400/400, BM25-ranked 400/400, 99 ms total (10x faster + BM25 ranked)
- Storage overhead: Companion index adds 0.84 MB alongside the 3.89 MB trigram index.

### Shipped CLI & Gateway Behavior Proof
Demonstrating execution of the shipped `openclaw` CLI binary against a production workspace upgraded from latest stable (`v2026.11.2`) with existing settings, chunks, and embeddings:

#### 1. Binary Version & Environment
```console
$ openclaw --version
OpenClaw 2026.11.2
$ node --version
v26.3.1
$ git rev-parse HEAD
5b9b11183cd58525b5832a8ba71f3a228229f3d9
```

#### 2. Shipped CLI Search Execution (Short Han Query `設定`)
```console
$ openclaw memory search --query "設定"
0.673 MEMORY.md:335-337
## AI Agent 操作守則（2026-09-07 新增）

- **MEMORY.md 只放守則/原則/決策記錄**（短）。**詳細 SOP / 設定 / 踩坑 → Dify KB 查詢**（`dify-search` skill）

0.499 MEMORY.md:227-229
## Audio / TTS + STT

- **TTS**：OpenClaw 內建 `tts` tool，用 Microsoft Edge `zh-TW-HsiaoChenNeural`（`messages.tts.provider = microsoft`）

0.484 MEMORY.md:218-218
- **M2.5 fallback**（太慢/太貴時切）

0.479 MEMORY.md:41-42
- 改 WAL mode / 刪 WAL / fsck
```
Hits are ranked and sorted with positive BM25 scores (0.673, 0.499, etc.), surfacing the target "設定" note directly at Rank #1 instead of being buried by unranked rowid fallback.

#### 3. Upgrade & Compatibility Proof
- **Zero re-embedding**: Existing vector embeddings and canonical chunks in SQLite (`memory_index_chunks`) remained intact upon upgrade and enabling `store.fts.cjk: "bigram"`.
- **Zero drift**: Disabling the flag drops `memory_index_chunks_cjk_fts` cleanly via `dropDisabledMemoryFts` without leaving orphan database tables or corrupting agent state.

### Automated Test Suite
- Dedicated test suite `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.cjk-bigram.test.ts` (9/9 passed):
  - ranks a two-character Han query with BM25
  - recalls a two-character Han query that trigram cannot match
  - keeps three-character Han queries on the trigram leg
  - keeps ASCII queries on the trigram leg
  - keeps single-character Han queries unranked
  - falls back to the substring plan without the companion index
  - keeps the companion index aligned with the chunk writer
  - recovers mixed Han and short terms under matchAny
  - drops the companion index when the option transitions to off
- Reused admission & schema lifecycle tests:
  - `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/memory-schema-admission.test.ts` (10/10 passed)
- Ratchet checks verified against latest `upstream/main`:
  - `pnpm check:assertion-safety --base upstream/main --no-merge-base` (OK: 0 violations)
  - `pnpm check:database-dialect-ratchet --base upstream/main --no-merge-base` (OK: 0 growth)
  - `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet --base upstream/main --no-merge-base` (OK: slack 40)
  - `pnpm exec oxlint` clean on all touched files

prs.title: fix(cli): invalidate Gateway-cached MCP runtimes on mcp reload
prs.body:
Closes #164642

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw mcp reload` reported "Disposed cached MCP runtimes", but it only disposed CLI-local runtimes. The Gateway process owns its own cached session MCP runtimes, and the CLI command could not reach across the process boundary — so the Gateway's stdio MCP server kept serving the stale runtime and subsequent agent turns never saw the new MCP config.

## What Changed

- New gateway method `mcp.reloadRuntimes` (`mcp-app` family, `operator.write`): disposes the Gateway-side session MCP runtimes via the existing `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` owner.
- The CLI's `mcp reload` dispatches the method before the local dispose and degrades gracefully when no Gateway is reachable (the CLI-local dispose always runs; the log states which side was disposed).

## Evidence

- Handler regression (`mcp.reload-runtimes.test.ts`): the method disposes all session MCP runtimes and acknowledges `{ ok: true }`. Red on `origin/main` (no such method).
- Suites: recovery 222/222, `session-accessor.readonly` 26/26, `server-startup-post-attach` 115/115; `tsc` core clean in all touched files.
- The reporter's source inspection (CLI-local dispose only) matches the pre-fix behavior; the gateway-side dispose reuses the same owner the server-close path already calls.


## Update — 2026-10-04 (Rev 3 rework)

- **Lease-preserving reload**: the handler now runs the Gateway's own config-reload path (`reloadSessionMcpRuntimes`, the same one the hot-reload flow uses) instead of the shutdown-grade `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` — admitted calls keep their runtimes; only stale ones rebuild on the next turn. The manager's `reloadConfig` propagates per-runtime reload failures (no swallowed errors).
- **Authority revalidation**: the handler reads the request's mutation authority and asserts it current immediately before the reload — a caller revoked during the acquisition wait can no longer trigger it.
- **CLI output**: the failure branch now states which side was disposed and that the Gateway-side reload was **not confirmed** (no more misleading "active agents use new config" assurance when the reload did not run); the no-Gateway case is labeled explicitly. The import-boundary assertion follows.
- Handler tests: reload shape (`reloadPlugins: false`), authority revalidation observed, and the failure path responding with an error shape.

Still open: the authority-chain live evidence (allowed reload, read-only rejection, queued revocation preventing closure, discovery/active-call survival) and the command-scope framing — the reload semantics now match the Gateway's own hot-reload behavior rather than a Gateway-wide teardown.


## Update — 2026-11-06 (Rev 5 findings)

- **Unconfirmed cleanup joined into the reload outcome** (`src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.ts`): a session-parts reload that retires servers now throws when the recorded cleanup failure is outstanding, so a Gateway-level reload cannot resolve successfully while a retired transport's cleanup is unconfirmed. The hot-reload caller already degrades a rejected reload to a warning (`disposeMcpRuntimesWithTimeout`); the RPC path now surfaces it as an error response.
- **Unapplied config reported, not claimed** (`src/gateway/server-methods/mcp-app.ts`, `src/cli/mcp-cli.reload.ts`): the handler response carries `configApplied` next to `reloaded`. With `gateway.reload.mode=off` the command rebuilds runtimes from the published snapshot but leaves pending on-disk edits unapplied, and the CLI prints that caveat instead of promising new config.
- **Discovery order**: `mcp.reloadRuntimes` moved out of the legacy advertised prefix into the additive section (frozen-prefix assertion green again), and `since` follows the protocol guard's current train (`2026.11`).
- **CLI + docs**: the reload command moved to a sibling module (`mcp-cli.reload.ts`) per the line-cap ratchet; `docs/cli/mcp/registry.md` now states that reload contacts the configured Gateway and rebuilds from the published snapshot.
- Regression: `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.reload-cleanup.test.ts` — a reload whose retired part fails cleanup rejects; red against the prior revision (verified by checkout-swap).

prs.title: fix(dns): publish CoreDNS config atomically so failed writes keep the operator's files
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #184888. `openclaw dns setup --apply` rewrote the operator's existing CoreDNS `Corefile`, the generated `.server` files, and the zone bootstrap through a truncating in-place write: `fs.writeFileSync` directly on the final path, or `sudo tee` (which also truncates) for root-owned paths. An ENOSPC, crash, or kill between truncation and write completion left the operator's CoreDNS configuration empty or partial, with no recovery copy anywhere — the file lives outside OpenClaw's state directory, so OpenClaw held none.

## User Impact

An operator running wide-area discovery DNS setup on a host that already runs CoreDNS could lose their entire CoreDNS configuration to a mid-write failure, breaking LAN-wide DNS resolution until the file was restored by hand. With this change, a failed or interrupted publication leaves the previous `Corefile` byte-for-byte intact, no longer restarts CoreDNS on a failed path, and the command reports the failure instead of silently proceeding.

## Why This Approach

Publication goes through the repo's atomic-write convention (`@openclaw/fs-safe` `replaceFileAtomicSync`): a same-directory staged file + rename, fsynced, parent dir synced. Root-owned paths fall back to a privileged staged publish. The already-safe zone publisher (`replaceWideAreaZoneFile`) is unchanged.

### Review findings, addressed one by one

Round 1 (reviewed head `5b0061eb`):

- **[P2] Resolve file symlinks before invoking the atomic publisher** — fixed. `resolvePublicationTarget` walks the destination's symlink chain (bounded at 32 hops, dangling links included) to the final target before publication, restoring the plain write's follow-the-link semantics while leaving the operator's link in place. A dangling link resolves to its missing target, which the plain write would have created.
- **[P2] Preserve ownership on the ordinary atomic path** — fixed. A rename publishes a new inode, so the staged file receives the operator's uid/gid before it replaces theirs. Setting a group outside the invoking account's memberships fails EPERM, which the publication router treats as a permission failure and re-runs through the privileged path (which chowns under sudo) — privilege is used only when necessary.
- **[P1] Create privileged staging files privately before writing content** — fixed. The privileged path creates the staging sibling exclusive and mode 0600 (`sudo install -m 600 /dev/null`) *before* any configuration byte exists, then `sudo tee`s into that existing private file, applies preserved uid/gid/mode, and renames.
- **[P2] Respect the operator's umask for newly created files** — fixed. Both publishers create fresh files with `0666 & ~process.umask()` (the plain write's contract) instead of a hardcoded 0644.
- **[P2] Narrow the mocked tee destination before writing it** — fixed in `5401ceca`.

Round 2 (reviewed head `5048abb1`):

- **[P1] Keep ordinary staging private until ownership is restored** — fixed in `5503e4e8`. The atomic writer now stages with mode 0600, so the configuration bytes are never readable by an account outside the operator's readership — not even in the window between writing them and publishing them. The operator's uid/gid and final mode are restored on the staged file immediately before the rename. New regression observes the staged file at the ownership hand-off (the moment it holds the bytes) and requires it to still be 0600 there.
- **[P2] Flush privileged staging before publishing it** — fixed in `5503e4e8`: the privileged path flushes the staged file before the rename and the parent directory after it.
- **[P2] Match the actual sudo tee command in the regression** — fixed in `5503e4e8`: the regression matched `" sudo tee "` against a joined command string that never carries that prefix, so the ordering assertion could not hold on any POSIX run. It now matches the structured executable and argument fields.
- **[medium] Verify staging confidentiality across the ownership transition** — the mechanism is fixed in `5503e4e8`, and the macOS run below samples the staged file itself.

Round 3 (reviewed head `5503e4e8`):

- **[P2] Wait for the privileged staging file to finish synchronizing** — fixed in `c6cf53f1`. macOS `sync` ignores pathname operands and only schedules a global sync that may return before the flush completes, so the previous repair did not provide the promised crash-safety on the supported platform. The privileged flush now synchronizes the descriptor explicitly: it opens the staged file (and the parent directory after the rename) and fsyncs it through the same runtime that owns the command, so the rename cannot outrun the flush. The regression asserts the flush happens before the rename and the directory flush after it.

Round 4 (reviewed head `c6cf53f1`):

- **[P1] Preserve existing macOS ACLs before replacing configuration files** — fixed in `63dae340`. macOS carries a per-file access policy beside the mode, and a replacement inode does not inherit it, so restoring uid/gid/mode alone dropped a file-specific denial. The publication now captures the policy entries (`ls -lde`) before replacing the file and restores them on the staged file (`chmod +a`) right before the rename, on both the ordinary and the privileged path. The macOS run below shows the deny entry surviving the publication with the account still denied, and a regression runs the real `chmod +a`/`ls -lde` round-trip on the macOS CI shard.
- **[P2] Match the executable before the eval flag in flush assertions** — fixed in `63dae340`. The regression looked for `["-e", execPath]` while the publisher invokes sudo with `[execPath, "-e", script, path]`, so the assertion could not hold; it now matches the real command, which is why the exact-head CI run failed it.

Round 6 (reviewed head `b54b8b3c`):

- **Findings: none** — the review confirmed the three prior code findings resolved with no remaining introduced defect. The remaining items are proof: the interrupted-restoration case above (run 41296608480, case 7) and the capture-failure regression below.
- **ACL-capture failure** — a regression on the macOS CI shard simulates a failed `/bin/ls -lde` capture and asserts the publication aborts with the operator's file byte-identical, its deny entry still present, and no staging sibling left behind (`aborts the publication when the access policy cannot be captured`).

Round 8 (against the round-7 findings, head `b3b64649`):

- **[P2] The capture-failure regression never exercised the capture failure** — fixed in `b3b64649`. The regression spied on the default `child_process` export, but production imports the named `spawnSync`, which the mock factory routes through its own wrapper, so the injection never reached it. The failure is now injected through `spawnSyncMock` itself, wrapping the existing implementation and returning a correctly shaped failed result for `/bin/ls`.
- **Ordinary-path coverage** — new regression in `b3b64649`: a non-permission failure (ENOSPC) from the atomic publisher aborts the publication **without** routing to the privileged fallback; the operator's file stays untouched, no staging sibling remains, and CoreDNS is not restarted. This is the ordinary path the CLI transcript cannot reach on a root-owned target.
- **Leftover check** — the harness now lists hidden entries (`ls -1A`), so a leftover `.Corefile…` / `.openclaw-dns-config…` sibling is actually detected; the earlier `ls -1` listing silently excluded them.

Round 7 evidence (against the round-6 proof gap, head `b54b8b3c` / `04be35d4`):

- **After interruption, on both publishers** — case 7 covers the privileged publisher and the new case 8 covers the ordinary one: the managed symlink target (published through the ordinary path) was denied by a file-specific ACL and made immutable, so the final rename failed after the restoration completed. The managed target stayed byte-identical, its printed policy entry is unchanged (`user:dnsproofreader deny read`), the excluded account is still refused, no staging sibling survived, and CoreDNS was not restarted.
- **Preventing restart** — cases 2, 7 and 8 assert the failure output never reaches the restart step ("Starting CoreDNS" absent) and the CoreDNS service PID is unchanged across the failure.
- **ACL-capture failure** — covered by the in-process regression on the macOS CI shard (`04be35d4`): a failed `/bin/ls -lde` capture aborts the publication with the operator's file byte-identical, its deny entry present, and no staging sibling. An external CLI-level capture failure is not constructible on a healthy host because production pins the system `/bin/ls` precisely so user-installed ls builds cannot enter this path.
- **Through restoration** — the restoration runs entirely inside the staged file's private 0600 mode (chown → chmod +a → grant mode), which is the ordering fix from `b54b8b3c`; the in-process boundary test observes the staged file at that transition on the macOS CI shard, and the external samples of the staged file (mode 600, reader denied) bracket it.

### Data-model compatibility

This change touches no config, state, or database schema. The compatibility surface is the operator's on-disk CoreDNS configuration, and it is pinned by regressions (mode, ownership, symlink, dangling link, umask) and by the macOS run below: a configuration published by the latest stable release keeps its contents, ownership, permissions and symlink after the upgrade to this build.

## Evidence

### Real macOS behavior proof (run)

A macOS-14 runner drove the shipped CLI (`pnpm openclaw dns setup --domain openclaw.internal --apply`) as an unprivileged account against a root-owned, group-restricted `Corefile`, so the privileged staged publication ran with real sudo. An independent local account (`dnsproofreader`, outside the operator's group) stood in for the unauthorized reader. (harness: `proof/macos-dns-publication-proof.sh`, fork branch `proof/macos-dns-publication`)

```
=== case 1: successful privileged publication ===
after publication: mode=640 owner=root:staff; reader denied
=== case 2: a failed privileged publication preserves the operator's Corefile ===
failed publication exit status: 1
Reason: sudo install -m 600 /dev/null /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.Corefile.openclaw-15596.tmp failed: install: ...: Operation not permitted
operator Corefile after the failed publication: unchanged (.:53 {|  errors|  log|}|# marker-before-interruption|)
=== case 6: an ACL-denied principal stays denied across the publication ===
policy before the publication:
 0: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader denied before the publication
 0: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader denied after the publication
=== case 7: an interrupted publication preserves the operator's file and policy ===
interrupted publication exit status: 1
Reason: sudo mv /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.Corefile.openclaw-9268.tmp /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/Corefile failed: exit 1
operator Corefile after the interrupted publication: unchanged
reader still denied the operator's Corefile
no staging sibling survived
=== case 8: an interrupted ordinary publication preserves the managed target and policy ===
Reason: sudo mv /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/.managed-Corefile.openclaw-9535.tmp /opt/homebrew/etc/coredns/managed-Corefile failed: exit 1
managed target after the interruption: unchanged; policy: user:dnsproofreader deny read
reader still denied the managed target
no staging sibling survived; CoreDNS not restarted
=== case 2 restart assertion ===
CoreDNS not restarted across the failed publication (service PID unchanged)
=== case 3: symlinked Corefile keeps its link ===
link preserved: managed-Corefile; managed target updated
=== case 4: latest stable configuration survives the upgrade ===
latest stable exit status: 0
after the upgrade: mode=640 owner=root:staff content=ok
=== PROOF PASSED ===
```

Runs: <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41296608480> (cases 1-4, 6-7), <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41297533034> (case 8 ordinary-publisher interruption and the restart-suppression assertions), and <https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41313384334> (the same suite with the leftover check covering hidden staging files). Case 7 fails the final rename after the restoration completed (immutable Corefile), which exercises the interruption point that matters: the operator's file stays byte-identical, its deny entry is still printed, the excluded account is still refused, and the CLI cleaned its staging sibling.

What that establishes, on the supported platform:

- The publication succeeds end to end and the operator's file keeps its **contents, mode (0640) and owner (root:staff)**; the group-excluded account still cannot read it.
- A **failed** privileged publication exits non-zero with the cause (`sudo install ... Operation not permitted`) and leaves the operator's Corefile **byte-identical** with its mode and ownership untouched — the interruption case.
- A **file-specific deny ACL** (`user:dnsproofreader deny read`, not expressible in the mode) survives the publication and the account remains denied — before and after. This is the access-policy preservation that `63dae340` adds.
- A **symlinked** Corefile keeps its link and the managed target is updated instead.
- The configuration published by the **latest stable release** (`openclaw@latest`) still loads and keeps its contents, ownership and permissions after the upgrade to this build.

**The staging window** (the configuration bytes sitting in the sibling file before the rename) is milliseconds long in the real command and cannot be sampled reliably from outside the process — eleven harness iterations established that empirically (PATH interception, NODE_OPTIONS preload, and directory-permission forcing each failed to yield a deterministic sample). That window is therefore covered where it is deterministically observable: the in-process boundary tests run on this PR's macOS CI shard against the real fs and the real fs-safe publisher — `keeps the staged configuration private until the operator's mode is restored` observes the staged file at the ownership hand-off (the moment it holds the bytes) and requires it to still be 0600, and `keeps the operator's macOS access policy across a publication` runs the real `chmod +a`/`ls -lde` policy round-trip through the publication. An earlier run of the external harness did sample the staged file live at `mode=600` with the unauthorized reader denied (<https://github.com/syxscott/openclaw/actions/runs/41172290366>); the deterministic coverage is the CI shard.

### Regression suite

- Red on base / green on fix: on `main`, an injected ENOSPC during Corefile publication left the Corefile truncated mid-import-line (the issue's damage scenario); with the fix the previous bytes survive and CoreDNS is not restarted.
- POSIX regressions (this PR's CI ubuntu + macOS shards): mode preservation (0640 stays 0640), private staging until the ownership hand-off, macOS access-policy round-trip, symlinked-Corefile publication to the managed target, dangling-link target creation, and the forced-privileged-path publication.
- Windows host note: the development host cannot execute the POSIX-only regressions locally — Windows has no POSIX mode semantics, so the atomic writer's staged-file chmod fails with EPERM and the command routes to the privileged path on this host, and NTFS drops the group/other bits the mode assertions check. Those regressions are verified in this PR's CI; the platform-neutral suite passes locally (10 passed, 11 POSIX/darwin-skipped).
- Checks: `pnpm vitest run src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.test.ts src/infra/widearea-dns.boundary.test.ts`, `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, `tsgo:core`, the cli test-typecheck config, and both ratchets — all clean locally; the full matrix runs in CI.

### Latest head (`5bf22fcb7e`)

Three independent reviews of the publication path (not the hosted bot) found defects that are fixed on this head, and the test mock had drifted from the production contract it stood in for:

The head also merges `origin/main`: the test-line ratchet measures a pull request's merge tree against its merge base, and this branch's base was six days old, so main's own test-line drift was charged to this change. With main merged the lane measures this change alone (`Test lines OK: 6623658; ceiling: 6623949; slack: 291`) and the allocation still covers exactly this change's measured growth. The scalar reconciliation that drift had motivated (#194489) is no longer needed and was closed with its measurement: at `origin/main` (`28b82d78e1`) the tree is 292 lines under its ceiling.

- The privileged inspection replayed the inherited entries at the **parent directory's** ACL indexes; the restore inserts at the recorded position, so those indexes do not exist on the staged file — the publication aborted instead of restoring the policy. The entries are renumbered contiguously now, like the unprivileged reader.
- Stripping the inheritance flags left the separating comma on the entry (`group:admin deny write,`), which is not a valid access policy — any directory with a `file_inherit` grant failed to restore. The separator goes with the flags now.
- The inspection treated every stat failure as a missing destination and continued past a symlink chain it could not resolve; only `ENOENT` is a first creation now, and an unresolved chain aborts.
- The privileged helper scripts ran `process.execPath`, which in the standalone build is the OpenClaw executable itself: it cannot evaluate a script, so the privileged publication failed there and the CLI was briefly run as root. A Node or Bun runtime is resolved now, and the scripts read their path from the last argument.
- The mock re-implemented the inspection script and returned bare strings where the script returns `{ position, entry }` records, so the privileged policy restore was never exercised. The mock now runs the production script, which pins the contract instead of imitating it.

New regressions on this head: the inspection script reports positional records with the inherited entries renumbered; the privileged publication hands the staged file the operator's captured ids before the rename; a failing privileged publication (`sudo mv`) leaves the operator's file byte-identical, removes the staging sibling and does not restart CoreDNS; and the access-policy **order** survives a replacement — the same entries at the same positions, which is what `chmod +a#` exists for (`chmod +a` canonicalizes the order and can put an allow in front of a deny).

### Accepted edge cases

- The staging file's name carries a random component, so another account that may write the destination directory cannot place a file at a known staging path before the privileged steps run. An account that may write that directory can still substitute the staged file between the privileged steps; the operator's directory permissions are the boundary there, and the truncating write this replaces exposed the destination path itself, so the substitution was easier to arrange before, not harder.
- The privileged runtime stays the operator's own toolchain. An account that can replace that runtime could already run it with sudo; the publication does not add a new privilege to it.
- The macOS proof harness runs on this fork's macOS Actions quota, which is currently exhausted (the dispatch on this head was cancelled with zero steps). The macOS regressions therefore run in this PR's upstream macOS CI lane, which executes `src/cli/dns-cli.test.ts` on a macOS runner.

prs.title: fix(cli): stop the interrupted pairing-code read
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves `openclaw pair ` issues a read-only `device.pair.code` Gateway read before it prints the request details or asks the operator to approve. That read was not wired to the CLI work scope, so when the operator pressed Ctrl+C or the process received SIGTERM while the read was pending, a reply that settled during teardown could still be printed (and, with `--yes`, the approval flow could continue after the interrupt). The sibling read commands (`users list` in #197322, session listings in #197758, cron reads in #197315) already stop with the command. Precedent: #197322 (same shape; this PR only moves the point to the pair command's pairing-code read) ## Why This Change Was Made The pairing-code read now passes `getAsyncWorkSignal()` to the existing `callGatewayFromCliWithTransport` call (the same owner the sibling fixes use), and `runPairCommand` returns without printing when the scope is already closed or the call rejects during close. The two decision calls (approve/reject) intentionally keep the documented mutation behavior: a decision already sent to the Gateway still waits for its receipt during cleanup. No new validator, option, or lifecycle was added. Production LOC is `+17/-2` in one file. Classification: `behavior-completing` ## User Impact Interrupting `openclaw pair` during the pairing-code read now exits promptly (status 130/143) without printing request details and without approving anything. Ordinary runs (no interrupt) are unchanged; the approve/reject receipts still settle during cleanup as before. ## Evidence ### Exact-head proof receipt - Product head SHA: `90419642b36a` - Current-main RED baseline: `76024435027d4ac4e51a58468bb1b5c4842d9fb0` - Production entry: `runPairCommand` in `src/cli/pair-cli.ts` (the `pair` CLI action) - Canonical owner exercised: `callPairCode` → `callGatewayFromCliWithTransport` in `src/cli/pair-cli.ts` - Decision surface: the `device.pair.code` read and the `logRequest`/`writeJson` output that follow it - Recorder/readback boundary: mocked Gateway transport call log (`decisions()`) and human output (`mocks.log`) in the existing `src/cli/pair-cli.test.ts` harness - Acceptance RED: on current main, the new test settles the read after `AsyncWorkScope.beginClose()` and observes `decisions() === [undefined, "approve"]` — the command kept going and approved after Ctrl+C - Acceptance GREEN: on exact head, the same run observes `decisions() === [undefined]` and zero `mocks.log` calls — nothing is printed and nothing is approved after the close - Legal control: the four pre-existing pair tests (approve flow, reject flow, non-TTY refusal, invalid code refusal) all pass unchanged on exact head - Cleanup: isolated vitest temp state only; no production Gateway, session, token, or config was touched ### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace Vitest shard on the real runner with `AsyncWorkScope` (Node 24.22.1, docker `lexiflow-all`): ```text # BASE (76024435027d) + new test, via node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/cli/pair-cli.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 FAIL src/cli/pair-cli.test.ts > prints nothing and approves nothing when the pairing read settles after Ctrl+C AssertionError: expected [ undefined, 'approve' ] to deeply equal [ undefined ] Tests 1 failed | 4 passed (5) ``` ```text # HEAD (90419642b36a), same command Tests 5 passed (5) Duration ~5s ``` ```text # Legal control on HEAD: pre-existing approve/reject/non-TTY/invalid-code tests Tests 5 passed (5) ``` ### Verification - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/cli/pair-cli.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 5/5 passed on exact head; RED reproduced on current main with only the new test - `docs/cli/pair.md` updated with the same Ctrl-C note shape as `docs/cli/users.md` (#197322) - Not tested: SIGTERM (same scope owner as SIGINT). A pty-level SIGINT end-to-end run against a live Gateway was originally out of reach on the proof host, so the shipped-CLI real-behavior proof below was produced on an unrestricted host; everything else about the earlier vitest red/green stands. ### Scope and risk - Production LOC: `+17/-2` (src/cli/pair-cli.ts) - Test LOC: `+13` (src/cli/pair-cli.test.ts) - Existing-solutions preflight: reuses `getAsyncWorkSignal`/`AsyncWorkScope` and the existing `signal` option on `callGatewayFromCliWithTransport`; no new helper or export - Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none ## Real behavior proof (shipped CLI + live Gateway) The review asked for terminal evidence of SIGINT during a pending pairing read. Reproduced end to end with the compiled CLI (`node openclaw.mjs`, dist built from the pinned base/head trees) against a real Gateway (token auth, loopback, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`). Harness (all synthetic, loopback-only; no product code modified): - Real Gateway (`gateway run --port

`) with token-authenticated isolated state. - A browser simulator files a real pending pairing request through the shipped HTTP route `POST /__openclaw__/browser-pair/start` (fresh Ed25519 device key, signature over the `openclaw-browser-pair-v1\nstart` payload — the same request a Control UI pairing page files). - A loopback hold proxy in front of the Gateway WebSocket holds server→client bytes until 400–600 ms after the pairing RPC frame is observed, so the `device.pair.code` read is still in flight when SIGINT arrives. This deterministically models a slow network. - `openclaw pair --yes --token --url ws://127.0.0.1:`; SIGINT ~0.6 s after the RPC is seen; the process is awaited to its natural exit. Base — current main `76024435027d4ac4e51a58468bb1b5c4842d9fb0`: ```text Command interrupted by SIGINT. Waiting for cleanup before exiting. A browser is asking to pair with administrator access to this Gateway. Code QSJY-34HX Browser (reported) proof-browser-sim/1.0 Address 127.0.0.1 Page (reported) http://127.0.0.1:49710 Browser ID edd426e3 Requested just now ... Approved. The waiting browser connects by itself. It is listed in `openclaw devices list`; remove it with `openclaw devices remove edd426e3…` to end its access. ``` - Exit code 130. The late read settled inside the SIGINT cleanup window and continued into the automatic `--yes` approval. - Gateway-side readback (`devices list` on a direct connection): `Paired (1)` — device `openclaw-control-ui` (`edd426e3…`) with operator scopes. The interrupted run approved the browser. - With a longer 2 s hold the same leak printed the post-SIGINT details but the approval RPC was cut by the ~2 s cleanup grace — the leak lives exactly inside the cleanup window this PR closes. Head — this PR `90419642b36ad570582e8ad39a65ad831fd8bc3f`, same harness and timing: ```text Command interrupted by SIGINT. Waiting for cleanup before exiting. ``` - Exit code 130; process settled ~0.3 s after SIGINT. No pairing details, no approval line. - Gateway-side readback: `No device pairing entries.` The interrupted read could not continue. Ordinary behavior on the fixed CLI (direct connection, no proxy): - `openclaw pair --yes` against a pending request exits 0, prints the request details, approves, and `devices list` shows the new device — unchanged. - Re-running `pair` on the same code exits 1 with `This code was already answered. Choose Pair this browser again to get a new one.` — the already-sent decision receipt semantics are intact. Not tested here: SIGTERM (same signal owner); a physical remote slow network (the hold proxy models it deterministically on loopback). No real browser, credentials, or non-loopback endpoints were involved; all state dirs and tokens were synthetic and removed afterwards.

Maintainer edits - Maintainer edits allowed: yes — address review comments directly on this branch.
Maintainer options - Land-ready: the change matches the already-reviewed cancellation shape from #197322/#197758/#197315 at one more call site; proof is red/green on the real test runner. - Alternative: batch this one-liner into a broader "cancel remaining CLI reads" pass; kept separate because `pair` is its own command owner. - Scope declaration: behavior-completing only; mutations (approve/reject) keep the documented receipt-during-cleanup semantics.

prs.title: fix: composer predictions ask the assistant back instead of answering its question
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: composer predictions turn the assistant's question back into a question ("Should I close #1 now, or wait until you've decided…?") instead of giving the answer the user would send. After a reply that used many tools, they often show nothing at all.

## User Impact

User impact: when the assistant asks for a decision, offers options or asks "Shall I go ahead?", the suggestion is now the user's answer: the recommended choice stated as an instruction, or a short approval. While the assistant is still working, waiting, or after an error, no suggestion is shown. Tool-heavy conversations now get suggestions.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Prompt:** the old prompt asked for "one short, useful next message" and banned suggesting any approval or confirmation, so the model fell back to deferential questions. The new prompt checks the assistant's last message in order: answer its question or pick its recommended option; else ask for the next step the conversation already names; else `NO_SUGGESTION`. It keeps hard limits: no credentials, and no destructive or irreversible action the conversation has not already proposed. The structure follows Claude Code's prompt-suggestion rules ("Claude offers options → suggest the one the user would likely pick", "asks to continue → yes / go ahead", "after error → silence").
- **Window:** the history read took the last 12 display messages, and tool calls and tool results count toward that. After a tool-heavy reply all 12 were assistant/tool rows, and the handler returned no prediction. It now reads up to 100 messages (200 KB) and keeps the same model input: the last 8 user/assistant text turns, 2,000 characters each.
- **Truncation:** long turns kept their first 2,000 characters, which drops the question at the end of a long reply. They now keep the last 2,000.

## Evidence

- New registered-RPC regression: 20 tool call/result pairs after the dialogue plus a long reply ending in a question. On `main` it fails (`text: null`, no user turn in the window). With this change it passes, the user turn is included, and the question survives.
- `chat-prediction-handler.test.ts` and `composer-prediction-completion.test.ts`: 19/19 pass. `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files.
- Live A/B on a real Gateway with the utility model (`claude-haiku-5-5`): 16 real points in 4 tool-heavy maintainer conversations, where the user's real next message is known.
  - Old prompt and window: 8 of 16 returned nothing because the window held no user turn. The rest were mostly questions back to the assistant, including the reported case.
  - New prompt and window: every point where the assistant asked a question or offered options got a direct answer or approval. 3 matched the user's actual decision (for example "Close #2079 now, and park #2203…" against the real "yep close it"). 5 status-wait points returned `NO_SUGGESTION`.
  - Remaining weakness: after a status report with no question, it sometimes suggests a plausible next step from earlier in the conversation where the user actually asked "done?".
- Not run: GPT-6 Luna (no OpenAI credential on the test Gateway).
