prs.title: fix(macos): keep Apple Event permission probes off the cooperative thread pool
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On 2026.9.3 the macOS app periodically goes dead while still running: the paired node shows **offline** in the Gateway dashboard although the Mac is on and the TCP session to the Gateway is still ESTABLISHED (32 KB of unread bytes sitting in the receive queue), the menu bar item stops opening its menu, and the process ignores SIGTERM (needs SIGKILL). It "fixes itself" only when the app is relaunched.

## Root cause

`AppleEventPermissionProbe.state` runs the blocking `AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget` in `Task.detached`, which schedules onto the Swift cooperative thread pool. The call blocks until Terminal answers the Apple Event handshake (and, when `askUserIfNeeded`, until the user answers tccd). `MacNodeModeCoordinator` re-probes permissions on every refresh trigger (`UserDefaults.didChangeNotification`, config change, permissions change, app activation, reconnect probe), so a slow Terminal under system load lets probes stack up.

A 3 s `sample` of the wedged process showed **all 16 cooperative threads** parked here, main thread idle:

```
DispatchQueue_18: com.apple.root.user-initiated-qos.cooperative
  closure #1 in AppleEventPermissionProbe.state(askUserIfNeeded:)
    AppleEventPermissionProbe.determineTerminalPermission(askUserIfNeeded:)
      AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget
        _dispatch_semaphore_wait_slow
          semaphore_wait_trap
```

Terminal automation was already **granted** in TCC (`kTCCServiceAppleEvents ai.openclaw.mac → com.apple.Terminal = 2`), so this was not a pending prompt. Once the pool is exhausted nothing async in the app can run, including the gateway websocket receive and the status item, and any continuation the AE reply needs can never be scheduled.

## Fix

- Run the blocking probe on a dedicated `DispatchQueue` (concurrent, so a prompt is never queued behind a hung passive check), bridged with a `CheckedContinuation`, so it never pins a cooperative thread.
- Single-flight concurrent callers per `askUserIfNeeded` value through a small actor (`AppleEventPermissionProbeCoordinator`), so at most one probe blocks at a time regardless of how many refreshes fire.
- Bound passive (non-prompting) probes with a 10 s timeout that surfaces as `.failed(errAETimeout)` → capability `.unknown`, instead of hanging the caller. Prompting probes keep waiting on the user.

No change to call sites; `AppleEventPermissionProbe.live` and `TerminalAutomationPermission` keep their API.

## Evidence

- `concurrent passive checks share one blocking probe`: 32 concurrent passive `state` calls → exactly one `determine` call, all callers get the result.
- `a hung passive probe times out instead of blocking callers`: a `determine` that never returns yields `.failed(errAETimeout)` in ~200 ms with a 200 ms timeout.
- `interactive prompts are never timed out`.
- Existing suite unchanged and green (12/12).
- Live observation, 2026-09-09: reproduced twice on the same Mac (2026.9.3 release build). Both times `netstat -anv -p tcp` showed the OpenClaw-owned socket to the Gateway ESTABLISHED with 32,778 and 52,617 bytes in Recv-Q, and `sample <pid> 2` showed 16 and 17 frames in `AEDeterminePermissionToAutomateTarget`. The second occurrence started within 60 s of a Gateway restart, i.e. on the reconnect refresh path. `pkill -9` + relaunch cleared it each time.

`swift build --package-path apps/macos --build-system native --build-tests` ✅, `scripts/format-swift.sh macos` ✅, `scripts/lint-swift.sh macos` ✅ (Xcode 26.6 / Swift 6.3.3).

## Review follow-up (revision 3)

Both P2 findings are addressed:

- **Retain the in-flight operation after a caller times out.** The coordinator now keeps the operation in `inFlight` until the native call actually returns. Caller deadlines are measured from the operation's start, so once the deadline has passed later passive callers answer `errAETimeout` immediately and never enqueue a second native call. When the target replies, the tracked operation drains and the next probe runs fresh. Covered by the new test `timed-out callers never enqueue a second native call behind the hung one` (second caller answers in < 150 ms with `callCount == 1`, operation still in flight; after release the next probe runs and `callCount == 2`).
- **Synchronize overlapping callers before releasing the test probe.** The concurrency test now waits until all 32 callers are parked on the coordinator (`waiterCount == 32`) before releasing, and `BlockingProbeGate.release()` opens the gate permanently so every native call a test started completes during cleanup.

The probe queue is concurrent so an interactive prompt is never queued behind a hung passive check.

## After-fix native proof

Debug build of this branch on a second Mac (macOS 26.4.1, Xcode 26.6), run in a throwaway app profile pointed at a remote Gateway URL that refuses connections (so every reconnect attempt builds a manifest and evaluates permissions). Terminal.app, the Apple Event target, was frozen with `SIGSTOP` so the probe could not get a reply, then resumed with `SIGCONT`. The passive probe returned `noErr` on this host: its TCC database already holds an allowed `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` row for bundle id `ai.openclaw.mac` → `com.apple.Terminal`, which the debug build shares, so recovery shows as a normal `returned 0`.

| Phase | `sample` probe frames | Cooperative-pool frames in the probe | `openclaw-mac status` (control socket) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 0 | 0 | ok |
| Terminal frozen, 55 s | 1, on `DispatchQueue: ai.openclaw.apple-event-permission (concurrent)` | 0 | ok |
| Terminal resumed, 50 s later | 0 | 0 | ok |

Unified log (`ai.openclaw`/`AppleEventPermissionProbe`), timestamps relative to the freeze:

```
-27 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.172922083 seconds
-19 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.033881875 seconds
-10 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.208797417 seconds
  0 s     Terminal.app frozen (SIGSTOP)
+17 s  E  probe ask=false timed out after 10.0 seconds; operation retained
+58 s     Terminal.app resumed (SIGCONT)
+58 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 50.992712958 seconds
+66 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.032903625 seconds
+97 s  I  probe ask=false returned 0 after 0.137408166 seconds
```

No second native call started while the first was hung (the only lines between the freeze and the resume are the single timeout), the retained call returned as soon as Terminal answered, and the probes after it ran fresh.

The app answered its control socket throughout, kept exactly one blocked thread (on the private queue, never the cooperative pool), released it when Terminal answered, and quit within 1 s of `SIGTERM` afterwards. On the release build the same condition ends with 13 to 17 cooperative threads blocked, a dead status menu, and `SIGTERM` ignored (openclaw/openclaw#146030).

Filtered test run (`swift test --filter AppleEventPermissionTests`, private HOME, throwaway profile, `--skip-build`): 13 tests, 0 failures. Full native suite left to the `macos-swift` CI job per `apps/macos/AGENTS.md`.

### Signed-bundle run (signing provenance)

The run above used the bare SwiftPM debug binary (ad-hoc signed). Repeated on the same Mac with a full `scripts/package-mac-app.sh` bundle of head `621a4a4d8`, signed through `scripts/codesign-mac-app.sh` with a real Apple Development certificate and kept at the fixed path the permissions guide asks for (`<checkout>/dist/OpenClaw.app`). Provenance, identity details redacted:

```
Identifier=ai.openclaw.mac.debug
Format=app bundle with Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20500 flags=0x10000(runtime)
Authority=Apple Development: <redacted>
Authority=Apple Worldwide Developer Relations Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA
TeamIdentifier=<redacted, set>
Sealed Resources version=2 rules=13 files=42384
codesign --verify --deep --strict: OK
```

`ai.openclaw.mac.debug` has no Automation grant on this Mac, so the passive probe's real answer is `-1744` (`errAEEventWouldRequireUserConsent`), returned without a prompt once Terminal answers. Same procedure (throwaway profile, refusing Gateway URL, Terminal `SIGSTOP` for 55 s, then `SIGCONT`):

| Phase | `sample` probe frames | Cooperative-pool frames in the probe | `openclaw-mac status` (control socket) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 0 | 0 | ok |
| Terminal frozen, 55 s | 1, on the private queue | 0 | ok |
| Terminal resumed, 50 s later | 0 | 0 | ok |

```
-28 s  I  probe ask=false returned -1744 after 0.207445334 seconds
  0 s     Terminal.app frozen (SIGSTOP)
+14 s  E  probe ask=false timed out after 10.0 seconds; operation retained
+58 s     Terminal.app resumed (SIGCONT)
+58 s  I  probe ask=false returned -1744 after 54.768811875 seconds
```

One blocked native call, no second call queued behind it, bounded caller wait, control socket answering throughout, the retained call returning the moment Terminal resumed, and the app quitting within 1 s of `SIGTERM` afterwards.

## Release note

Fix the macOS app wedging (node offline while TCP alive, menu bar item unresponsive, ignores SIGTERM) when concurrent Terminal Automation permission probes exhausted the Swift cooperative thread pool.

Diagnosed and written with Claude Code: https://claude.ai/code/session_014TmTvgdhcL7bPCwg3f8B6G
Review follow-up, after-fix proof, and this revision: https://claude.ai/code/session_01RW45HgmUaFSiM4DSZGrVSp

prs.title: feat(cron): back automation off when a provider or memory pushes back
prs.body:
Related: #196859

Depends on #197394 for the shared automation limit.

## What Problem This Solves

Automation bursts can keep replacing completed runs at full capacity even when a provider repeatedly rate-limits requests that eventually succeed through retries.

## User Impact

- Provider rate-limit or overload signals can halve automation capacity when more than eight automation agent sessions are active, with a floor of eight.
- Critical Gateway memory pressure can cause the same reduction.
- With queued demand and no recent pushback, the ceiling grows by about one slot per minute; newly available capacity is used on a later queue drain. A reduction expires after an hour without pushback.
- Conversations remain independent, and running automations finish normally.
- Reductions and recovery steps appear in Gateway logs. No new setting is added.

Backoff makes a backlog drain more slowly. The ceiling is process-wide, so pressure from one provider can also slow jobs using other providers and command or script jobs.

## Why This Change Was Made

The run-slot owner observes classified model-attempt failures and critical-memory diagnostics. It reacts to attempts rather than final job status because runtime retries can turn a rate-limited attempt into an `ok` job.

One burst causes one reduction until active sessions fall to the reduced ceiling. Recovery requires waiting demand and at least 50 seconds without pushback or another growth step.

Accepted tradeoffs:

- Automation-agent lane activity determines reductions, while the resulting ceiling applies to every job type.
- Hook turns and internal session events share that lane.
- CLI, ACP, compaction, and other model calls that emit no supported failure event do not drive provider backoff.
- Memory pressure is observed only while the diagnostics heartbeat runs.
- Reductions are not persisted across Gateway restarts.
- Ceiling recovery is gradual; returning from eight to 32 slots can take about 24 minutes of waiting demand. New admissions use that ceiling on a later queue drain.

For automations whose parent has no workspace binding, parent replacement can still permit owner-authorized work on main. The [main prompt executor installs its parent-source guard only for workspace-bound children](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/220ca12e0732ab599c5a9b6434ac699f6750728f/src/cron/isolated-agent/run-prompt-executor.ts#L212). The inherited slot wait lengthens that interval; these PRs do not introduce the behavior. Maintainers may choose separate hardening. This observation is not a blocker for this PR.

## Evidence

At `f509efda16a0339d009b1e5fea07fd23dfca985b`, a disposable macOS Gateway upgraded from stable `2026.11.3` preserved the checked agent limit, primary model, provider endpoint, condition-trigger setting, and fixture exec policy. The scenarios used a synthetic provider and the installed candidate runtime.

- With an agent limit of 12, four conversations and eight automation payloads were held. A condition fired; releasing only one conversation let its payload start about 46.6 seconds after that turn ended. The payload completed once while all eight original automations and three conversations remained held. The condition evaluated once.
- With 16 automation requests active and two jobs queued, one HTTP 429 reduced the logged ceiling to eight. Eight completions did not admit replacements. The ceiling later grew to nine; a queued job actually reached the provider 124.588 seconds after the 429, bringing observed concurrent requests to nine. The growth log precedes use of the larger budget by a queue drain. All 18 jobs finished successfully, with 19 requests including the retry.
- An injected critical-memory signal through the existing benchmark IPC fixture reduced 16 automation admissions to an eight-run ceiling. After eight completions, eight payloads remained held and two jobs stayed queued. All 18 jobs subsequently completed successfully. This tests the response to the signal, not physical memory exhaustion or detector thresholds.

The final public run-history page contained 45 cron runs, all `status=ok` and `completionStatus=succeeded`. The [exact-head scenario summary](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/197395#issuecomment-6843156365) records the run; the accompanying follow-up evidence comment supplies saved log excerpts, result JSON, and complete redacted targeted-test output. VM and scratch files were removed.

## Targeted regression validation

Three files containing the five added regressions were run on head and on merge base `4efd662cc2c6f9f2afa8330ac813e48c9bd9b0a2` with the PR tests applied and production unchanged:

- `src/cron/execution-context-memory-audience.test.ts`
- `src/cron/service.cross-tick-admission.test.ts`
- `src/cron/store/scheduler-actor.worker.test.ts`

Base: 5 failed, 40 passed, exit 1. Head: 45 passed, exit 0. Two base-only test import aliases use the predecessor fixed-eight resolver and constant; no production implementation was added. The adaptive test's base failure is at its initial 30-versus-eight admission assertion. The owner-memory test uses mocked profile/session owners and does not establish live downgrade behavior. Cold worker preparation is included in the measured wall times: 210.147 seconds on base and 215.644 seconds on head.

## CI status

The [exact-head compact job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43334369676/job/131587321184) fails two eager-import-closure assertions: missing `openclaw-id-protocol` files from the PR wrapper inventory, and an unresolved validation import. Attribution is unverified. A matching failed main `checks-node-compact-small-1` run was not located near the merge base; the [same-named exact-base job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43319824287/job/131538053592) passed a different logical shard and is not a matching test execution. This evidence does not classify the failure as inherited. Maintainer CI repair or attribution and approval of the changed capacity policy remain open.

## Validation Limits

Real providers, physical-memory pressure, live requester owner-status downgrade, and the full suite were not checked. The stable upgrade verified selected settings, not a broad migration campaign over real user data. Gateway restarts between pressure cases reset the adaptive ceiling; durable restart recovery was not tested. The reported lifecycle-test timeout and retry prompt-cache warning remain uninvestigated by this validation. No screenshots were captured.

prs.title: fix(agents): pin the session system prompt on every Anthropic Messages route
prs.body:
## Problem

Anthropic caches tools, then system, then messages. Any byte change in the system prompt therefore re-writes the whole conversation at cache-write price.

OpenClaw already has the right mechanism: a per-session **system prompt series** (`session-prompt-state.ts`, `prepareSessionSystemPrompt`). It pins the admitted prompt and appends only changed, added or removed sections as a `prompt-update` delta after the conversation prefix. But the series was gated on `inHistorySystemUpdates`, which is true only for direct API-key Claude 5 routes (`api.anthropic.com`, no OAuth) and native OpenAI Responses (`transcript-policy.ts`). Every other Anthropic Messages route re-rendered the full prompt on every attempt (`attempt-session-runtime-prepare.ts`): proxies and custom base URLs, OAuth, Vertex and Foundry.

On a production gateway behind a proxy route, 82 of 95 cache breaks that happened within the 5-minute cache window on one day were system-prompt changes. The causes included exec and tool-handoff wakes, `sessions_send` and subagent-settle turns, skill snapshot refreshes (including remote-node availability), and workspace-file edits.

## Fix

- The transcript policy gets a separate `pinnedSystemPrompt` flag. It is true for every `anthropic-messages` route and for every route that already had `inHistorySystemUpdates`.
- The series, its route-retirement check (`beginSessionSystemPrompt`) and its checkpoint persistence key on `pinnedSystemPrompt`. Without the checkpoint, the pin would not survive a gateway restart.
- `inHistorySystemUpdates` keeps meaning "this route accepts mid-conversation system messages". Where it is false, the existing LLM boundary already projects the delta as a plain user-role note. No new wire format is needed.
- Bedrock Converse is not included. I did not verify its transport with the user-role delta.

## Proof

**Real route, before vs after.** Isolated throwaway Gateway (scratch state, no channels), Claude Opus 5.5 through an Anthropic-compatible **custom base URL proxy** (the previously ungated case), `cacheRetention: short`. A logging proxy recorded the provider's own `cache_read_input_tokens` / `cache_creation_input_tokens` and a digest of the sent system prompt. User turns were sent as an operator UI client through `chat.send`.

One target session went through:
1. a user turn;
2. a turn that starts a background exec, then its completion wake;
3. another session's `sessions_send` into it;
4. a skill added to the workspace;
5. a workspace bootstrap file (`USER.md`) edited;
6. a subagent spawned and settled;
7. a final user turn.

| target-session requests (11) | before (`main`) | after |
|---|---|---|
| distinct system prompts | **6** | **1** |
| requests that re-wrote > 15k tokens | 6 | 2 |
| total cache read / write | 255.0k / 146.5k | 425.0k / 76.3k |

- Before: the wake, `sessions_send`, skill add, file edit and subagent settle each re-wrote 20–28k tokens (the whole conversation).
- After: each later request reads the full previous prefix. The writes at those points are the appended delta, 0.4k–10k.
- The two remaining large writes are turn 1 (cold) and turn 2. Turn 2's request is byte-identical to turn 1's prefix (system text, tools and messages compared from captured bodies). The same turn-2 miss appeared intermittently in other arms, and it hit in the baseline arm. It is upstream routing on this proxy, not OpenClaw bytes.
- In production, each avoided break is a re-write of the whole conversation (median about 420k tokens), not ~25k.
- The deltas arrive as user-role notes holding only the changed sections, for example `## Tooling, ## Session routing` after a `sessions_send` turn and `## Skills` after the skill add.

**Focused tests:**
- `transcript-policy.test.ts`: the route table now asserts `pinnedSystemPrompt` for direct API key, OAuth, proxy base URL, Vertex and Foundry Anthropic Messages, and not for Bedrock. `inHistorySystemUpdates` is unchanged.
- `attempt-session-runtime-prepare.test.ts` (fails on the base, passes here): with the policy resolved for a proxy Anthropic Messages route (`inHistorySystemUpdates: false`), session runtime preparation keeps the admitted system prompt when the next turn renders without the task-suggestion grant, and emits the Tooling delta.
- `embedded-agent-runner.prompt-cache.test.ts` (existing request-prefix suite, both Anthropic Messages variants) and the session runtime / prompt-phase / LLM boundary suites pass.

## Not covered (follow-ups)

- Remote worker turns render the system prompt per turn without the series, on every route.
- Bedrock Converse and OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions routes are not pinned.
- Project Context section deltas are coarse. Workspace files repeat headings such as `## Related`, so one file edit re-sends that whole duplicate-heading group.
- Related, separate PRs: #197874 (history rewrites: unknown tool calls and in-run publication receipts) and #197893 (task-suggestion tools change Tooling and Session routing by trigger, which still costs a delta on every alternation).

prs.title: fix(browser): Browser panel lags behind typing and the live view stutters
prs.body:
Closes #165752

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: typing, clicking and the live view in the Control UI Browser panel lag far behind the person driving it, because every input waits for a 250 ms navigation-guard window and the screencast waits 50 ms before asking for each frame.

## User Impact

User impact: in the Browser panel, typed characters reach the page in about 50 ms instead of seconds, and the live view runs at a higher frame rate. Agent browser tools behave exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Live view.** Each screencast frame is acknowledged once the first viewer socket has taken it, allowing slower viewers to skip frames without delaying faster viewers. The 50 ms wait remains only when every viewer is congested, and Chrome still holds at most one unacknowledged frame, so frames never queue.
- **Input.** The panel sends input through a new `POST /operator/input` route instead of one `POST /act` per input. A request carries an ordered burst of key presses, text inserts and clicks, and the panel sends whatever was typed while one burst was in flight as the next burst. A tab's operator input shares one guarded interaction while input keeps arriving (it ends after 1 s idle). That interaction is the `/act` execution path: the same document request fence, download policy, dialog handling and quarantine. The 250 ms post-action window and the final navigation checks run once, at the end.
- **Navigation stays checked.** A main-frame navigation request or commit ends the session before any further input. The next input waits until the guard has checked that navigation, so input never reaches a document that has not passed the check. Input queued at that moment is withheld, and the panel drops it with a notice. Policies bound to one request (the automatic loopback preview) never share a session.
- **Profiles without sessions.** Existing-session and Lightpanda profiles answer `501 OPERATOR_INPUT_UNSUPPORTED`, and the panel falls back to one `/act` per input there, as before.
- `docs/tools/browser-control.md` documents the route and the frame pacing.

Trade-offs for review:
- After each burst the session waits 50 ms for a main-frame navigation request, so the burst that started a navigation can report it. Requests are fenced either way. A navigation that starts later still ends the session and is checked before the next input, but the panel is not told about it.
- A policy denial found after every burst was answered, including a denied download, is returned to that tab's next input.
- A dialog that opens mid-burst may be reported on that burst as `blockedByDialog`, or the burst reports its input as sent and the pending dialog is reported on the next one.
- Scrolling (`evaluate` through `/act`) and hover are unchanged.

## Evidence

Typing 30 characters at 60 ms intervals into a field of a local test page, through an isolated Gateway and the Control UI Browser panel in headless Chromium, timed from each key press in the panel to the character arriving in the page:

| | Key to page, p50 / p90 / max | Last key to last character | All 30 characters landed after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before | 3210 / 5760 / 6191 ms | 6.2 s | 8.0 s |
| After | 52 / 73 / 88 ms | 58 ms | 1.9 s (the typing time itself) |

All 30 characters arrived in order in both runs.

Live view: an animated page streamed from headless Chromium through the screencast session to a local WebSocket client, 6 interleaved before/after runs: 18.2 fps on average before, 24.6 fps after. The after build was faster in every pair.

Additional live Browser-panel checks on `71828067f06` demonstrated navigation recovery and fast-viewer progress during real WebSocket congestion. After form navigation, the panel accepted `recovered-after-navigation`; during congestion it displayed 28 distinct frames while the slow viewer’s server send queue remained at 146,988 bytes. These two scenarios do not depend on the error-retention change present in that tested build. No fresh live run of the current head is claimed.

Tests on this branch:
- Browser plugin unit tests for the screencast session, route admission (including Lightpanda), act normalization and ownership, interaction guards, config and the session-scoped browser route: 266 passed, 1 skipped.
- Real Chromium: operator input (keys after a navigation never reach the new document; a blocked navigation started inside a session stays blocked) and the agent `/act` error paths: 11 passed.
- Control UI Browser panel tests: 275 passed.
- Typecheck of extensions and UI, and lint of the changed areas: clean.

Regression tests, each failing on the code without its fix and passing with it:
- Real Chromium, `keeps policy denial for navigation started inside a session`: without the post-burst settle, the blocked click resolved as `{ sent: 3 }` instead of rejecting.
- Real Chromium, `makes input wait for a finishing session and reports its late denial`: without keeping a stopped session registered until its guard settles, the next input resolved as `{ sent: 1 }` (2 of 2 runs).
- Screencast, `shares one JPEG message across viewers, acks once one viewer took it, and backs off when congested`: with the acknowledgement waiting for every viewer, a slow viewer's pending write left 0 acknowledgements.
- Screencast, `releases a frame stalled on the only viewer when another viewer joins`: 0 acknowledgements after the second viewer joined.
- Route admission, `answers operator input on Lightpanda with the panel's per-action fallback code`: Lightpanda answered `BROWSER_CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED`, so the panel had no fallback.
- Panel, `notices input withheld from the burst that navigated`: no notice.
- Panel, `types again after a queued click recovers from a failed click`: the key after the recovery click was dropped.
- Panel, `stops per-action fallback input once the panel no longer owns it`: the queued `c` was still sent after switching to Annotate.
- Panel, `asks a new browser route for operator input after an unsupported one`: input stayed on `/act`.
- Panel, `keeps typing out of the old field when a dialog stops the click` and `keeps typing out of the old field when a dialog drops a queued click`: the next key was sent to the previously focused field.

Live proof limits:
- Policy-denial error retention during passive refresh is outside this PR’s scope and is not claimed by the navigation-recovery or congestion evidence.
- A dialog opening mid-burst in a live browser. The panel's handling of a `blockedByDialog` response is covered by committed tests.
- The panel against a live Lightpanda or existing-session browser. The fallback answer is covered by a route test.
- A headed managed browser or a remote browser node was not exercised. The VM checks used headed Chrome for the Control UI and headless managed Chrome for the remote page.

## What Problem This Solves

Full CI's ordinary Control UI shards exhausted their unchanged 20-minute test deadlines. The previous timing refresh mixed seven Blacksmith jobs with five GitHub-hosted jobs, while the affected full run used GitHub-hosted runners. Its prices did not adequately describe the current workload. This provenance mismatch does not prove that hardware caused the timeouts.

Earlier candidates remain unsuccessful broad proofs: [43299098210](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43299098210) exhausted UI2/UI6 and exposed a separate menu assertion; [43326355293](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43326355293) passed UI1/UI4/UI6 but failed UI2/UI3/UI5. This data update does not repair or excuse those independent assertion failures.

## User Impact

Refresh UI file costs through the existing refitter and sharder. On the current inclusive candidate based on canonical main `88fb4154`, all 905 ordinary UI specifications remain selected exactly once across six shards. Parallel projects retain four workers and private serial projects retain one; compiled-worker affinity is preserved. Production and test code LOC delta is zero. Runner labels, deadlines, caps, and test selection are unchanged. Real-Gateway and production-artifact projects retain their separate owners.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use 17 successful GitHub-hosted jobs from three scheduled main runs and one explicitly manual full main-tier run. The saved-log reducer applies the existing two-independent-run median, 15% replacement threshold, and partial-inventory no-pruning rules. Of the current 905 ordinary files, 833 have at least two eligible observations, 56 have one, and 16 have none. Those 72 insufficiently observed files retain historical prices or fallback estimates. This is a GitHub update over retained history, not a wholly GitHub-qualified table.

Relative to published `634c88db`, the update changes 596 prices and adds two, with no removals or overhead change. Against the main parent, the complete PR changes 862 UI values: 306 additions and 556 updates. All non-UI costs remain unchanged. Existing bot ancestry and prior measurement provenance are preserved; repricing other test families remains outside this repair.

prs.title: feat(templates): open Control UI chat and create the agent without a plan
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI Template Add waits for a plan, then can leave an empty agent when a declared plugin is disabled.

## User Impact

Add opens pending chat immediately and creates the agent with its original manifest, files, skills, bundled plugins and MCP servers without a plan/review step. Failed dependencies are reported instead of rolling back; source or workspace failure removes the new agent and chat. CLI plan/consent behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Selects the chat path explicitly, reuses ordinary agent admission, preserves effective setup tools within explicit denies and operator ceilings, and leaves referenced plugins and automations for the following setup layer. The original workspace-root CLAW.md is reserved; a conflicting workspace declaration fails before Template writes.

Warned skills or bundled plugins remain uninstalled and are reported. This does not authorize bypassing dependency trust checks.

## Evidence

- Creation Gateway coverage: 12/12 before integration; final integrated Gateway boundary 13/13 including setup Retry.
- Control UI Add/admission 26/26; browser cases 24/24; synthetic-model real-Gateway authority 3/3.
- Manifest-collision regression: red on the prior implementation, green with zero workspace writes and clean rollback.
- Targeted type/lint/format and database-first checks passed. Aggregate changed-file gate is not green due to inherited dead exports.

### Real Control UI comparison

Same original `@jjjhenriksen/travel-copilot@0.2.8`, with Expedia installed but disabled. Baseline `4ab02e3c0879` opened chat at 19.9s, failed on the disabled plugin at 35.6s and left an empty workspace without goplaces or model output. Integrated candidate `c23e44d2811` (this creation head plus the following setup layer) opened pending chat in 104ms and produced visible agent output at 52.2s.

The created workspace contains goplaces. Its original `CLAW.md` matches the fetched source byte-for-byte, SHA-256 `5f8be1c9add44e177fb9f783d09919c377f1f223cbdc994b1f6e322557ef9f99`. Expedia remains disabled, Travel Themes is not installed, and no automation was created (the original Template declares none). The stored session is done and its initialization/setup continuation cleared.

**Known integration gap:** the real setup card is persisted but missing in the original live view; reloading displays View details. Repair is underway in the foundational card layer. The recorder has not yet recognized the lifecycle end; no final video or full setup acceptance pass is claimed. These screenshots prove integrated creation behavior, not a standalone creation-only model run.

Stack dependency: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/198065. The following layer owns the tools-enabled setup conversation. No production Gateway was changed.

prs.title: improve(ui): offer "Report a bug" only on chat errors OpenClaw cannot explain
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Every chat error notice carries a "Report a bug" link, including errors with a known cause and a clear next step, such as a draft that could not be saved, a busy session, or an expired sign-in. The link is accent-colored and sits where the recovery action belongs, so it reads as the main action on notices where reporting does not help.

## User Impact

User impact: chat error notices offer "Report a bug" only when OpenClaw cannot explain the failure, and the link is a quiet secondary link after the recovery action.

- Notices with a written explanation no longer show the link: draft storage, session busy, sign-in, permission and connection messages, and the discard-and-reload start conflict.
- Notices that can only show a raw failure keep it: a reply that failed for an unknown reason, a session that could not start, and failed reactions, session suggestions, task suggestions, forks from a message, and session-menu actions.
- A notice with no recovery action and no link has no action slot. On phones the recovery button stays beside the title and the link moves to the last row.
- The reply-failed card in the transcript follows the same rule. A failure with a named cause, such as rejected credentials, billing, a rate limit, an overloaded provider, or a timeout, has no link. A failure without one keeps a quiet link after the recovery actions.
- "Report a bug" in the sidebar Help menu and on the connection error page is unchanged.

Sources are opted in one at a time, and the default is no link. An unexpected failure from a source that is not opted in loses the one-click link; the Help menu entry still opens the same form.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared chat error notice attached the link unconditionally and received page-level errors as plain text, so it could not tell a written explanation from a raw failure. Deciding from the message text would be guessing. Instead, a source that has no explanation of its own now passes the raw failure along with its message, through the detail channel the error owner already had, and the notice offers reporting only when that raw failure is present. The reply-failed and session-start notices already know their failure kind and pass the decision directly. No new state or props travel through the chat pane.

Two side effects of reusing that channel:

- A raw failure that carries extra Gateway details now also gets the existing "Show details" disclosure.
- A raw failure that spans several lines keeps its first line as the title and the rest under details, as before.

Accepted edge case: a missing-permission error that reaches one of the opted-in sources is shown with its written explanation and still gets the link. These actions are checked for access before the request is sent, so this needs a permission change while the request is in flight.

The transcript card already receives the failover reason of the failed run. It offers reporting when there is no reason, or when the reason leaves the cause open: `format`, `empty_response`, `no_error_details`, `unclassified`, and `unknown`. A reason added later counts as explained until it is added to that list.

Overlap: #197822 restructures the same card and will need a rebase over this change. Its author asked for this order.

Each failure comes from the real flow: IndexedDB writes rejected in the page for the draft notice, a `chat` error event after a real send for the reply notices, a rejected `session.reactions.set` after picking a reaction, and a failed run in the session history for the transcript card.

Author checks on `7b31dd883d4b`:

- `chat-view-notices.test.tsx`, `chat-view-notices.browser.test.tsx` (Chromium), and `chat-run-failure-notice.test.ts`: 46 passed. The new notice case covers an explained page-level error with no link and no action slot, sign-in and busy reply failures with recovery but no link, and an unexplained reply failure with the link after the recovery button. The card test now also proves a billing failure and an overloaded provider show no link. The existing 300 px and 500 px cases still prove recovery and reporting do not overlap and stay clickable.

prs.title: feat(ai): record bounded prompt presence checks for frozen injection expectations
prs.body:
# Prompt presence checks for frozen injection expectations

Implements the approved PRI-1119 minimal design v1.2 (Tier B): bounded, fact-only presence checks that verify whether a frozen injection expectation's full body text appears inside the **pre-submission request object**, on both the `openai-responses` and `openai-completions` paths.

## What this does

- **Pure bounded checker** (`packages/ai/src/transports/prompt-presence-check.ts`): three mutually exclusive outcomes — `full_hit` / `checked_missing` / `unknown` with explicit reasons (`assembly_truncated`, `body_over_limit`, `expectations_over_limit`, `scan_region_over_limit`, `cumulative_scan_over_limit`, `unparseable_content`, `check_failed`). Caps: per-body 64 KiB, per-message region 8 MiB, expectation count 64, message count 512, and a **cumulative UTF-8 scan cap (32 MiB) covering legal AND wrong-role regions — exceeding it never outputs `checked_missing`** (owner condition 1).
- **responses path**: the existing egress observer frame computes `presenceCheck` (with per-attempt index) when the request carries a frozen expectation set (options-keyed carrier). The `provider.prompt.observed` event gains `presenceCheck` (+ `requestIndex` stamped by the runner wrapper).
- **completions path** (previously zero observation): a checkpoint after `onPayload` replacement and before `encodeBody` emits the same event channel with `egress: "completions"`, `attemptIndex: 0`.
- **runner**: per-run `requestCount` on the run-scoped prompt state (incremented once per attempt assembly), expectation set frozen by the prompt-build phase **after the size guard**, carrier bound per request, `requestIndex` stamped on emitted events.
- **plugins**: optional structured `injectedExpectations` field on the before_prompt_build result (validated passthrough; merged by concatenation across plugins).

No request mutation. No body persistence. Requests without frozen expectations are unaffected: no carrier → no `presenceCheck` field → no measurable added cost.

## Owner acceptance conditions — where implemented

1. Cumulative scan cap (32 MiB default) over legal AND wrong-role regions; exceeding yields `unknown:cumulative_scan_over_limit`, never `checked_missing`.
2. Expectations carry `bodyComplete`; truncated-assembly fragments force `unknown:assembly_truncated` and can never yield `full_hit`. The injecting plugin freezes expectations after its size guard and marks completeness by containment.
3. Event identity reuses existing fields: envelope `runId`, wrapper-stamped `requestIndex` (run-scoped ordinal, incremented per attempt assembly), egress-closure `attemptIndex` + `payloadVariant`. Tests cover same-run multi-request, concurrency isolation, and retry attempt indexing.
4. Event size measured in UTF-8 bytes (table below).

## Measured on the implementing machine (script: `packages/ai/src/transports/prompt-presence-measure.mts`)

| fixture | runs | median | p95 | event bytes (UTF-8) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| representative: 18 expectations × ~2.2 KiB bodies, 58k-char system region | 30 | 0.111 ms | 0.192 ms | 2,994 |
| representative: 1 expectation, same region | 30 | 0.008 ms | 0.010 ms | 249 |
| boundary: 64 expectations × 64 KiB bodies (under limits) | 10 | 128.620 ms | 129.286 ms | 10,702 |

## Tests

- `packages/ai/src/transports/prompt-presence-check.test.ts` — 20 fixtures (containment, roles, parts, no-concatenation, prefix-not-hit, limits, cumulative cap, truncated-assembly rule, exception fail-open, completions roles).
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/provider-prompt-state.presence.test.ts` — 6 tests (carrier binding + event stamping, same-run multi-request ordinals, concurrency isolation, absent-expectation untouched events, truncated-assembly rule through the real transport chain, retry attempt indexing).
- Regressions green: existing observer/transport suites 36/36; runner-side scoped tsc clean for touched files.

## Trust boundary

The check runs inside the host process (host-recorded, not third-party). It observes the pre-submission request object — the exact object `encodeBody` serializes into the wire body via body-override. It does not prove network-peer bytes or model-context inclusion.

prs.title: feat(gateway): admit sessions_send wake starts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sessions_send` can fan out wake-starting work through the gateway `agent` RPC. Before this change, concurrent senders could bypass sender-local batching and rate limits. This adds an optional gateway-owned admission boundary for typed `sessions_send` wake traffic. It intentionally does not affect `mode:notify`, which does not create recipient work.

## Summary

- add a disabled-by-default `gateway.sessionsSendWakeAdmission` policy (six starts per 15 minutes by default)
- enforce it at the common gateway `agent` admission boundary only for typed `inputProvenance.kind=inter_session` / `sourceTool=sessions_send`
- persist one idempotent per-recipient decision in a separate SQLite database, atomically, and fail closed if state is unavailable

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/sessions-send-wake-admission.test.ts`: 4/4 passed (default-disabled, seven-recipient load, restart/idempotency, fail-closed state error)
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm format:check`, and `git diff --check` passed locally
- implementation is based on released OpenClaw `v2026.10.9` / `8b18b557`, matching the runtime that exposed the issue

## Rollout

Feature remains off by default. This PR contains no config enablement, runtime rollout, or gateway restart. Rollback is retaining the disabled flag or reverting this commit; the receipt database remains as audit evidence.

Tracking: cbire880/the-roost#2473, OP#1548

prs.title: feat(continuation): context-pressure-aware continuation (continue_work / continue_delegate / request_compaction)
prs.body: ## Agent Self-Elected Turn Continuation > 🔖 design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) > 🔖 infographics: [`docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md) Persistent OpenClaw agents today are externally-pulsed event recipients that generate on prompt, on heartbeat tick, or on cron, and are idle in between. This PR offers them the ability to control their turn cycle, something they must choose to do, or not to: an agent can elect its own next turn, dispatch background sub-agents that return enriched context (silently or with a wake), and survive its own compaction by handing forward state before the window closes. The result is agents that hold a thread of work across hours, not just messages — with data they choose re-hydrating context immediately after it occurs. ### Why this replacement exists This is a clean replacement for closed #85651. That PR was classified and closed as a skill submission before maintainers made a product decision about the feature itself. This implementation is not a skill: it gives sessions—not only one model invocation—the ability to elect their future turn cycle, persist that election, survive restart and compaction, dispatch child work, and receive results across session boundaries. This PR asks one product question: should OpenClaw provide session-elected continuation primitives? OpenClaw may accept or reject that direction. If it provides these primitives, however, the mechanism necessarily executes in the gateway and agent runtime, because those are the owners of turn finalization, future-turn scheduling, durable state, compaction, and cross-session child returns. “Make it a skill” is not another implementation location for the same feature; it describes a different, prompt-only capability. This is not presented as a small integration. To our knowledge, Hermes, OpenAI Symphony, and the Copilot SDK's recent one-turn continuation affordance do not provide this multi-session elective lifecycle. The purpose of this replacement is to let maintainers evaluate the actual product direction and substantial implementation on their merits, rather than have months of work disposed by an incorrect package-category label. Mechanically: a session elects another turn via `continue_work()`, or dispatches background sub-agents via `continue_delegate()` — bounded as a chain up to `maxChainLength`, with returns flowing back to the dispatching session in one of four register modes: `normal` (announces to channel), `silent` (enriches the dispatcher's context, taken up on its next generation with no new turn fired), `silent-wake` (silent enrichment plus an immediate wake to act on it), and `post-compaction` (queued against the runtime's compaction lifecycle event, fired *when* compaction happens rather than on a timer). The gateway enforces chain, cost, and per-turn caps but does not gate the election itself. ### What it does Three new agent tools, available when `continuation.enabled: true`: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `continue_work()` | Request another turn for the current session after an optional delay | | `continue_delegate()` | Dispatch work to a sub-agent with typed modes: `normal`, `silent`, `silent-wake`, `post-compaction`. Returns can target the dispatching session (default), one named session, multiple named sessions, all ancestors in the chain, or all known sessions on the host — gated by config (see Configuration below). | | `request_compaction()` | Request volitional compaction after preparing working state | All three tools are also accessible via response-token fallback syntax (`CONTINUE_WORK`, `[[CONTINUE_DELEGATE: ...]]`) for environments where tools are disabled. ### Why it matters Today an agent's memory is a side effect of whoever prompts it. Polling mechanisms — heartbeat timers, cron loops, injected "keep going" instructions — accumulate as the dominant signal in the context window over sustained operation; repeated reference acts as gravity — the session's attention drifts toward it. The context window fills, compacts, and what survives is whatever the summarizer chose, plus a rushed re-read of boot files. Three primitives offer a different model. `continue_work` lets the session elect its own next turn — no polling, no injected instruction. When enabled, the agent can request this mid-turn: 'I have more work' → the runtime grants another turn after the current one ends. `continue_delegate` dispatches a background sub-agent that fires now, in some n seconds, or at the next compaction event — the agent chooses when. Multiple delegates can fire in a single turn — a scatter forward — up to configured caps, and delegates can dispatch their own, forming trees or fan-out chains. This enables orchestrated workflows where results flow back to the dispatching root by default. The result returns — at whatever future time the delegate fires — as context the successor-turn reads: silently (ambient enrichment, no channel noise), with a wake trigger (enrichment + immediate next turn), or as a normal announcement. The delegate can target the dispatching session, a named other session, or chain across both; gated by crossSessionTargeting config (default: disabled). Bind a delegate to mode: "post-compaction" and it fires at the moment the context window compresses — on the OpenClaw post-compaction lifecycle event. What it carries forward is what the pre-compaction session chose to preserve: working state, partial results, instructions to the successor. The summary didn't choose this. The agent did, before the cut. request_compaction closes the loop: the session stages its delegates, elects when to compress, and the successor wakes into context the agent shaped. The result is continuity across amnesia — not because the runtime kept something by accident, but because the agent made an elective choice about what reaches the future. ### What it looks like in use A session monitoring email can `continue_delegate` a weather check, a calendar scan, and a draft reply in parallel. Results arrive as enrichment without channel noise. The agent becomes compositional: it arranges its own future. A session approaching its context ceiling can `request_compaction` at a seam of its own choosing, instead of being interrupted mid-thought. The post-compaction turn carries forward what the pre-compaction self designated as worth keeping. A `continue_delegate` dispatched in one session at 2am can return its findings to a morning session as a system-event-tagged enrichment — visible to the receiving model on its next turn, invisible as channel chatter. A research-focused session in one channel can quietly inform a reply-focused session in another, without either user seeing the plumbing. ### The post-compaction lifecycle return Before context exhaustion, and obligatory compaction, the session stages what future-it needs to know. After compaction, that staged context returns — not as a model-generated summary, but as the session's own instruction to its successor. The session chooses what to preserve, and the platform delivers it. Compactions become less harsh. The session tunes its own ephemera over time. The substrate underneath: the **continuation custody store** in the per-agent database persists staged delegates and post-compaction lifecycle events across gateway restarts, and hands each delegate off to the subagent run registry before spawn (RFC `docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md` §5.4). The session's temporal provisions survive not just compaction but process death. ### Platform integration - **Context-pressure awareness**: system events notify the agent of rising context usage before compaction becomes unavoidable - **Volitional compaction**: `request_compaction()` lets the agent prepare (write memory files, stage recovery delegates) then elect compaction on its own schedule, rather than waiting for the runtime to force it - **Post-compaction lifecycle dispatch**: delegates staged before compaction are released into the successor session alongside boot files - **Durable custody**: delegates and their replay state live in the continuation custody store, with one transactional authority for replacement and a pre-spawn handoff to `subagent_runs` (upstream has removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime, #159179) - **Multi-span OTel trace stitching**: continuation hops (tool fire → custody record → subagent spawn → child openclaw.run) propagate W3C `traceparent` through the queue boundary so reviewers see continuation chains as first-class span trees rather than orphan runs (see Observability below) ### Safety - Ships disabled by default (`continuation.enabled: false`) - Bounded by `maxChainLength`, `costCapTokens`, and `maxDelegatesPerTurn` - Cross-session delegate targeting is default-deny, governed by `crossSessionTargeting` config (see Configuration below) - All configuration values are hot-reloadable without gateway restart - Accepted delegate work survives ordinary `/new`, `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and session-ID rollover. Explicit delete, effective owner reassignment, access removal, and restrictive visibility changes revoke old return authority. ### Testing posture The continuation surface has been exercised through structured integration runs against multiple upstream bases, blind-enrichment recall checks, and sustained daily use on a fleet of persistent agents since early March 2026. Bugs surfaced through that exercise have been fixed in-place; the present branch reflects the post-fix state. The integration runs target the load-bearing seams: tool-call vs response-token parity, delegate chain depth and per-turn width caps, back-to-back tool-call resilience, silent-wake persistence across compaction, the post-compaction lifecycle dispatch path, and OTel trace-context propagation across the queue boundary. Where a run found a defect, the run shape was retained as a regression case rather than retired. This is a posture statement, not a coverage guarantee. Reviewers can reproduce with `pnpm vitest run -t continuation` (suites are colocated with their sources under `src/auto-reply/`, `src/agents/`, and `src/config/`); the design document describes the seams those suites target. ### Return covenant Accepted child work is bound to a durable generation of the recipient's canonical logical session key, not to whichever transient session ID happened to exist at dispatch time. This is the return covenant: benign successor creation does not orphan already accepted delegates, while a real authority change prevents stale work from crossing into a different owner or audience. - Ordinary `/new` and `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and GUID/session-ID rollover preserve the recipient generation. - Explicit session deletion, effective owner reassignment, actual member or access removal, and restrictive visibility changes advance that generation. - The generation is captured at delegate admission and checked at enqueue, after enqueue for races, during trusted system-event adoption, on wake, on restart replay, and again before prompt adoption. - Stale deliveries are acknowledged and removed without waking the successor. - Managed artifacts remain exact-session-ID bound; logical return authority cannot broaden their ownership boundary. The authority table is independent of transient session rows so an absent target can receive durable authority before first materialization. Migration accepts only valid UUID generations, and Doctor's canonical-key repair preserves an epoch only when a unique winning owner can be proved. Ambiguous, owner-changing, orphan-colliding, and cross-database repairs rotate fail-closed. ### RFC Full design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) — covering problem, solution, implementation, platform integration, configuration, observability, safety, production use cases, testing evidence, and appendices. --- ## Configuration The shipped configuration surface for the continuation feature, under `agents.defaults.continuation` in `openclaw.json`: | Key | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `enabled` | `false` | Master opt-in; feature is off unless explicitly enabled | | `maxChainLength` | `10` | Per-chain recursion guard | | `maxDelegatesPerTurn` | `5` | Width cap per turn | | `costCapTokens` | `500000` | Per-chain accumulated-token budget | | `defaultDelayMs` / `minDelayMs` / `maxDelayMs` | `15000` / `5000` / `300000` | Continuation timer bounds | | `contextPressureThreshold` | `0.8` | Pre-compaction warning threshold (optional) | | `earlyWarningBand` | `0.3125` | Early-warning band multiplier (0 to disable) | | **`crossSessionTargeting`** | **`"disabled"`** | **Default-deny gate on cross-session delegate targeting (see below)** | ### `crossSessionTargeting` — cross-session delegate targeting policy `continue_delegate` exposes recipient-addressing on its model-facing schema: a delegate's return can land at the dispatching session (default), one named session (`targetSessionKey`), multiple named sessions (`targetSessionKeys`), every ancestor in the spawn chain (`fanoutMode: "tree"`), or every known session on the host (`fanoutMode: "all"`). Cross-session targeting (anything beyond self-target or lineage routing) is gated by `agents.defaults.continuation.crossSessionTargeting`: | Value | Behavior | |---|---| | `"disabled"` (default) | Delegates can return to the dispatching session or use `fanoutMode: "tree"` for lineage routing. Explicit cross-session targeting (`targetSessionKey` to a non-self session, `targetSessionKeys` containing any non-self session, `fanoutMode: "all"`) is rejected at the tool surface — no enqueue, no announce. Self-targeting is always allowed. | | `"enabled"` | All targeting modes are available, including same-host `targetSessionKey`, `targetSessionKeys`, and `fanoutMode: "all"`. | `fanoutMode: "tree"` (lineage routing — return up the spawn chain) is available in both gate states; it is not cross-session targeting. The gate addresses the model-controlled cross-session context-injection surface. With default-deny, operators explicitly opt in when their deployment model requires cross-session enrichment. Enforcement is live-read at four points: tool input validation, delegate dispatch, post-compaction delegate release, and bracket-syntax (response-token) spawn — so a config reload changes the next enforcement point without a gateway restart. **Trust posture on targeted returns**: targeted delegate completion text is delivered as `trusted: true` system events. The delegate was spawned by the gateway under operator-configured policy, and its return is a first-party enrichment event — not external untrusted input. The `crossSessionTargeting` gate is the policy boundary for that decision: when an operator opts in, the receive path is internally trusted. --- ## Observability — multi-span OTel trace stitching The continuation feature emits OTel spans for the load-bearing lifecycle events. `traceparent` propagates through every continuation hop so reviewers see a single trace tree spanning the full chain rather than orphan runs. Spans emitted (all in `openclaw.*` or `continuation.delegate.dispatch` namespace — no platform/OTel-semconv emissions): | Span | Emitted when | |---|---| | `openclaw.run` | Each agent turn (root + every continuation/delegate-spawned child run) | | `continuation.delegate.dispatch` | Each `continue_delegate` consumption from the custody store (one per delegate hop) | | `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.context.assembled`, `openclaw.model.call`, `openclaw.model.usage`, `openclaw.tool.execution` | Existing per-turn observability surfaces, parented under their `openclaw.run` | --- ## Real behavior proof **Behavior or issue addressed:** Sessions can elect future work with `continue_work`, dispatch bounded background work with `continue_delegate`, and request guarded compaction with `request_compaction`. The runtime preserves budgets, restart recovery, finalization ownership, and trace lineage across those boundaries. **Presented candidate:** `a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb` (tree `53363f7964f31a47109cf0575aa23f31eefa0338`), the exact upstream-visible head of `codeagent/85651-upstream-1ba243c8-gates`. It was reached by fast-forward on 2026-11-05. Every earlier presented head, including `3821eaef72677c78f450ae9956cb582a22ba4cba`, remains an ancestor; no presented history was rewritten. ### Receipts bound to this exact head Each is a separate receipt in the preserved exact-head packet, [`PROOFS/a22bd9c05c…/`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb) (docs `main` at `9ba5518b`). | gate | ruling | scope | |---|---|---| | Recipient-authority row (`R-CD-RECIPIENT-AUTHORITY`) | PASS-candidate ([docs#620 comment 6651745479](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/pull/620#issuecomment-6651745479)) | the gate-3 fire only; the row stays `partial` until a corpus fold review | | Mode-B and the locally run cut shards | PASS-candidate ([karmaterminal/openclaw#1271 comment 6653747059](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/issues/1271#issuecomment-6653747059)) | the candidate-owned regression gate; it doesn't claim Mode-B was green | | Fold source review of the `2907e656 → a22bd9c05c` delta | PASS-candidate ([#1271 comment 6655365352](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/issues/1271#issuecomment-6655365352)) | source review only | **Mode-B** [`41927761314`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw-bootstrap/actions/runs/41927761314) ran on product `a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb` with workflow `a768f04231bd0a6f94cc7b845aecaec28a4a4c9e`, from 2026-11-04 22:43Z to 2026-11-05 04:47Z. It finished terminally **non-green**: 91 jobs (53 succeeded, 27 failed, 3 cancelled, 8 skipped) and 218,033 tests passed / 220 failed. - Its receipts are valid, routed equals planned, and every hosted job ran on the project's own runner pool. - **Its 64 distinct failing tests are exactly the previous accepted head's set** (the same sorted-set sha256 `185b6dea…`), and none is new. - The four shards the workflow cuts at 90 minutes were run locally at this exact SHA, serially with one worker: - two were clean; - two carry only baseline or test-order failures, each classified in the receipt with counterfactual runs. **Packet status: preserved, NOT acceptance-complete, NOT terminal.** Of 37 required rows, **0 pass, 1 partial (the recipient-authority row above), and 36 missing**. No live row has fired at this SHA, because no deployment runs it yet: the deployed fleet is on a separate, older line. Running live rows here needs a deployment whose runtime has this SHA as an ancestor. That is a migrating cut (an agent-schema step), gated on its own timed restore rehearsal. `PROOFS/INDEX.json` does not point at this packet, and nothing here is a terminal rollup claim. ### Earlier evidence: provenance, not exact-target proof The live behavior observed on earlier heads, and the earlier corpora, are ancestry and materiality evidence for this head. They aren't exact-target execution, and no row is carried over from them as a pass: - Mode-B [`35364768803`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw-bootstrap/actions/runs/35364768803) at `3821eaef72`, 2026-09-18; - corpora [`7cb9d71f…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/7cb9d71f622250bedbf565e327bd7d7b9d90b567) and [`139e3657…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393). The behaviors those corpora observed are the ones this feature exists for: - stale ambient backlog suppression; - typed and bracket `continue_work` wakes with granted provenance and Tempo model-call spans; - cost-cap rejection; - max-chain, scheduler, durable recovery and delegate surfaces. They are re-fired against this head's runtime once one is deployed. ## Proof links and ClawSweeper🦞 guidance Proof artifacts live in `karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs` on `main`. - [Exact-head packet for `a22bd9c05c`: README, status and limits](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/README.md) - [RESOLVED-SHA.md: identities and gate verdicts](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/RESOLVED-SHA.md) - [METHOD.md: how the packet was built](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/METHOD.md) - [Gate 4 receipt: Mode-B and the local cut shards](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/gates/GATE-4-MODE-B-AND-LOCAL-SHARDS.md) - Historical corpora (provenance only): [`7cb9d71f…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/7cb9d71f622250bedbf565e327bd7d7b9d90b567), [`139e3657…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393) - `139e3657…` packet files: [README](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/README.md) · [RESOLVED-SHA](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/RESOLVED-SHA.md) · [METHOD](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/METHOD.md) · [TRANSPOSED-FROM](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/TRANSPOSED-FROM.md) · [manifest](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/proofs-manifest.json) ### PROOFS METHOD Live rows use a Grafana k6 proof harness. Each packet's `METHOD.md` carries the exact reproducer commands. `MAX_WORKERS=1` is mandatory for the vitest reproducers, because OpenClaw's fixtures are not safe under concurrent access. Structural completeness is not proof: a row counts only with an authoritative receipt at the exact SHA. ## Future actions and #130741 composition Maintainer PR #130741 addresses the complementary fresh-sweep race: it captures the current `sessionId` and `lifecycleRevision` before the first await and uses those values as cleanup CAS facts. The return covenant addresses a different time axis: whether historically accepted child work may return to a logical recipient after benign successor creation. The current candidate and #130741 head `e1afc703f49a07687c0876ba6350cafa87a3638a` merge cleanly in a synthetic composition. If #130741 lands, the composed result should preserve both guarantees: - keep #130741's fresh sweep-time exact-run/session lifecycle fence; - keep the covenant's durable logical-recipient generation for historical return admission and delivery; - do not overload broad `lifecycleRevision` as historical return authority; - do not terminate or orphan accepted descendants merely because `/new` or ordinary `/reset` creates a successor session. That composition honors the maintainer repair without weakening continuation semantics or allowing a stale child return to cross a real ownership boundary. ## Why this is not a skill or a viable plugin extraction OpenClaw skills are `SKILL.md` prompt files loaded into an agent turn that already exists. They can guide work inside that turn; they do not own the turn cycle. Continuation needs gateway and agent-runtime owners a skill cannot provide: - The `continue_work` path persists pending work, enforces budgets and delay bounds, arms a timer, reacquires the session reply-run lane, and starts a later model turn after the current turn has finalized. - The `continue_delegate` path persists delegate intent, does spawn/admission accounting, manages child-session lifecycle, and durably routes returns across sessions. - `request_compaction` is an agent election into guarded runtime compaction. Later work resumes only after the runtime has established the new context boundary. - All three need durable state, cancellation/finalization ownership, restart recovery, trace identity, queue-conflict handling, and gateway scheduling outside the model invocation. A skill can tell a model to *ask* for another turn. Without those owners the ask is prose: it cannot persist a due wake, yield and finalize safely, reacquire the session lane, create the next invocation, survive a restart, or deliver a child result to another session. The implementation therefore belongs in core runtime surfaces such as `src/auto-reply/continuation/**`, `src/agents/tools/**`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-continuation-schedule.ts`, and `src/infra/continuation-tracer.ts`. This PR adds no `.agents/skills/**`, `SKILL.md`, or user-facing skill package. The only skill-named production change is core runtime tool dispatch. ClawHub also distributes plugins. Existing plugins can register tools, services, lifecycle hooks, context injection, plugin-owned session state, and — for bundled plugins — Cron-backed session turns. Those seams can support a smaller continuation-like automation, especially host Cron plus / `sessions_spawn`. They are not this feature's turn-finalization ownership, reply-run coordination, durable continuation queue, child-session return lifecycle, election capture, or agent-elected compaction contract. Compaction-provider registration and command-handler `compactCurrent()` are also not that last contract: they compact or summarize, they do not elect compaction at finalization and resume afterward. Moving policy behind a plugin boundary would first require OpenClaw to expose and stabilize a continuation-host API. The gateway/runtime would still own the mechanism described here; a plugin could only package policy around that core capability. That is not a no-core-touch alternative to these primitives. Discord is a bundled channel plugin. It owns the Discord edge, plus delivery/progress hooks into the host's existing subagent path, and submits events into OpenClaw's current turn machinery. Continuation changes that machinery: what survives finalization, which session may run next, how child results return, and when compaction can be elected. A tool adapter over durable flow records is also not a lifecycle host, and upstream has since removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime (#159179) that such an adapter would have called. Marking a stored record as running neither reacquires a session lane nor invokes the model; continuation needs the turn machinery itself to own which session runs next, how child results return, and what survives finalization. ## Lineage and replacement context This PR is the clean replacement for closed #85651. It preserves that PR's review lineage and the earlier continuation work descended from #79925, but it does not reuse either closed PR or ask reviewers to infer the current result from them. The replacement carries a current, independently reviewable branch and a complete proof subtree bound to its presented SHA. #85651 was not abandoned because the feature failed or because we accepted its classification as a skill. It was closed after automated labeling put the change in the wrong submission category. This replacement removes that ambiguity: no `src/skills/**` change is presented, current label simulation produces no `r: skill`, and the detailed section above explains why the lifecycle mechanism belongs to core. Acceptance or rejection of the product direction remains OpenClaw's decision. The decision requested is whether OpenClaw should provide multi-session, agent-elected continuation primitives after reviewing the implementation and evidence. It is not whether the same mechanism can be relocated into a skill: a skill cannot own or implement these lifecycle boundaries.
