prs.title: fix(codex): keep the Codex migration plan usable when a memory file is unreadable
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw migrate codex --from <codex-home> --dry-run --json` fails outright with `EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<codex-home>/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md'` when a single Codex memory file cannot be inspected, so the user gets no migration plan at all — skills, auth, config, and plugin items are all dropped — and the onboarding wizard silently discards the Codex migration because its `detect()` exception is only written to a debug log. One unreadable memory file should never take down the entire Codex source.

- Problem: `discoverCodexMemoryFile` (extensions/codex/src/migration/source-files.ts) treats every `fs.lstat` rejection except `ENOENT` as fatal. The two memory candidates are discovered via `Promise.all`, so a single `EACCES`/`ENOTDIR` rejects `discoverCodexSource`; `buildCodexMigrationPlan` and the wizard `detect()` have no per-source degradation channel. Sibling discovery in the same file (`discoverSourceDirs`) already tolerates unreadable directories, and plugin inventory failures already degrade into `pluginDiscoveryError` plus a plan warning.
- Solution: an `lstat` failure is now neither "absent" nor fatal. The candidate is retained carrying a `probeError`, and `buildCodexMemoryItems` emits a `status: "error"` migration item that surfaces the real errno, so the rest of the plan is still produced and the unreadable file is visible rather than silently omitted.
- What changed: extensions/codex/src/migration/source-files.ts (keep the candidate with `probeError` on non-ENOENT lstat failure, while preserving the existing symlink / non-regular-file hard rejections) and extensions/codex/src/migration/plan.ts (emit a `status: "error"` item with the errno reason).
- What did NOT change: `ENOENT` still means "no such memory file"; symlink and non-regular-file candidates are still hard-rejected (pinned by existing tests); `hasCodexSource` / `found` still treat an unverifiable memory as present; no copy is attempted for an uninspected source; no new migration item kind or status was introduced.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the minimal, behavior-preserving fix. The failed `lstat` boundary is exactly the spot where sibling plugin/source discovery already degrades instead of aborting, so reusing that pattern keeps the Codex memory path consistent with the rest of the codebase.

- Best fix: degrade at the item level using the existing `MigrationItem` `status: "error"`, rather than swallowing the error into a vague provider-level warning. The per-file errno is the information the user actually needs to fix the source.
- Alternative considered: return `undefined` (treat "unreadable" as "not found"). Rejected because it would report "Codex state was not found" for data that is present but unreadable — silent data loss, which is exactly the symptom we are fixing.
- Risk / edge cases: an `ELOOP` / `ESTALE` / `EACCES` / `ENOTDIR` memory candidate is now kept as an `error` item instead of aborting the whole plan. `apply` never selects `status: "error"` items (src/commands/migrate/selection.ts and extensions/codex/src/migration/apply.ts only act on `planned`/`conflict`), so no copy of an uninspected path is attempted. The control (readable) case is unchanged; on Windows the fix only changes error handling at the same `lstat` boundary that sibling tolerant discovery already relies on.

## User Impact

A Codex home with one unreadable or malformed memory directory now still produces a full migration plan: skills, auth, config, and plugins remain planned/migrated, and the unreadable memory file appears as a clearly labeled `error` item with its errno, instead of the whole Codex source silently disappearing. This also keeps the onboarding wizard from dropping the Codex provider when it cannot inspect a memory file.

## Compatibility

- Preserved: `ENOENT` still means "no such memory file" (no item emitted); symlink and non-regular-file memory candidates are still hard-rejected (unchanged code paths, pinned by existing `provider.test.ts` cases); `hasCodexSource` / `found` still report an unverifiable memory as present (fail-closed, unchanged); `apply`/selection still only act on `planned`/`conflict` items.
- Related: the degradation pattern reuses the file's existing tolerant sibling (`discoverSourceDirs` already `.catch(() => [])` on unreadable directories) and the provider-level `pluginDiscoveryError` channel — no new behavior shape introduced.
- Not claimed: no change to how readable memory files are read or copied; no change to non-Codex migration providers; no Windows-specific behavior added (only the same `lstat` boundary that sibling tolerant discovery already relies on).

## Evidence

### Live command verification (real `discoverCodexSource` boundary)

A `node --import tsx` probe imports the production `discoverCodexSource` and runs it against real temp filesystems (no mock of the `lstat` boundary). This is the same-worktree before/after method: the production `source-files.ts` is swapped between `origin/main` and the fix while every other file stays identical.

**Behavior matrix**

| input form | pre-fix result | post-fix result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: `memories/` mode `000` (EACCES) | `discoverCodexSource` rejects → `migrate codex` aborts with no plan | candidate kept with `probeError`; plan still built; memory item `status: "error"` carrying `EACCES` |
| B: `memories` is a regular file (ENOTDIR) | `discoverCodexSource` rejects → `migrate codex` aborts with no plan | candidate kept with `probeError`; plan still built; memory item `status: "error"` carrying `ENOTDIR` |
| C: readable `memories/` (control) | plan built, 2 memory items | identical — no behavior change |

**User-visible before/after**

| scenario | before fix (user sees) | after fix (user sees) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| one memory file unreadable (EACCES / ENOTDIR) | `migrate codex --dry-run` fails: no plan; skills/auth/config/plugins all dropped; wizard silently drops Codex source | full plan (skills/auth/config/plugins still planned/migrated); unreadable memory shown as an `error` item with its errno |
| all memory files readable (control) | normal plan | identical |

Pre-fix output (production `source-files.ts` reverted to `origin/main`):

```text
A eacces-memories THREW code=EACCES message=Error: EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/eacces/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md'
B memories-is-a-file THREW code=ENOTDIR message=Error: ENOTDIR: not a directory, lstat '<case>/notdir/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md'
C control-readable OK memories=memory:codex:MEMORY.md,memory:codex:memory_summary.md probeErrors=- | - sourceConfidence=high sourceMemoryItems=2
```

Post-fix output (fix in place, same probe shape):

```text
A eacces-memories OK memories=memory:codex:MEMORY.md,memory:codex:memory_summary.md probeErrors=EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/eacces/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md' | EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/eacces/.codex/memories/memory_summary.md' sourceConfidence=high sourceMemoryItems=2
B memories-is-a-file OK memories=memory:codex:MEMORY.md,memory:codex:memory_summary.md probeErrors=ENOTDIR: not a directory, lstat '<case>/notdir/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md' | ENOTDIR: not a directory, lstat '<case>/notdir/.codex/memories/memory_summary.md' sourceConfidence=high sourceMemoryItems=2
C control-readable OK memories=memory:codex:MEMORY.md,memory:codex:memory_summary.md probeErrors=- | - sourceConfidence=high sourceMemoryItems=2
```

### End-to-end CLI (real shipped entry, `migrate codex --dry-run --json`)

Before the fix (memories directory mode `000`), the entire command aborts:

```console
$ env -i HOME=<case>/home OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=<case>/state \
    node --import tsx --import ./probe-env.mjs src/entry.ts migrate codex \
      --from <case>/.codex --dry-run --json
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "type": "cli_error",
    "message": "EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md'"
  }
}
[openclaw] The CLI command failed.
```

After the fix, the same unreadable memories directory yields a complete plan; the two memory files are reported as `error` items and everything else is still planned:

```json
{
  "providerId": "codex",
  "summary": { "total": 6, "planned": 2, "migrated": 0, "skipped": 2, "conflicts": 0, "errors": 2, "sensitive": 2 },
  "items": [
    { "id": "memory:codex:MEMORY.md", "kind": "memory", "status": "error", "reason": "EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md'" },
    { "id": "memory:codex:memory_summary.md", "kind": "memory", "status": "error", "reason": "EACCES: permission denied, lstat '<case>/.codex/memories/memory_summary.md'" },
    { "id": "auth:openai", "kind": "auth", "status": "skipped", "reason": null },
    { "id": "auth:openai:api-key", "kind": "auth", "status": "skipped", "reason": null },
    { "id": "skill:tweet-helper", "kind": "skill", "status": "planned", "reason": null },
    { "id": "archive:config.toml", "kind": "archive", "status": "planned", "reason": null }
  ]
}
```

### Unit tests (vitest, the extension-database-workers shard)

The regression cases live in a sibling `provider.memory-probe.test-support.ts` module (the owner `provider.test.ts` is over the 1000-line cap), registered from the existing `describe("buildCodexMigrationProvider")`.

Pre-fix (production files reverted to `origin/main`, tests kept):

```console
Test Files  1 failed (1)
     Tests  2 failed | 40 passed (42)
FAIL  keeps other Codex migration items when memory probing fails with EACCES
FAIL  keeps other Codex migration items when memory probing fails with ENOTDIR
```

Post-fix (candidate):

```console
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  42 passed (42)
```

### Gates

`oxfmt --check` clean on all four changed files; `check-line-cap-ratchet` and `check-test-lines-ratchet` (slack 27) pass against the rebase target; `read_lints` clean. Typecheck is deferred to CI (the worktree `node_modules` is a symlink and the native `tsrs` binary is unavailable on this host).

### What was not tested

- Windows: only the `lstat` error-handling boundary changes, which sibling tolerant discovery already relies on for all platforms; no Windows-specific behavior was added.
- A live `migrate codex` apply (copy) of an `error`-status item: only the plan-level degradation is unit-tested; `apply`/selection already skip non-`planned` items (verified by reading the selection/apply code, not a live copy run).
- Full Gateway/CLI end-to-end beyond `--dry-run --json`: the dry-run reproduction above is a real shipped-entry run; the CI shard runs the vitest suite.
- `tsc` type-check is deferred to CI (worktree `node_modules` is a symlink and the native `tsrs` binary is unavailable on this host); `read_lints` and `oxfmt --check` are clean on the changed files.

### Environment note for the live CLI command

The `./probe-env.mjs` `--import` preload only works around a checkout-local dependency resolution issue on this machine (`unicorn-magic`'s package "exports" map is unresolved under Node 24.19.0), mapping its bare specifier to its file. It does not patch any migration code or behavior; the same shipped `migrate codex` command runs unchanged on CI.

Searched open PR topics and scanned changed-file lists for `extensions/codex/src/migration/source-files.ts`, `extensions/codex/src/migration/plan.ts`, and `extensions/codex/src/migration/provider.test.ts`. prs.title: fix(android): keep realtime Talk alive through slow audio acknowledgments
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/182602

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Android realtime Talk over the Gateway relay ends with "Talk failed: request timeout" when the Gateway's answer to one audio append takes longer than 8 seconds, on the phone and through a paired Watch.

## User Impact

User impact: a short network stall or a busy Gateway no longer ends an Android realtime Talk call. Audio past about three seconds in flight is dropped, Talk says "Realtime audio input fell behind; repeat the last part", and "Microphone input recovered; repeat the last part" once the Gateway catches up. A paired Watch shows its own shorter text ("Audio fell behind. Repeat the last part.", "Audio recovered. Repeat the last part.") in place of the elapsed time; each notice stays until the next Talk state change, as on the phone. Talk still ends on an explicit Gateway error, a lost connection, or an append left unanswered for 30 seconds.

## Why This Change Was Made

The browser relay and the Apple apps already follow this contract (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/155839, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/180572, `docs/nodes/talk/realtime-sessions.md`); https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/180572 did not reach Android. Both Android relays sent every frame with an 8 second deadline, no limit on audio in flight, and ended Talk on the first timeout.

A small `RealtimeInputAudioBudget` owns the three-second budget and the two notices, and both relays use it: the phone's append loop in `TalkModeManager` and the Watch relay in `WearRealtimeTalkController`. To release audio from the budget when the Gateway answers, `GatewaySession.sendRequestFrameForEndpoint` gains an optional success callback, and the Watch relay's send callback now reports success as well as errors. The append deadline is the 30 second liveness limit from the same contract. The Watch shows the notices from its own strings: the relay's snapshot gains an optional `notice` field (older watches ignore it), and the Watch Talk screen shows it in place of "Listening · 0:00" while listening. The notices are registered for translation; the docs page now says Android follows the same budget.

Trade-off: a Gateway that keeps the socket open but stops answering is now noticed after 30 seconds instead of 8, as https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/180572 states for the Apple apps.

## Evidence

Tested at `328b08f350f`, which merges `upstream/main` `c424ad1b0bf` into the branch. Upstream's microphone mute (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187722) now wraps each captured frame with its microphone generation, so the append loop counts `frame.bytes.size` against the budget; the change is otherwise the same as before the merge. The Before run below used the base the PR was first opened on (`315fba74e12`) and was not repeated on `c424ad1b0bf`; at the new base the failure is shown by the regression test, which fails there (see "Checks at this head"). The After run used a build of `f9a3db57d9e`, an earlier revision of this branch whose production code is the same as `7751b8a3321` (which only adds a test assertion); the stall run was repeated on a build of this head (see "Re-run at this head").

Real app: the Android app (play debug build of each side) on an Android 16 emulator, paired with an isolated Gateway (empty state directory, loopback port, no outside traffic) whose realtime Talk provider is a local fake that only counts audio. The Gateway is an older source build (2026.9.6, `19afe35954`) on both sides; the bug and the fix are in the Android client. A local WebSocket proxy between the app and the Gateway sets the answer delay: while a stall is on, it holds each `talk.session.appendAudio` answer for a fixed time and logs every 50th held answer as `hold`. Same steps on both sides: open the chat, start realtime Talk, let audio flow, turn the stall on.

Proxy lines are UTC; logcat lines are the emulator's local time (UTC+9), whose clock runs about 1.06 s behind the proxy's. On the proxy clock, Talk closes 8.0 s after the stall starts on the base and 30.0 s after it in the 40 second run.

Before (base `315fba74e12`, 12 second stall per answer):

```text
11:58:35.244Z req   talk.session.create
12:00:20.447Z hold  held=1   stallMs=12000
12:00:25.441Z hold  held=51  stallMs=12000      (every frame still sent)
21:00:27.401 (UTC+9) W TalkMode: realtime appendAudio failed: request timeout
12:00:28.448Z req   talk.session.close
screen: dialog "Talk failed: request timeout"
```

After (`f9a3db57d9e`, same phone-side code as this PR, same stall):

```text
12:17:39.337Z req   talk.session.create
12:17:48.405Z hold  held=1   stallMs=12000
screen: "Realtime audio input fell behind; repeat the last part"
screen: "Microphone input recovered; repeat the last part" (held answers start coming back, about 12 s in)
(stall turned off by the operator at about 12.7 s, not logged)
12:18:03.915Z append appends=151
12:18:13.912Z append appends=251
no talk.session.close, no append failure in logcat, Talk stays on

40 second stall per answer:
12:19:02.948Z hold  held=1   stallMs=40000
21:19:31.897 (UTC+9) W TalkMode: realtime appendAudio failed: request timeout
12:19:32.953Z req   talk.session.close
```

![Before: dialog "Talk failed: request timeout"](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/before.png)
![After: "Realtime audio input fell behind" notice during the stall](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/after-fell-behind.png)
![After: "Microphone input recovered" notice, Talk still on](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/after-recovered.png)

Re-run at this head (`328b08f350f`, its own play debug build on a wiped emulator, same Gateway, fake provider and proxy, each held answer delayed 12 s; screenshot times are the host clock, which matches the proxy's):

```text
18:31:19.005Z req    talk.session.create
18:31:34.549Z append appends=151      (50 per 5 s before the stall)
18:31:37.863Z hold   held=1   stallMs=12000
18:31:43      screen: "Realtime audio input fell behind; repeat the last part"
about 18:31:50 screen: "Microphone input recovered; repeat the last part", Talk still on
18:32:02.760Z append appends=251      (stall still on: frames past the budget are dropped, not sent)
18:32:16.855Z append appends=301
(stall turned off by the operator at 18:32:18.876Z)
18:32:30.951Z append appends=351
18:32:50.952Z append appends=551      (50 per 5 s again)
18:32:55.412Z req    talk.session.close   (the operator ended Talk)
no append failure in logcat
```

![Head: "Realtime audio input fell behind" during the stall](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/merged-fell-behind.png)
![Head: "Microphone input recovered", Talk still on](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/merged-recovered.png)

Watch display (rendered by `WearVoiceLayoutTest` under Robolectric, round 192 dp, not on a watch): before this commit the Watch shows "Listening · 0:00" while the relay reports the notice; now it shows each notice.

![Watch before: "Listening · 0:00" while input fell behind](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/watch-before.png)
![Watch after: "Audio fell behind. Repeat the last part."](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/watch-fell-behind.png)
![Watch after: "Audio recovered. Repeat the last part."](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261024-finding-android-talk-append-timeout/watch-recovered.png)

Mixed versions with the latest stable (`v2026.10.9`, `8b18b5578f6`): the new `notice` field crosses the phone-Watch protocol in both directions while one side still runs the stable release. A throwaway JUnit test (not committed) ran in `:wear-shared` of each tree and passed the real encoded bytes between them: this head's `WearProtocolCodec.encode` of a Talk event with each notice, decoded by the stable `WearProtocolCodec.decode` and `WearRealtimeTalkCodec.decode`, and the stable encoding of a listening event decoded by this head.

```text
head wrote    {"type":"event",...,"event":"talk","payload":{...,"status":"LISTENING",...,"notice":"INPUT_FELL_BEHIND"}}
stable read   WearRealtimeTalkSnapshot(attemptId=attempt-1, active=true, listening=true, speaking=false, status=LISTENING, statusText=Listening, conversation=[])
stable read   (same for INPUT_RECOVERED)
stable wrote  {"type":"event",...,"event":"talk","payload":{...,"status":"LISTENING",...,"conversation":[]}}
head read     WearRealtimeTalkSnapshot(..., status=LISTENING, statusText=Listening, conversation=[], notice=null)
```

An updated phone with a stable Watch keeps Talk working and the Watch shows its usual status text; a stable phone with an updated Watch sends no notice and the Watch shows "Listening · 0:00" as before. In the stable release both codecs already share `WearProtocolCodec.json`, which sets `ignoreUnknownKeys = true` and `explicitNulls = false`.

Upgrade from v2026.10.9 (same emulator, same isolated Gateway and proxy, no stall): the stable play debug build was installed on a wiped Android 16 emulator, paired with the Gateway (operator and node approved), and the Talk speaker set to "Muted" in Voice settings. This head's build was then installed over it with `adb install -r` (no uninstall; both builds are version code 2026080201, `firstInstallTime` unchanged, `lastUpdateTime` changed).

```text
14:57:11.572Z close  who=client code=1006   (the install stops the stable app)
14:57:14.909Z req    connect                (same device ID, no pairing request, no onboarding)
screen: Overview with Gateway "Online"; Voice settings still show "Enable speaker · Muted"
14:57:44.825Z req    talk.session.create
14:58:05.492Z append appends=201            (Talk "Listening")
```

After the upgrade the Overview's Nodes row shows "Review node access" instead of "1 online": `openclaw nodes list` on the same Gateway shows the node in `pending-reapproval` with the same 7 caps and 14 commands as approved and one changed permission, `microphone` false to true, because the microphone was granted after the node was approved and 14:57:14 was the first reconnect since; the stable build, installed back over this head, reconnects into the same `pending-reapproval` and shows the same row, so it does not come from this change.

Observed result: on the base, Talk ends 8 seconds into the stall; with this PR it drops audio past the budget with the notice, recovers when the answers arrive, and ends only after an append is unanswered for 30 seconds.

Regression tests: `TalkModeManagerTest.stalledAppendsDropInputPastThreeSecondsWithoutEndingTalk` feeds 31 frames while every append is unanswered, expects 30 appends, the fell-behind notice and Talk still on, then answers one append and expects the recovered notice and the next frame sent. It fails on the base (the 31st frame is sent) and passes with this PR. `WearRealtimeTalkControllerTest` has the same case for the Watch relay and also asserts the 30 second deadline on every append, which pins the deadline constant both relays share; it changes the relay's callback type, so it does not compile on the base. It also asserts the notice the relay sends to the Watch. `WearVoiceLayoutTest` has two new listening cases with each notice; they fail with the previous Watch screen code (the notice text is not on screen) and pass with this PR, and they check the text fits the round screen at font scale 1 and 1.3 in English and in the German locale (which shows the English text until the native locale refresh adds the translation).

Checks at this head: `TalkModeManagerTest` on the base `c424ad1b0bf` (with the test file carried over) and on this head: the new test times out at 31 appends on the base and passes here, and the other 121 tests pass on both sides. `./gradlew :app:testPlayDebugUnitTest --tests 'ai.openclaw.app.wear.*' --tests 'ai.openclaw.app.gateway.*'` (384 tests), `:wear:testDebugUnitTest` (347), `:wear-shared:testDebugUnitTest` (14), `:wear:lintDebug`, `:app:assemblePlayDebug`, `:app`, `:wear` and `:wear-shared` `ktlintCheck`, all with 0 failures; `node scripts/check-native-state-schema-version.mjs`; `pnpm native:i18n:verify`; `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet`; `git diff --check`. The broad suites run in this PR's CI.

CI: an earlier head failed `preflight` with "Native generated locale artifacts must be isolated from source changes", and `openclaw/ci-gate` failed because of it. That head carried English placeholders in 21 Watch `values-*/strings.xml` files. Since `170d5c59956` the branch leaves those files unchanged, so the native locale refresh workflow fills them; `pnpm native:i18n:verify` passes at this head.

CI at the previous head `170d5c59956` ([run 41094221772](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41094221772)): `preflight`, `android-test-play`, `android-test-third-party`, `android-test-wear`, `android-ktlint` and `android-access-native (16384, google_apis_ps16k)` passed. `android-access-native (4096, google_apis)` [failed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41094221772/job/124196671436) while installing the Android Emulator, before the emulator started or any test ran: `sdkmanager` reported "Error reading Zip content from a SeekableByteChannel" while preparing the Android Emulator package, and the job uploaded no test results. `openclaw/ci-gate` is red only because of that job. The same job passed on main in [run 41123124777](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41123124777/job/124295092007) (that run is red for unrelated Node and UI jobs). `pnpm test:ci-failed` classifies it as a new job failure with the matching main job passed and no test failure to rerun. This head's CI runs it again.

The CI seconds below come from that run's JUnit reports of `android-test-play` (phone files) and `android-test-wear` (Watch file). CI tests the PR merged into main, where `TalkModeManagerTest` has 113 tests.

| Test file | Local wall (Gradle, `170d5c59956`) | CI seconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apps/android/app/src/test/java/ai/openclaw/app/voice/TalkModeManagerTest.kt` | 0.84 s for the new test (file 17.8 s, 112 tests, Gradle `--max-workers=4` with other modules running) | 0.77 s for the new test (file 14.8 s, 113 tests) |
| `apps/android/app/src/test/java/ai/openclaw/app/wear/WearRealtimeTalkControllerTest.kt` | 0.16 s for the new test (file 1.1 s, 26 tests) | 0.01 s for the new test (file 0.38 s, 26 tests) |
| `apps/android/wear/src/test/java/ai/openclaw/wear/WearVoiceLayoutTest.kt` | two more cases in the existing layout loop (file 7.9 s, 12 tests) | file 4.5 s, 12 tests |

Simplify pass: no change. One budget type serves both relays instead of two copies of the policy, and each new test covers a different relay. Against the merge base: production +147/−15 lines, tests +135/−6, docs +2, Watch English strings +2, translation source +4.

Local review: autoreview (Codex gpt-6.1-sol, medium), base `c424ad1b0bf` to head `328b08f350f`, priority P0–P1: scoped-clean, no remaining findings.

<!-- openclaw-preflight:v1
{"v":1,"repo":"openclaw/openclaw","base":"c424ad1b0bf3de37868a9bc4645cde6f4d05419a","head":"328b08f350ff3f5be8bbf329a4968195d172543b","tool":{"name":"autoreview","version":"source-a120e048f9fc"},"completion":"complete","summary":"Threshold P1; lower priorities not assessed; status scoped-clean; accepted 0; priority-filtered 0; scope/attribution-rejected 0; missing-required 0. Self-reported; see native report."}
-->

Not covered: no real phone and no real Watch. The phone runs used the Android 16 emulator. No Wear OS device is available; the emulator host has only phone and tablet emulators (Android 13 and 16) and no Wear OS system image, and pairing a Wear OS emulator also needs the Play Store companion app and a Google sign-in on the phone side. So there are no Watch screenshots or recordings with transport logs from a live call. The phone-side Watch relay is proven by its unit test, the Watch screen by Robolectric renders, and the phone-Watch payload against the latest stable by the codec run above. The device runs used an older Gateway build (see above); the change is client-only. Non-English locales show the English notices on both the phone and the Watch until the native locale refresh translates them.

prs.title: fix(signal): inbound message bursts pile up in memory and are lost on restart
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/127383

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a burst of inbound Signal messages piles up in Gateway memory, and is lost on restart or crash, because each message waits for its own database write and drain pass before the next one is stored.

This addresses part of the linked issue: the lasting pile-up and the loss. It adds no bound on memory (see the accepted edge cases below), so the bound that issue asks for stays open there.

## User Impact

User impact: a Signal account that receives a large burst (signal-cli pulling its backlog after a reconnect, or a busy group) moves the whole burst into the durable inbound queue within seconds. Nothing is dropped. A restart, shutdown or crash right after the burst loses none of the messages OpenClaw has read. The stored backlog is then delivered in order, at the same per-message speed as a small one.

This replaces the earlier revision of this PR, which paused the WebSocket while a message was stored. The signal-cli-rest-api container drops messages for a client that does not keep up (see Evidence), so the client must keep reading at full speed and the backlog has to go to the durable queue, not back to the container.

## Why This Change Was Made

On `main`, the Signal receive handler awaits `admit` for one event and then `waitForPumpIdle`, a full drain pass, before the client hands it the next frame. That is about 55 messages per second here. Everything the socket reads in the meantime stays in the client's promise chain, in memory, until its turn.

Now:
- The container client hands each decoded frame to the receive handler in arrival order without waiting for earlier ones. A shared promise still joins them for close and failure.
- The Signal ingress groups the events that arrive while one append runs into the next `admitBatch` transaction (up to 10,000 rows, about 0.4 s). Receive settles at the durable append; claiming and dispatch run on the drain as before. If a batch append fails, its events are appended one by one, so only the event that cannot be stored (or all of them, if the store is down) rejects.
- A graceful stop first appends every event the socket already read, then stops the monitor. If that takes longer than the client's 1.5 s shutdown wait, the client log now says the ingress stop still stores the events, instead of "messages may be lost".

The per-receive `waitForPumpIdle` came from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111449, so that messages accepted just before shutdown were not abandoned before their durable claim. `monitor.stop()` already awaits the admission tail and the pump before it returns, so that shutdown guarantee stays. A row appended just before stop is not claimed in that process, but it is durable and is claimed on the next start.

Storing the whole burst needs two changes in the shared ingress:

**Lane order in admission.** Pending rows drain by `(receivedAt, eventId)`, and one batch shares one `receivedAt`. In a group lane, event ids come from different senders, so a lane's arrival order need not be its id order. Shared admission now keeps each lane's last `(receivedAt, eventId)`:
- An event keeps its arrival time unless an earlier admission had a later one, or it would sort ahead of its lane's last row; then it steps 1 ms past that row. Other lanes keep their own time.
- Stepped rows can run ahead of wall time, so the lane tails are read from the queue once, before the first admission. A restart inside the step window cannot let a new event overtake older rows of its lane.
- Matrix seeded its own arrival time from the queue at start for the same reason. That copy is removed; Matrix now uses the shared admission.
- The SDK docs for `admitBatch` say so.

**Drain cost.** Each drain pass listed every unsettled row, so with 100,000 rows stored it took about 3.3 s per pass and delivered 66 rows in 120 s. The drain now reads the backlog in pages of 100 pending rows that skip lanes it already knows are blocked (claimed, retry-delayed, or started in this pass), with every claim in the same read snapshot. A lane stays blocked for the whole pass, so lane order and FIFO are unchanged. A pass ends when it has started its limit or the backlog ends. When only blocked lanes have pending rows, the read ends after one probe per blocked lane on the existing lane index instead of walking their rows. Channels that derive lanes, supersede pending work or prioritize (Telegram, Slack, Discord and others) still read one whole snapshot, as before.

### SDK addition

`ChannelIngressQueue.listUnsettled` takes three optional fields: `pendingLimit`, `after` (a `{ receivedAt, id }` cursor in `orderBy` order) and `excludeLaneKeys`. They bound one read's pending rows; every claim is still returned. A queue may ignore them and return every unsettled row, and the drain then behaves as before. The change is additive: no existing caller or queue changes, and no schema, index or migration changes. `docs/plugins/sdk-runtime/state-and-system.md` names the fields.

Accepted edge cases, also named in the code:
- There is no bound on received events waiting in memory. While SQLite keeps up, the wait is short: the 100,000-frame burst below was durable in 7.6 s. If the state database stalls (full disk, broken database), later events wait in memory without limit, as they do on `main`. A bound would have to drop events or stop reading. Dropping recreates the loss this PR removes, and the container has no flow control: a client that stops reading makes the container drop instead (see Evidence). So the stall is made visible instead of bounded: past 50,000 waiting events (about 200 MiB of decoded messages) the ingress logs one error naming the state database, and logs again if the backlog drops and comes back. Nothing is dropped.
- Admission reads the whole unsettled queue once per monitor start, at the first admission, to seed the lane tails: about 3.3 s at 100,000 rows, nothing on an empty queue.
- While other lanes have pending rows, a page read still walks the index past the rows of a large blocked lane; only a read where nothing else is pending ends early.
- A page read excludes at most 1,000 blocked lanes, sent as one `NOT IN` list as `claimNext` already does, so it stays far below SQLite's bound-parameter limit. Past that limit the read returns rows of the other blocked lanes, and the drain skips them itself, so order is unchanged.

## Evidence

Tested at `c729be7e269` (base `upstream/main` `210d3df7f65`). The burst, crash and container measurements below were taken at `eda993f7f21`; the later changes are in admission ordering and the drain, outside the receive and store path they measure. Delivery was measured again at `2c9eb8f4977`, at the previous head `377edf16faf`, and on the base; the later commits change no drain path those runs take (the shared lane-tail read in admission, a bound on the excluded lanes that these one-lane runs stay far below, lint fixes, and a test-only change).

Harness: the plugin's real `streamContainerEvents` client and real `startSignalIngressMonitor`, writing to a real SQLite state database in an isolated state directory. Node 24, Linux x64. A local `ws` server in a worker thread stands in for the container's `/v1/receive` endpoint and sends synthetic receive frames of about 1 KB. The agent dispatch handler holds the first event, so the numbers measure receiving and storing. No Signal account.

100,000 frames, one direct-message lane: base stored 4,939 in 90 s; this PR stored all 100,000 in 7.6 s.

<details><summary>100,000-frame table</summary>

| | base | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| frames read by the client | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| durable in SQLite | 4,939 after 90 s | 100,000 after 7.6 s |
| heap growth | +129.4 MiB, still held at 90 s | peak +344 MiB during the first second, back to −1.3 MiB at 8 s |
| graceful stop | 93,207 receives failed with "Channel ingress monitor is stopped"; drain timed out, "messages may be lost" | nothing waiting |

</details>

The same run with 7 senders in one group lane: all 100,000 durable after 7.7 s, rows in arrival order, heap back to −1.3 MiB. The backlog warning fired once in both runs. The higher transient peak is the decoded burst plus the batch being written; on `main` the same burst stays in memory for as long as it takes to store at about 55 per second (about 30 minutes for 100,000). A smaller batch does not lower the peak: with 1,000 instead of 10,000 events per transaction it was +351 MiB instead of +356 MiB in a rerun at `c729be7e269`, and storing took 13% longer.

Crash (`kill -9` mid-burst, then reopen the state directory and count rows):
- This PR: killed at 1.35 s with 31,046 receives settled. After restart, SQLite has 31,046 rows, contiguous from the first frame. Every appended frame survived.
- Base: at 30.9 s only 3,000 were durable while all 100,000 had been read. After restart, 3,001 rows; the other 96,999 were only in memory.

Delivery after release (burst stored while dispatch is held for 30 s, then delivered for 120 s; every run delivered in order per lane):

| | base `210d3df7f65` | previous head `377edf16faf` | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100,000 frames, one direct lane | 6,033 stored by the end; 3,250 delivered in 120 s, the rest of the burst still in memory | 100,000 stored; 66 delivered in 120 s | 100,000 stored; 49,709 delivered in 120 s |
| 2,000 frames, 7 senders in one group lane | 2,000 in 24.3 s | 2,000 in 24.4 s | 2,000 in 5.3 s |

Delivery no longer depends on how many rows are stored. The 2,000-row run is faster too, because base and the previous head also listed every unsettled row for each pass.

Real container: `bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api:latest` (0.101) in json-rpc mode, with the signal-cli daemon inside it replaced by a synthetic JSON-RPC stand-in that sends receive notifications. The container itself drops messages. Its JSON-RPC reader hands each notification to the WebSocket handler with a non-blocking send, and drops it when the channel cannot take it:
- At 0.101, the image used here and the latest release, the receive channel is unbuffered ([`jsonrpc2.go` line 276](https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/blob/0.101/src/client/jsonrpc2.go#L276)), so a notification that arrives while the handler is still writing the previous one is dropped, however fast the client reads.
- At https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/commit/787d204e155d0c73840a615a5e90c697bacaa6f1 on `master`, the channel holds 64 entries ([line 378](https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/blob/787d204e155d0c73840a615a5e90c697bacaa6f1/src/client/jsonrpc2.go#L378)). The buffer came with https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/commit/ad0c2310325154b59b8bb5523e29a132a82326f8 (a manual receive mode) and is in no release yet. Once 64 are waiting behind the handler's write, the next one is dropped the same way.

In both versions, a client that pauses keeps the handler's write blocked, and every notification after that is dropped. That is why this PR keeps reading.

Measured through the container (0.101):
- 100,000 notifications at full speed: the container passed about 13,500 to OpenClaw on both sides. This PR stored all 13,594 it received, with +0.7 MiB heap. Base had stored 2,851 of 13,465 after 30 s, and its stop timed out with "messages may be lost".
- Paced at 20 notifications every 10 ms (20,000): the container still passed only 2,514; this PR stored all of them.
- One notification every 10 ms (2,000): this PR received, stored and delivered all 2,000 in order.

That loss is in the container and needs an upstream fix.

Regression tests (each fails on base and passes with this PR; the other tests in these files pass on both):
- `extensions/signal/src/signal-ingress.test.ts`, "appends a burst of received events in a few transactions, not one each": 50 concurrent receives, at most 2 appends. Base: `expected 50 to be less than or equal to 2`.
- `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.admission.test.ts`, "keeps each lane in arrival order across a restart when event ids do not sort that way": a stepped batch, a new monitor on the same queue, then one event in the stepped lane and one in another lane. The previous head drains `sender-a:0` ahead of the older rows of its lane; base drains the lane out of order.
- `src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts`, "starts a lane behind blocked busy lanes without reading their backlog": 5,000 rows behind a claimed head and 5,000 behind a retry-delayed head, then one row in a third lane. The pass starts only the third lane and reads fewer than 1,000 pending rows; base and the previous head read all 10,000 (`expected 10000 to be less than 1000`).
- `extensions/signal/src/client-container.websocket.test.ts`, "drains accepted and socket-buffered events before resolving shutdown", now also asserts that frame 2 reaches the receive handler while frame 1 is still held. Base: `expected [ 1 ] to deeply equal [ 1, 2 ]`.

Two guards pass on base and on this PR, and protect the new read: `src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts`, "ends a pass when the queue ignores the page bounds" (a queue that returns every row for every read still ends the pass; without the check the pass never ends), and a `src/state/sqlite-query-plan.test.ts` case that keeps the lane probe on the covering lane index.

Checks:
- The touched test files pass.
- So do the other durable-ingress suites in `src/channels/message`, and the consumers of shared admission and the drain: Signal (`extensions/signal/src`), LINE `webhook-spool`, Matrix `monitor/ingress` and Telegram `polling-session`, plus the ingress tests of the other channels that use the shared drain.
- `pnpm check:changed` against `upstream/main`: typecheck, lint, the ratchets and the guards pass. Its two red lanes come from files outside this diff on `main`: changelog attributions in `CHANGELOG/records` and unused exports in `extensions/deep-research`.

<details><summary>Test cost</summary>

Test cost (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`, local; CI seconds come from this PR's run):

| Test file | local | new test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extensions/signal/src/signal-ingress.test.ts` | 10.8 s (9 tests) | 501 ms |
| `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.admission.test.ts` | 3.3 s (18 tests) | 38 ms |
| `src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts` | 17.1 s (29 tests) | 518 ms (blocked lanes), 472 ms (page bounds) |
| `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.test.ts` | 14.9 s (41 tests) | none new; one existing scan gate now waits for a read with pending rows |

</details>

Test-lines ratchet: these regressions and guards add 120 lines, so this PR adds `config/test-lines-allocations/signal-receive-batch-order.txt` for exactly those lines and leaves the shared baseline unchanged. `scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base 210d3df7f65` passes.

Simplification: shared admission now reads its lane tails through the same unsettled read as the drain, and Matrix's own arrival-time seeding is gone (-29 lines in Matrix). Against `main`: production +394/-176 (+325/-107 ignoring the re-indented drain loop), tests +127/-7 (the ratchet counts 120), docs +3/-1. Since the previous head `377edf16faf`: production +320/-180, tests +107/-38. The remaining growth is the paged read (new `ingress-drain-backlog.ts`, 61 lines, and the bounded branch and lane probe in the SQLite queue) and the lane tails in admission.

Not covered:
- A real Signal account or a real signal-cli daemon; the container run uses a synthetic daemon stand-in.
- A full Gateway with a real agent and model: dispatch is held during the burst and is a stand-in after release, because the change is in receiving, storing and selecting rows.

prs.title: feat(ui): offer conversation starters from BOOTSTRAP.md
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

New agents need setup-specific first prompts alongside their bootstrap instructions instead of generic conversation suggestions.

## User Impact

Authors can add `conversationStarters` to `BOOTSTRAP.md` YAML frontmatter. The Control UI shows these as clickable prompts and reuses the existing agent description. Opening a chat sends nothing.

```markdown
---
conversationStarters:
  - Connect my calendar
  - Set up a repository
  - Walk me through setup
---

# First-run setup

Help the user connect their tools and choose their preferences.
```

Templates preserve this frontmatter with the first-run instructions. Missing, empty, invalid, or unreadable metadata keeps the default suggestions. Removing `BOOTSTRAP.md` restores defaults when the agent list refreshes; no config migration is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep first-run prompts with the file that owns bootstrapping rather than introducing another agent setting. The existing welcome renderer handles the selected agent, recents, incognito, phone layouts, model setup, and terminal guidance. Local file observation avoids rereading unchanged metadata on every agent-list request.

## Evidence

- Focused metadata/lifecycle, agent-list, protocol, Template Add, welcome, and draft-welcome tests pass. The browser regression fails on the base and passes with this change, including desktop, 390/320 px phones, click-only submission, incognito, and terminal retargeting.
- Production UI build, core/UI and source/UI-test typechecks, targeted lint/format/style checks, Control UI controller guard, protocol generation/native determinism/since checks, and documentation links pass.
- Independent Auto Review of the complete local candidate against `07c8e1411b79b481f2e096c52ea11a2b428f7e0d` (P0–P2): no actionable functional or lifecycle findings. Simplification keeps one metadata owner and adds no config field or separate renderer.
- **Draft: asset-budget gate remains open.** The base already exceeds the New Session JS cap: 806,988 B gzip versus 805,886 B. This change measures 807,174 B (+186 B), exceeding the unchanged 64-byte variance allowance. Startup JS is unchanged; CSS adds 59 raw bytes / 11 gzip bytes. No budget increase is included.

Screenshots from the production-built Control UI with synthetic data:

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| ![Generic first prompts](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/df5410c7-9c6d-4e61-96e3-fd6d930e8cd8) | ![Agent description and BOOTSTRAP conversation starters](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5c9dddcd-8315-4e67-9ac6-1f3799da689c) |

<details>
<summary>Phone layout and validation cost</summary>

![Conversation starters on a phone](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/255ccc5f-eead-429c-b377-4e39f9ac2da3)

Vitest file wall times: metadata 2.25 s, agent-list 48.91 s (mostly compiler setup), protocol 1.24 s, Template workspace 22.54 s (9.6 s test execution, including fresh-process recovery), welcome 2.21 s, draft-welcome 2.40 s, focused browser invocation 15.49 s. CI timing is not yet available.

Production delta against the merge base: +162/−27 lines; tests: +313/−2 lines. The remaining growth is the optional metadata path, observed-file lifetime, and shared welcome presentation; no separate renderer or config setting was added.

</details>

Contributor credit: requested and shaped by Miguel Branco.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/6912d561-4185-4e5d-9918-9eadd835c9f2)

## Worked on by

- @miguelbranco80

prs.title: fix: configure, classic onboarding and agents add save new channel tokens as plaintext in openclaw.json
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/175333

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a channel token entered in `openclaw configure`, classic onboarding (and the Gateway's default `wizard.start` flow, which runs the same setup), `openclaw agents add` or the chat's channel setup in Control UI is saved as plaintext in `openclaw.json`. The same token entered through `openclaw channels add` goes to the protected secret store since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169732. Doctor then warns about plaintext secret-bearing fields, and the prompt's plaintext option says "Stores the credential directly in OpenClaw config".

## User Impact

User impact: a new or changed channel credential entered through any of these setup paths is saved as a protected entry in the shared secret store, and `openclaw.json` keeps a `store` SecretRef, as with `openclaw channels add`. The plaintext entry option now reads "Saves the credential in the protected secret store". Existing config is not rewritten: only credentials that differ from the config the setup started from are moved, so plaintext tokens, SecretRefs and env references saved by earlier releases stay as they are.

`--secret-input-mode plaintext` (the onboarding default) still means typing the value in. Channel credentials entered that way now go to the store as well, as they already do in `channels add`.

## Why This Change Was Made

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169732 put the protected-store step inside `persistChannelPluginConfig`, the save path of `channels add` and the Gateway's channels wizard. The other setup paths run the same `setupChannels` prompts but commit config through their own writers, so they never reached it.

What changes:
- The store loop moves unchanged out of `persistChannelPluginConfig` into `storeChannelSetupCredentials` in the same module. `persistChannelPluginConfig` calls it as before, so `channels add` keeps its retained-entry notice and its authority checks.
- `configure`, onboarding, `agents add` and `runHostedChannelSetup` call it at their config commit point, comparing against the config the channel step started from. The hosted chat setup passes its existing `beforePersistentApply` and live-owner assertion, so a stale chat session still cannot write.
- The Gateway's `wizard.start` setup flow passes the wizard session's cancellation lock and liveness check into that store write, as its channels flow already does: if the client cancels after the token prompt and before the store write, the write throws and nothing is saved; once the write has begun, cancellation is refused until the next prompt. Because setup keeps prompting after the channel step, it takes that preparation lock rather than the permanent one. A setup session cannot be replaced mid-flow: setup admission rejects a second setup session as busy.
- `wizard.ts` composes that liveness check with the `assertCurrent` callback `startGatewayWizard` gives the session. Since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/183777, that callback checks the starting operator's retained grant, so a revoked device, a lost operator scope or a rotated shared credential now fails the check. Both `wizard.start` flows use it, so this also closes the same window in the existing channels flow.
- The check runs at the store writer's admission and inside the config writer's `assertBeforePublish`, the synchronous hook `config.patch` uses. Before, both flows checked once before awaiting the config commit, and an isolated Gateway showed the commit publishing after a device removal while it waited on locks. A store write already admitted settles; its entry then stays unreferenced (see the first accepted limit).
- The Control UI chat follows the same rule. `ChatWizardHost.forTurn` binds each queued chat turn to its Gateway request's `hasCurrentClientAuthority`, and the host's persistent-effect check, already used at the hosted store write, now also fails once that authority is gone. `runHostedSetup` runs the channel setup's check in the same `assertBeforePublish` hook. CLI chat has no request scope and passes no authority, as before.
- The plaintext option's hint and `docs/start/wizard-cli-reference.md` describe where the credential goes.

The store step runs where each path commits config, not inside `setupChannels`: a later prompt, a cancel or a failed check before the commit then leaves no store entries behind.

Accepted limits:
- If the config write fails after the store write (including a requester whose authority ends between the two), `configure`, onboarding, `agents add`, the Gateway setup flow and the hosted chat leave unreferenced store entries without the "retained" notice that `channels add` prints. The entries are unused and the config keeps its previous value; a retry stores the credential under a new name.
- Like `channels add`, the store step covers credential paths registered as channel secret-input targets. A plugin credential outside that registry is still saved as entered, under the same option hint.
- While the store write holds the preparation lock, `wizard.cancel` is refused and returns `status: "running"`; the cancel is not queued, so the client cancels again at the next prompt.

<details><summary>Writers and overlapping PRs</summary>

Writers that skipped the store step: `writeWizardConfigFile` in `configure` and the hosted chat setup, `commitSetupConfigFile` in onboarding and Gateway `wizard.start` setup, `createAgent` and `commitConfigWithPendingPluginInstalls` in `agents add`.

Open PRs touching the same files (none changes the channel save step):
- `src/wizard/setup.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/127083, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163527, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166573
- `src/commands/configure.wizard.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166573, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/131153
- `src/commands/agents.commands.add.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/174857, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175069, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168268
- Draft https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/121563 adds a shared credential-mode hint in `src/channels/plugins/setup-wizard-credential-mode.ts` that still says "Stores the credentials directly in OpenClaw config"; whichever lands second should use this PR's wording.

</details>

## Evidence

The CLI built from this branch and from the base `19c5e58c2e8`, each run in a fresh `HOME` and state directory under `env -i`, with synthetic tokens. The prompts were driven in a pseudo-terminal by the same step file on both sides. Runs that start the Gateway or the bundled Codex app-server were in a network namespace with only loopback.

Re-run on 2026-10-30 at the head `e268f2377da`, after merging `main` `885e57e9f9d`, with the same scripts on Node 24.22.1:
- `configure`: `botToken` is a `store` SecretRef, `openclaw.json` holds no copy of the token, the entry option says "Saves the credential in the protected secret store", and `secrets audit --check` exits 0, clean.
- Gateway `wizard.start`: the forbidden, cancel and complete scenarios match the first table below. With the answering device removed 2 to 100 ms after its last answer, 0 of 23 runs published the token to config. At 2 and 15 ms (10 runs) the removal cut off the answer before it reached the session, so nothing was written. From 25 ms on (13 runs) the session ended with one unreferenced store entry each (the first accepted limit above).
- Hosted chat: the forbidden and complete steps match the hosted chat table below. With the answering device removed at its last answer, 0 of 5 runs published config or stored an entry.

The hosted chat table no longer lists a second `operator.admin` device answering the admin's step. Since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176587, shared-token operator connections share the Gateway owner profile, so a second shared-token admin device is the same chat owner on `main` too. This PR does not change session ownership.

The tables below keep the commits they were first measured at.

`openclaw configure --section channels`, Telegram, "Enter Telegram bot token":

| Check | Before (`19c5e58c2e8`) | After (`dd48b4790aa`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry option hint | "Stores the credential directly in OpenClaw config" | "Saves the credential in the protected secret store" |
| `channels.telegram.botToken` in `openclaw.json` | **the token** | `{"source": "store", "provider": "default", "id": "CHANNEL_SETUP_…"}` |
| `doctor --lint` `core/doctor/security` plaintext warning (`Paths: channels.telegram.botToken`) | **present** | absent; the other five findings are unchanged |
| `secrets audit --check` | **exit 1, plaintext=1** | exit 0, clean, unresolved=0 |

`openclaw onboard --classic --flow quickstart --mode local --auth-choice skip --skip-…`, Telegram at "Select channel (QuickStart)", After at `6719dd19adc`:
- Before: exit 0; the token is in `openclaw.json` and `openclaw.json.bak`.
- After: exit 0; `botToken` is a `store` SecretRef and only the state database holds the token. `secrets audit --check` lists only `gateway.auth.token`, which onboarding generates and which this PR does not touch.

`openclaw agents add helper` on the onboarded state (After only, `6719dd19adc`), Discord at "Set up a chat channel now?": exit 0, "Agent "helper" ready.", `channels.discord.token` is a `store` SecretRef, resolves, and only the state database holds the token.

Gateway `wizard.start` setup, built at `786f6bc8daf` (the production code of the then-head `080097ce070`, which added one test-only commit): an isolated Gateway with token auth and a driver on the real `callGateway` client, answering each `wizard.next` step and reading the config file and `secrets.store.list` after each scenario.

| Scenario | Result | `channels.telegram.botToken` | Store entries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| client with `[operator.write]` calls `wizard.start` | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| admin client enters the token, cancels at the next prompt | `cancelled` | absent | none |
| admin client completes QuickStart setup | `done` | `store` SecretRef | exactly the referenced entry |

The cancel above stops at a prompt, which the flow already honored. The new guard covers a cancel that lands after the last prompt and before the store write; the `wizard.test.ts` case below shows that window.

Device revoked after the last prompt, same Gateway setup: a client with its own paired device answers every step. At "Set up administration from your own chat account?", the last prompt before the store write, it sends its answer, and an admin client removes that device with `device.pair.remove` at once. Each run used a fresh state.

| Gateway build | Runs | Token stored after the removal | `wizard.status` after the answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `6719dd19adc` (session hooks only) | 5 | **5** (config published 154–173 ms after the removal) | `running` |
| `fcc798f1332` (client check before the awaited commit) | 5 | **1** (config published 167 ms after the removal, after a lock wait) | `running` in the stored run, once `error` "Gateway caller authority is no longer active.", otherwise already ended |
| `3e378f75424`, a local build of `70078921176`'s production code before a test-only amend; it differs from `080097ce070` only in `src/system-agent` and `setup.test.ts` (check at publication) | 10 | 0 | already ended and collected |

Hosted chat in Control UI (`openclaw.chat`), the same isolated Gateway setup, built at `786f6bc8daf`, the production code of the then-head `080097ce070`. A chat session needs a verified model before it starts, so a loopback stand-in for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint answering "OK" was the default model; it was called once, for that check. The admin, a client with its own paired device, sent "connect telegram" and answered each hosted wizard step with `wizardAnswer`, as Control UI does.

| Step | Result | Config field | Store entries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[operator.write]` client sends "connect telegram" | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| at the admin's token step, an `[operator.write]` client answers it | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| the admin answers through the last step | "Done — telegram is configured." | `store` SecretRef | exactly the referenced entry |

Hosted chat, answering device removed at its last chat answer ("Set up administration from your own chat account?"), a fresh state per run. Counted runs are those where the removal closed the answering request (4001); two `786f6bc8daf` runs where the request completed instead are listed in the proof file and excluded. In one, the answer's connection was silently re-paired on loopback after the removal. In the other, its handshake finished as the removal ran. `device.pair.remove` closes only registered connections, so a connection whose handshake completes during the removal keeps its capture, and loopback silent pairing can approve the device again; that is an existing Gateway race outside this PR.

| Gateway build | Removal | Counted runs | Config published after the removal | Store entry left |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before the hosted fix (`wizard.start` fixes only) | at once | 5 | **3** | 3 |
| `786f6bc8daf` | at once | 13 | 0 | 0 |
| `786f6bc8daf` | after 30 ms | 10 | 0 | 10, admitted before the removal; unreferenced (first accepted limit) |

Upgrade from the latest stable, v2026.10.6: the published package (`npm install openclaw@2026.10.6`, `fe06181`, empty HOME) wrote a state with a plaintext Telegram token, a Discord `env` SecretRef, a Slack `store` SecretRef and `env` SecretRef, a store entry, and gateway/model settings. On copies of it, the head `7b1c2db75d5` ran `doctor --fix --non-interactive` first: its `configure` refuses a state database that has not had the client credential migration from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/174599 (on `main` since 2026-10-19, not in v2026.10.6) and names `openclaw doctor --fix`; `openclaw update` runs that Doctor step after installing the candidate, so the run applied it by hand. Doctor migrated the state database and added five unrelated defaults without changing any release value. `configure` then added Zalo:
- Entered token: only `channels.zalo.*` and `plugins.entries.zalo.enabled` change; the other 26 config values, including the plaintext Telegram token, both env refs and the release store ref, are identical. The store keeps the release entry and gains one `CHANNEL_SETUP_…` entry.
- "Use external secret provider" → Environment variable: an `env` SecretRef, no store entry.
- `secrets audit --check`: `unresolved=0` after both runs; `plaintext=1` for the pre-existing Telegram token, as v2026.10.6 reports it on its own state.

An earlier run of the same steps from v2026.10.4 (`383c124`), with `configure` built at `6719dd19adc` and no Doctor step needed, kept the same values and store entries.

Tests:
- `src/cli/program/register.configure.persistence.test.ts` (new case): runs the registered `configure --section channels` command with a fixture channel plugin and checks that the file holds a `store` SecretRef and the store returns the token.
- `src/system-agent/hosted-setup.runtime.test.ts` "rejects stale hosted channel authority at config revision" now expects the `store` SecretRef in the hosted write, reads the token back from the store, and checks that a stale write phase leaves the store empty. Two new cases run the chat engine's turns in a Gateway request scope whose authority ends after the last answer, before the store write or while the config commit waits: the reply names "Gateway caller authority is no longer active.", nothing is published, and the store is empty or keeps only the admitted entry.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/wizard.test.ts` (new, four cases): the real `wizard.*` handlers and `WizardSession`; the `wizard.start` request carries a real device-revocation capture, which the session retains. The setup flow running, cancelled after the token prompt, and with the starting device revoked before the store write; the channels flow with the device revoked. Running: the store holds the token. Cancelled: `cancelled`. Revoked: `error` "Gateway requester authority changed". In the last three, no store entry and no config write.
- `src/wizard/setup.channel-authority.test.ts` (new, two cases): `runSetupWizard` with the real channel store step and a config-writer stand-in that runs `assertBeforePublish` as the real writer does. A rejecting `beforePersistentEffect` stops it before it saves the channel token; authority that ends once the channel config commit has started stops its publication. `setup.test.ts` is over its line cap, so the cases live in this sibling file and `setup.test.ts` is unchanged from `main`. Since `a7cf9a6d65c`, its migration, workspace, Gateway configuration and onboarding-helper mocks spread the real module through `importOriginal`; the channel registry mock keeps the process-global registry out of the fixture and says so in a `mock-isolation` comment, as `setup.test.ts` does.
- `src/commands/channels/plugin-config-persistence.test.ts` (new case): with the real config writer and store, authority that ends at the commit's last await before publication leaves no channel config. It fails on the base, whose channels flow checked before the commit.
- The new cases and the changed hosted-setup assertions fail on the base with this branch's test files and pass on this branch; the changed `channels.add.test.ts` case passes on both and guards the write ownership. At `a7cf9a6d65c`, a fail-to-pass run of the six changed test files against `main` `885e57e9f9d` gives 11 cases that fail on `main` and pass here, and 66 guard tests that pass on both. On `main` no authority check stops the setup flow: it runs past the channel step into workspace and session preparation, which rejects with "Shared-state admission requires the host broker" instead of the expected authority error. At `080097ce070`, eight wrong fixes were caught; the two `setup.ts` variants were checked again with the new mocks at `a7cf9a6d65c`, each failing its own case:

Each changed test file, timed with `node scripts/test-projects.mts <file> --maxWorkers=1` (what `pnpm test` runs) and a warm transform cache, at the head `e268f2377da` on a loaded host (`setup.channel-authority.test.ts` at `a7cf9a6d65c`). prs.title: fix(ui): stabilize idle command palette browser test
prs.body:
Related: #192730

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/6a1b6fef-8de4-46d1-8db7-8a8e43aa305c)

## What Problem This Solves

The idle command-palette browser regression intermittently fails when keyboard dispatch takes longer than the 200 ms search debounce between characters.

## User Impact

No runtime behavior changes. CI can consistently check that usage updates leave idle searches settled and genuine command/model updates still refresh results.

## Why This Change Was Made

Control the timeout clock while typing, then advance the debounce after the full query and after each usage event. Keep every existing assertion, including exactly one session search. This changes one test file (+8/-1 lines), with no production changes.

## Evidence

- Confirmed the supplied Chromium CI annotations: expected one session-list call, received four and two on unrelated branches.
- One unmodified main-baseline run at `b6efe7be`: 1/1 passed (359 ms test time; 5.049 s command wall time).
- Deterministic reproduction: split typing into `zzidle` and `query`, advancing the timeout clock 200 ms between fragments. Both session-list calls occurred **before** usage events; the strict assertion failed with two calls. Three usage events added zero calls (211 ms test time; 2.807 s wall time).
- One fixed named-file run: 1/1 passed (153 ms test time; 2.698 s wall time). All three runs used the repository UI test command for this file, one at a time with a 120 s timeout. No repeat loops or CI reruns.
- The latest three scheduled main runs (`43310185262`, `43300241896`, `43290071255`) have all nine `checks-ui` shards green; no matching main failure observed.
- Focused lint, a typecheck rooted at this test file, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass. The normal type-aware lint wrapper timed out during package-declaration preparation before linting; its supported focused mode passed. Broad checks are left to PR CI.
- Requested local autoreview of the final change snapshot against `b6efe7be` completed through P2 with no findings. The simplification pass retained only the timeout control and cleanup needed by this test.

This is Chromium browser-unit proof with synthetic Gateway events. The original CI keyboard timings were not captured, and the original multi-file shard order was not replayed. The controlled reproduction establishes that intermediate-query debounces alone produce the reported failure.

prs.title: fix: keep worker creation tied to its original caller across restarts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes pending worker creation continuing with an outdated caller after access changes or a Gateway restart.

## User Impact

Worker creation keeps its original caller through preparation, allocation, and initial bootstrap. Retrying the same key cannot replace that caller. Ready workers keep their existing maintenance behavior.

Shared state advances to schema 40. Older readers refuse the upgraded database. Pending legacy creation intents without recoverable caller evidence stop; uncertain allocations retain their cleanup identity. Recreate affected pending work after cleanup settles. Rollback requires the matching pre-upgrade backup and build.

## Why This Change Was Made

Store the original caller on the existing allocation intent and restore it through the authentication owner. Confirmed refusals settle unallocated work or request exact cleanup. Temporarily unavailable identity reads leave recovery pending without allocating or destroying resources. Initial bootstrap stays bound to creation until first readiness.

The existing lifecycle owner still handles provisioning and cleanup; the continuation moves to one resume module. No separate authority store or cleanup implementation is added. Migration, recovery, and reader fencing form one complete repair. The 547-line test allocation covers the exact excess above the standard allowance (947 net test lines), for distinct admission, replay/restart, cleanup, transient-reader, migration, reader-fence, and build-swap compatibility contracts.

Historical SQLite catalogs remain resolvable across an in-place build swap, as required by #196800. An already-loaded updater may read the replacement JSON after activation. The generator now retains the immediate pre-provision-source schema and all four runtime variants, alongside the earlier historical inputs. All 112 base catalog layouts are preserved exactly after resolving their generated table indices. Five fixed-hash regression cases fail before regeneration and pass afterward.

The CI repair also restores the wrapper's runtime source closure, removes a type-import cycle without adding another schema owner, fixes canonical test routing, and updates PostgreSQL preparation expectations for schema 40.

## Evidence

Validated source: `bfb4774af27d3514b7bcc55247f68daf614154dc`, tree `c2e19f899186c894422056073e9442df9246e249`. All 64,467 selected files match the validated snapshot before and after the final build. Build metadata identifies the preceding commit plus that dirty snapshot; its blobs map exactly to this final committed tree.

- Original regressions fail before the repair. Compiled-app qualification additionally exposed a missing OpenClaw ID origin marker and confirmed-refusal classification; both were repaired and covered by regressions.
- Final worker, principal, recovery, and SQLite migration batch: **68 tests across seven files pass**, two canonical shards, 120.56s wrapper.
- Catalog equivalence: **200 pass**, 3.88s wrapper. Wrapper closure: **23 pass**, 29.01s. Cold provisioning/private-state: **32 pass, two capability skips**, 357.11s. These run through the canonical wrappers with real fixture Git and state engines.
- PostgreSQL 17 preparation: **three pass**, 39.87s wrapper. PostgreSQL migration and old-reader refusal previously passed through the canonical conformance runner. The current build retains that migration unchanged.
- Previously qualified shared scheduled-work, queued-input, channel-recovery, and service-work consumers: **101 tests across nine files pass**. Their code is unchanged by this repair batch.
- Targeted production/test/tooling types, lint/format, migration SQL inventory, test ownership, generators, and native schema ceiling checks pass. Canonical Madge reports **zero import cycles**.
- Full compiled build: **passes in 3m 47.9s**. Compiled CLI/Control UI composition: **passes in 65.909s**, using real OTP, owner enrollment, membership approval, UI device removal, same-key retry, graceful restart, abrupt exit, and signed removal through actual Discovery while offline. Valid allocation/destroy controls work before and after.
- Installed stable `2026.11.3` → candidate compiled Doctor: **schema 22 → 40 passes**, preserving four synthetic worker rows, preferences, and existing settings. Stable CLI initialized the database and settings; worker/preference rows were seeded offline. All original worker columns remain exact. Doctor adds only its existing missing-skill disables, run bookkeeping, and two migration markers. Candidate config and sessions commands work afterward. The installed stable Doctor then refuses schema 40 (it supports 22).
- Local autoreview fallback: original complete repair received five P0–P2 passes; this incremental CI/catalog repair received four complete P0–P2 passes, no actionable findings. The final snapshot maps to the committed tree above. [Hosted ClawSweeper re-review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/197875#issuecomment-6833927116) completed on this exact head: both previous findings resolved, no new actionable findings, ready for maintainer review.

<details>
<summary>Sanitized terminal and receipt evidence</summary>

Actual canonical-check output, with ANSI formatting and local paths removed:

```text
Madge import cycle check: 0 cycle(s).
Wrapper closure: Test Files 1 passed; Tests 23 passed
Provisioning/state: Test Files 2 passed; Tests 32 passed | 2 skipped
Worker/principal/migration: Test Files 1 passed + 6 passed; Tests 1 passed + 67 passed

Catalog equivalence: Test Files 1 passed; Tests 200 passed

restart-browser-completed
completed
{"status":"passed","receipt":"[isolated composition receipt]"}
```

Selected fields from the actual compiled-app receipt (identifiers and paths omitted):

```json

  "liveRemoval": {

  },

```

Actual upgrade receipt:

```json

  "fixtureBoundary": "Stable CLI initialized config and SQLite; worker/preference rows seeded offline. Candidate compiled Doctor upgraded it."

```

</details>

The offline composition holds effect-free preparation until canonical removal is observed. It proves refusal after that removal, not that mailbox processing precedes every startup task. The external synthetic worker never provides a runnable node. All execution uses isolated synthetic services; this does not qualify real cloud allocation, deployed services, npm candidate packaging, or native macOS execution.

Final-head [CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43294790488) has completed: **166 jobs passed, 19 skipped, two failed**. All branch-related repairs passed, including architecture guards, the previously failing compact-large jobs, and all four PostgreSQL lanes. Separate Swift and iOS Periphery workflows passed. No checks remain pending.

The only failing test is the inherited [Codex Bun command-execution assertion](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43294790488/job/131451171094). The original six-file shard reproduces identically on this head and original base `a3d5baaabd2ce88ace4b5d1c45a9577a61dbc08a` (80 pass, one fail; `node-app-server.runtime.test.ts:268`, expected marker/exit 0, received empty stdout/exit 1). The final source was restored and reverified afterward. The second failed job is the aggregate CI gate. The subsequent [automated policy workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43299749586) completed successfully; its dependency and sensitive-change checks passed, while its aggregate CI status correctly remains failed because the primary CI gate failed. This inherited failure remains a deferred CI blocker; no unrelated repair or rerun was performed. The first run's inherited workflow-size failure did not recur in the final run.

Hosted review and CI closeout are complete. The PR remains open with auto-merge disabled. No merge is requested.
