prs.title: feat(database): hold Gateway state ownership in PostgreSQL on all-PostgreSQL installs
prs.body:
Part of #196156

Related: #196154, #196155, #196157

This is the ownership half of #196156 (item 2). Store identity (item 1) is not in this PR; see "Store identity: what blocks it" below.

## What Problem This Solves

On an all-PostgreSQL install, Gateway state ownership is still a local lock file keyed by `state/openclaw.sqlite`. It only excludes processes that see the same state directory on the same host, and its refusals name a SQLite file that holds no application data.

## User Impact

Operators can set `database.postgres.ownership: "installation"`. It is opt-in and accepted only when `database.engine` is `postgres` and no family overrides to `sqlite`. The default, `"state-directory"`, keeps today's local lock file. The setting only changes Gateway state ownership. Store anchors, `client/credentials.sqlite`, `control/services.sqlite`, the local lock files and the journals stay local.

- A second Gateway, maintenance owner, or offline CLI owner (such as `openclaw config set` with no Gateway on its own state directory) with the same database and schema prefix is refused on any host. The refusal names the schema prefix and the holder's PID, host and PostgreSQL backend PID. A waiting Gateway logs the holder once.
- If the owner's PostgreSQL session ends (crash, terminated backend, network loss) or a heartbeat fails, the running Gateway retires its state ownership at once. New and queued state work is refused, and the Gateway closes. PostgreSQL releases the lock, and the next Gateway can start.
- On a silent network failure the Gateway finds out from the next heartbeat, within about 20 s (10 s interval plus 10 s query timeout). The docs ask operators to keep server-side dead-connection settings above that, so PostgreSQL cannot release the lock while the former Gateway still admits work.
- A successor on another state directory starts on its own stores, because store identity is still the local anchor. It does not take over the former Gateway's data until store identity moves (see below).
- Connection startup and every owner query time out after 10 s, so an unresponsive server cannot hang startup.
- Nothing new is stored: no file, no schema, no table. The database and `database.postgres.schemaPrefix` name the installation, so the runtime role needs no new privilege.
- The owner connection must be direct or go through a session-mode pooler. Session advisory locks do not work through PgBouncer in transaction mode.
- The default and mixed installs behave exactly as before: no PostgreSQL lock, unchanged messages.
- Downgrade: releases without this setting validate `database.postgres` strictly (2026.11.3 does), so remove `ownership` before rolling back to one. Installs that never set it are unaffected.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `acquireGatewayLock` also takes a session-level `pg_try_advisory_lock` on one dedicated `pg` connection outside the pool. The key is a hash of the schema prefix with its own namespace, so it never collides with the per-store writer locks. Advisory locks are per database, so the database and prefix together scope it.
- CLI owners that resolve the configured engine only after taking the lock (`runWithLocalStateOwner` with `databaseEngine: "configured"`, as `openclaw config set` does) take the PostgreSQL lock through the same handle once that selection is in scope, before the command reads or writes any state. Contention is refused like any other offline owner refusal. Its loss retires the same process owner. A cold config-only repair (`databaseAccess: "none"`) skips this call and touches no database. Database port maintenance and recovery owners go through the same call; only the `configured` path has its own test.
- Losing that session aborts a custody signal passed to `acquireGatewayStateOwner`. That retires the existing process owner, which is the one owner that admission (`captureStateDatabaseAccess`), queued workers and the server lifecycle (`captureGatewayStateOwner(...).signal` in `server.ts`) already observe. There is no parallel loss flag.
- The PostgreSQL session lives exactly as long as the process owner's physical custody. When uncertain child cleanup keeps a borrowed lease after the lock is released (`runWithLocalStateOwner` on `CommandProcessCleanupError`), the session stays open until that lease ends, so no successor can start under live child work. The owner ends it through a release hook (`onReleased` in `acquireGatewayStateOwner`).
- The holder is read from `pg_locks` and `pg_stat_activity`. The owner session sets `application_name` to `openclaw-gateway-owner:<pid>:<host>`, so there is no diagnostic row to go stale or to fail on release.
- Release never rejects: it ends the session (bounded by the same 10 s), which releases the lock, so local custody is always released after it.
- Contention reuses `GatewayStateOwnerContentionError`, so the existing wait and retry behavior applies unchanged.
- The existing local file owner stays in place. It still provides in-process custody for SQLite handles; the PostgreSQL lock adds cross-host exclusion on top of it.
- The setting lives under `database.postgres` and is named for what it changes (the scope of Gateway ownership), not for a later state with no local files. Earlier revisions of this PR called it `database.localStores: "none"`; that name was never released.

### How this lock relates to the `state_leases` gateway-owner lease

Both exist with `ownership: "installation"`, and they cover different scopes:

- The advisory lock is per installation and is taken first, inside the ownership acquisition loop. A Gateway that cannot get it never reaches the lease.
- The `state_leases` `gateway-owner` row lives in the state store's namespace, which is still per state directory because the state anchor is local. It carries the listener facts (port, mode, supervisor) used for restart and update handoff.

When PostgreSQL ends the owner session, the client is told at once and retires the owner. In the recorded run below that took about 0.1 s, before the successor acquired. On a silent network failure the client finds out within about 20 s, and PostgreSQL holds the lock until it ends the session itself. With server-side dead-connection settings above 20 s, the former Gateway stops before the lock is free.

From the code, offline lease recovery (`gateway-lock-recovery.ts`) and the Windows task probe (`schtasks-process.ts`) still take only the local owner; this is not separately tested. They act on one state directory after its holder is gone, and they never admit Gateway work.

### Decision needed

This adds a config option, so it needs a maintainer's yes before it lands.

**Question:** should this ownership-only phase ship as the opt-in `database.postgres.ownership: "installation"`?

**Options:**

1. **Approve as is (recommended).** Opt-in, default unchanged, no new persisted state or privilege, and cross-host exclusion works now for all-PostgreSQL installs.
2. **Approve with a different name or place**, for example a top-level `database.ownership`. The rename is mechanical: schema, one runtime field, tests and the guide.
3. **Defer** until store identity can move too, so all of #196156 lands at once. That work is blocked on a file-independent admission identity (below) and would not change this contract.

**What approving means:**

- **Installation identity.** The database plus `database.postgres.schemaPrefix`. Nothing new is persisted. Two installations in one database must use different prefixes, as they already must for their store schemas.
- **Local custody.** The local lock files and process owner stay and keep their current role.
- **Pooling.** The owner connection must be direct or through a session-mode pooler.
- **Disconnect.** Session loss stops the Gateway. A silent network is noticed within about 20 s, so server-side dead-connection settings must stay above that.
- **Offline recovery.** Offline lease recovery keeps using only the local owner.

Later, separate question: should the `state_leases` gateway-owner lease merge into, or defer to, the lock once store identity moves?

### Store identity: what blocks it

Moving the state store's identity into a PostgreSQL registry and opening the store on an in-memory anchor fails. The reason matters for the shape decision: the anchor file does more than record identity.

- The process-wide admission cache (`sqlite-database-admission.ts`) keys every store's admission facts on the anchor's file identity. An in-memory anchor gets no admission (`Missing PostgreSQL state admission`).
- The client credential receipt in `client/credentials.sqlite` binds to the state anchor's path, device and inode (`readClientCredentialFileIdentity`).
- Agent-store callers treat "anchor file exists" as "store exists" in roughly ten places.

So removing anchors first needs a non-file admission identity, and the credential binding has to move with or before the state anchor. Proposed order:

1. This PR: ownership.
2. A file-independent admission identity.
3. The registry for state and agent identity, offline anchor retirement, and registry writes from `database port` and `backup restore`.
4. The fixed-local stores (#196157).

## Evidence

All runs used PostgreSQL 17.11 on macOS (arm64), Node 24.22.2, and a build of this branch. The scratch database had `unaccent`, `pg_trgm` and `vector` installed, as the operator guide requires. Hosts, paths and anchor IDs are redacted; timestamps are as logged. Both Gateways ran on one machine with separate state directories and ports, which is what a second host sees: a different state directory and the same database.

**Upgrade from the latest stable release (2026.11.3).** Stable ran on default SQLite storage with `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds: 321`, and a cron job was added through its CLI:

```
d1fa9142-05ff-4569-b27b-40f89d415c0e -   upgrade-proof   every 1d   in 1d   -   idle   main ...
```

After stable stopped, the branch followed the documented path: `openclaw doctor --fix` (exit 0, "Doctor complete."), then `openclaw database port --to postgres`, which ported the state and agent stores and set `database.engine` to `postgres`. Then `ownership: "installation"` was added and the branch Gateway started on the same state directory:

```
== config database section
{"engine": "postgres", "postgres": {"connection": {"source": "env", "provider": "default", "id": "OPENCLAW_DATABASE_DSN"}, "schemaPrefix": "proof196237", "ownership": "installation"}}
Config valid: <root>/a/openclaw.json
== branch ready
== cron job written by 2026.11.3
d1fa9142-05ff-4569-b27b-40f89d415c0e -   upgrade-proof   every 1d   in 1d   -   idle   main ...
== setting written for 2026.11.3
321
== owner lock
openclaw-gateway-owner:78133:<host> backend=78169
== schemas
proof196237_agent_<id>
proof196237_state_<id>
```

The job and the setting are unchanged. The only schemas are the two the port created; enabling the setting created none.

**Validation.** With `engine: "sqlite"`, `openclaw config validate` refuses the setting and exits 1:

```
- openclaw.json:2 - database.postgres.ownership: database.postgres.ownership "installation" requires database.engine postgres and no family overrides to sqlite., got: "installation"
```

**Authority chain after session loss.** Gateway A (port 19631) held ownership. Gateway B used its own state directory and port 19632 on the same database and prefix. A's owner backend was then terminated with `pg_terminate_backend` while A kept running.

```
== 20:17:16.911 owner lock:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78482:<host> backend=78518
== B log while A holds:
20:17:26.291 [gateway] state ownership is held in PostgreSQL schema prefix proof196237: Gateway pid 78482 on host <host> holds it (PostgreSQL backend 78518).
20:17:26.292 [gateway] waiting for Gateway state ownership held by another OpenClaw process, up to 300 s
== 20:17:26.677 pg_terminate_backend(78518) (A's owner session)
== A log after termination:
20:17:26.775 [state] PostgreSQL Gateway ownership was lost (terminating connection due to administrator command); state work is refused and the Gateway stops. Check the PostgreSQL connection, then restart the Gateway.
20:17:26.778 [admission] closed: restart-signal fence
20:17:26.786 [admission] closed: restart (SIGUSR2: Error: PostgreSQL Gateway ownership was lost ...)
20:17:26.876 [audit/events] audit event persistence failed: PostgreSQL Gateway ownership was lost ...
== 20:17:31.376 A exited
== B log after termination:
20:17:27.263 [gateway] state ownership acquired after 1.0 s
20:17:31.182 [gateway] ready
== owner after:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78726:<host> backend=78816
```

A logged the loss and closed admission about 0.1 s after the terminate, and its in-flight audit write was refused. B acquired 0.59 s after the terminate, after A had closed admission. A had exited 4.7 s after the terminate (no supervisor ran, so it stayed down). B's state directory is separate, so it started on its own stores.

**Cold CLI owner.** Gateway A held ownership. A fresh `openclaw config set agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds 321` then ran with its own state directory (`<root>/b`) and the same database and prefix. It resolves its engine only after taking its local lock.

```
== cold CLI on <root>/b while A holds
Cannot admit config set for agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds in state root <root>/b/state: OpenClaw state database is busy at PostgreSQL schema prefix proof196237. Gateway pid 78482 on host <host> holds it (PostgreSQL backend 78518). ... No local mutation was attempted. ...
exit 1
== b agents config after refusal:
None
== (A terminated and B stopped as above) owner after B stopped: []
== same cold CLI on <root>/b with the lock free
Updated agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.
exit 0
{'defaults': {'timeoutSeconds': 321}}
== owner sessions in PostgreSQL connection log order:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78482:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78695:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78726:
openclaw-gateway-owner:78976:
```

While A held the lock, the CLI was refused, named A, and wrote nothing. With the lock free, it opened its own owner session (78976) and wrote the setting. 78695 is the refused attempt and 78726 is Gateway B. The refusal text after "holds it" is the existing contention guidance; part of it speaks of "the same state directory", which does not fit a holder on another state directory.

**Tests**, run with `scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs` against PostgreSQL 17.11, `src/infra/gateway-postgres-owner.postgres.test.ts`, 7/7:

- A second Gateway (separate state and lock directory, same database) is refused. The error names the schema prefix and the holder's pid and host, and not `openclaw.sqlite`. Releasing twice is safe, and the next Gateway then acquires.
- Session loss: after `pg_terminate_backend`, the former Gateway's owner signal aborts. A process-owner handle captured before the loss (as queued work holds one) fails `assertCurrent`. `captureGatewayStateOwner` and new `captureStateDatabaseAccess(...).prepareAccess()` are refused. A successor acquires, and exactly one backend holds the lock.
- Silent network: a TCP proxy stops forwarding both ways without closing. The next heartbeat times out and reports the loss (2.1 s with a 100 ms interval and 2 s bound).
- A server that accepts TCP but never answers fails acquisition with a timeout, and the attempt's socket is closed (241 ms with a 200 ms bound).
- Cold CLI: with no engine selection installed, `runWithLocalStateOwner` for another state directory reads `ownership: "installation"` from its config and is refused while a Gateway holds the lock. `runLocal` never runs. After the Gateway stops, the same CLI holds exactly one owner session during `runLocal` and none after it returns. Without the new call in `local-state-owner.ts`, this test fails (`promise resolved "'ran'" instead of rejecting`).
- Retained lease: a lease borrowed before the lock is released (as uncertain child cleanup does) keeps the PostgreSQL session open. A second host is refused until the lease ends, and then acquires. With the lock releasing the session directly, as in an earlier revision of this PR, this test fails.
- Default mode: two Gateways with separate state directories both acquire, and no lock is taken.
- Without `connectionTimeoutMillis`, the silent-server test hangs until the 120 s test timeout. Without the loss-to-owner wiring in `gateway-lock.ts`, the session-loss test fails (`expected false to be true` on the aborted signal). Both checks ran against the 4-test revision of this file.

`src/config/zod-schema.database.test.ts` covers the setting: it is accepted with all families on PostgreSQL, `"state-directory"` is accepted anywhere, and it is refused without `engine: "postgres"`, with a family on `sqlite`, or with an unknown value. Against the previous head (with `database.localStores`), the three accept cases fail (`Tests 3 failed | 26 passed (29)`); on this head it passes 29/29.

**Gates.** The PR diff was checked merged onto main `277e32c668a`. main `2cfd5ceab3d` was merged later; it changes none of this PR's files except the generated config baseline. The first group below was then re-run on this head.

prs.title: fix(state): PostgreSQL updates to builds with Template bootstrap deferral are refused as schema drift
prs.body:
Closes #196966
Related: #197008 (SQLite clean-close seals invalidated by the same column)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: PostgreSQL-backed installs cannot update to any build from caa978ca (#196392) onward. The update is refused at `database-engine-preflight` with "PostgreSQL schema drift detected against generated DDL".

## User Impact

User impact: PostgreSQL installs update past 2026.11.2 again, whichever valid schema-39 shape their store holds. The store moves to shared-state schema 40 with its workspace setup rows and stored values intact. SQLite installs migrate the same way.

Required action: none. As with every state schema bump, older builds refuse a schema-40 store, and downgrade means restoring the verified pre-upgrade backup with its matching binary.

## Why This Change Was Made

#196392 added `workspace_setup_state.bootstrap_deferred` as a first-use column. SQLite admission tolerates a missing first-use column, but PostgreSQL stores have no first-use columns. The generated PostgreSQL DDL declares the column, so every existing PostgreSQL store sealed without it no longer matched the candidate's contract.

This PR makes the column part of state schema 40, following the single-column v39 precedent (`retention_json`). Two valid v39 shapes exist in the field:

- **Column absent:** stores sealed before #196392.
- **Column present:** PostgreSQL stores freshly bootstrapped from main at or after #196392 (`bigint`), and SQLite stores whose first-use writer added it (`INTEGER`).

The v40 step accepts exactly those two shapes. It adds the column only if it is missing, so stored values are kept. On PostgreSQL it refuses any other definition (for example `integer`, a default, or `NOT NULL`) as drift. The change touches these places:

- **Migration step:** may declare `alsoFromSchemas`, additional exact predecessor shapes. The runner and existing-version inspection select the stored shape through `selectPostgresMigrationSource`.
- **Port descriptor:** may declare `sourceVariants`. Port admission (snapshot, backup, restore) selects the variant the source holds, comparing only the tables where the variants differ. The v39 descriptor carries the column-present variant.
- **SQLite:** adds the column if it is missing. The predecessor transforms keep v39 admission, backups, ports and the historical v13 rebuild on the exact pre-v40 shape.
- **Workspace writer:** no longer calls `ensureColumn`. On PostgreSQL that call would have added an `integer` column against the generated `bigint` contract.

### Maintainer decision

This PR makes `bootstrap_deferred` a schema-40 column on SQLite and PostgreSQL. It replaces the first-use install that #196392 chose. Both exact schema-39 shapes migrate with their stored values kept. Older binaries refuse a schema-40 store, as with every state schema bump. Downgrade means restoring the verified pre-upgrade backup with its matching binary.

Why not keep first-use: PostgreSQL has no first-use columns. It adds columns to existing tables only through versioned transitions (v28, v35, v37 to v39). The other options also change the #196392 storage design:

- **First-use companion table:** moves the flag into its own table. Stores already bootstrapped with the column would then drift.
- **First-use columns in PostgreSQL admission:** a new admission and seal concept that loosens exact catalog checks.

A versioned column is the smallest change that reuses the existing schema, migration and backup owners and keeps admission exact.

## Evidence

All local runs below are on tree `551c0c97e2a4` (this head), PostgreSQL 17.11 with `max_locks_per_transaction=512` and the `unaccent`, `pg_trgm` and `vector` extensions, as in CI.

**Discriminating PostgreSQL regression:** `src/state/openclaw-state-workspace-bootstrap-migration.postgres.test.ts`, run with `node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --connection <disposable> -- <file>`.

```
main 29c445e7: × upgrades a v39 store with the column absent … → PostgreSQL schema drift detected against generated DDL.
               × upgrades a v39 store with the column present … (main has no v40; the store stays at v39)
               ✓ still refuses … integer   ✓ … bigint DEFAULT 0   ✓ … bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
this head:     5 passed (5)
```

**SQLite, both v39 shapes:** `src/agents/workspace-state-store.test.ts`.

- Column absent: the column is added, `user_version` reaches 40, and setup rows are unchanged.
- Column present with `bootstrap_deferred = 1`: the store opens at 40 and keeps the value. If the v40 step instead adds the column unconditionally, this case fails with `duplicate column name: bootstrap_deferred`.

**Real CLI, PostgreSQL** (run by the author on `fdf476ea`; this head changes only `src/agents/workspace-state-store.test.ts` and the test-lines allocation on top of `8da0de95`): isolated git installs with all three families on PostgreSQL, onboarded and seeded with `agents add probe`. Each runs `openclaw update --yes --no-restart --channel dev` against a local mirror whose `main` is pinned to the target.

- **Column absent:** installed 2026.11.2 (`0a9d8c71`).
  - Before, main `25bf99f6`: refused at `database-engine-preflight` with "PostgreSQL schema drift detected against generated DDL"; exit 1.
  - After: `✅ OpenClaw updated to 2026.11.3 (fdf476ea) (from 2026.11.2 (0a9d8c71))`, exit 0. Schema 40, column added, 2 retained rows. `agents add probe2` writes a setup row (3 rows), and a `doctor` reopen shows version 40 and all three agents.
- **Column present:** installed 2026.11.3 (`041c3b71`), which bootstrapped the store at v39 with the column. Before the update, one retained row was set to `bootstrap_deferred = 1` with SQL; I found no offline product path that drives Template deferral.
  - Before, an earlier revision of this PR: refused at `database-engine-preflight` with the same drift error; exit 1, and the store stays at v39.
  - After: `✅ OpenClaw updated to 2026.11.3 (fdf476ea) (from 2026.11.3 (041c3b71))`, exit 0. Schema 40. Values were `1,null` before the update; after a new setup write they read `1,null,null`, and after the reopen still `1,null,null` at version 40. All three agents are listed.

**Latest stable → fix (SQLite, run by the author on `f5abb2d5`, an earlier revision with the same SQLite path):** `npm install -g openclaw@latest` (2026.11.3), onboarded and seeded. The stable binary's own `openclaw update --channel dev` to the fix gives `✅ updated`, exit 0. The store ends at `user_version 40` with `bootstrap_deferred` present and its 2 rows kept, and agents and `gateway.port` are preserved.

**Focused checks on this head:**

- PostgreSQL conformance, file by file:
  - `openclaw-state-workspace-bootstrap-migration` 5/5
  - `doctor-migration` 26/26
  - `openclaw-state-db.postgres` 13/13
  - `database-prepare-state` 3/3
  - `schema-admission` 15/15
  - `readonly-admission` 6/6
  - `config-preflight` 1/1
  - `state-port` 2/2
  - `agent-port` 9/9
  - `port-command` 5/5
  - `port-provider` 1/1
  - `git-backup-secrets` 4/4
  - `update-cohort-restore` 1/1
  - `postgres-generation` 2/2
  - `startup-client-credentials` 7/7
  - `client-credential-migration` 3/3
  - `client-credential-startup.gateway` 1/1
  - `logbook-port` 5/5, logbook and workboard transports 1/1 each
- `src/agents/workspace-state-store.test.ts` and `src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts`: 73 passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test`: passes. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on the changed test: clean.
- Test-lines ratchet: `Test lines OK: 6645167; ceiling: 6645186; slack: 19.` The +119 net test lines are covered by `config/test-lines-allocations/postgres-workspace-bootstrap-deferral.txt`. Main's 19 lines of slack are unchanged.
- PR wrapper inventory: `scripts/pr-lib/wrapper-components.txt` lists the new v40 module.

**CI on `8da0de95` (run 42972390862):** each remaining failure is unrelated to this change.

| Failing check | Classification | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.native-hook-relay.test.ts` ("relays native tool results through Codex result middleware") | Pre-existing | Fails the same way locally on main `29c445e7`. Same failure on other PRs' CI: runs 43024779027, 43009841575, 43008868345, 42999561346 |
| `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/telegram-message-tool-failure-settlement.e2e.test.ts` | Pre-existing | Same assertion on another PR's CI: runs 42998401262, 42991776111. No frame touches state schema |
| `PostgreSQL conformance (1/3)` | Job time limit | Every conformance file passed (`passed 9 Vitest shards in 1460.35s`), and the PG16 Gateway smoke passed 8/8. The job reached its 30 minute limit while that step exited. The shard's file list is the same on main. Other PRs hit the same cancel: runs 42991997194 (1816 s) and 42982947108 (1808 s) |
| `openclaw/ci-gate` | Aggregate | Fails because of the rows above |

**Gaps**

- The native Swift shared-state ceiling and its test constant moved to 40. The Swift tests were not run here.
- There is no stable PostgreSQL upgrade to prove: latest stable 2026.11.3 rejects `database.*` config, so the stable→fix run is SQLite-only.
- `archive-restore`, `git-backup` and `port-command-refusals` need a built `dist/` and were not rerun on this head.

**pr-simplify:** each hunk serves one of three things: the v40 column, its two exact predecessor shapes (migration source and port variant), or removing the first-use path. The two new optional fields are the smallest way I found to make one schema version accept two exact shapes in both the migration runner and the port layer, without loosening any exact-catalog check. The new PostgreSQL tests live in their own file because `doctor-migration.postgres.test.ts` is at its 1000-line budget.

prs.title: feat(google): add Gemini 4 Hydrogen to the catalog
prs.body:
## Problem

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen (`gemini-4-hydrogen`) today. OpenClaw resolves `google/gemini-4-hydrogen` only through the Gemini 4 forward-compat rule (`GEMINI_4_TEMPLATE_IDS = ["gemini-4-argon"]`), which copies Argon's row. That row has no price, so usage on main is unpriced. Main is the source for the hosted catalog (published every 4 h), so a manifest row here reaches released installs through hosted v1/v2 and main through v3, with no release.

## Change

- `extensions/google/openclaw.plugin.json`: new `gemini-4-hydrogen` row after Argon, in the same shape as the other Gemini rows:
  ```json
  { "id": "gemini-4-hydrogen", "name": "Gemini 4 Hydrogen", "reasoning": true,
    "input": ["text", "image"],
    "cost": { "input": 1.5, "output": 7.5, "cacheRead": 0.075, "cacheWrite": 0 },
    "contextWindow": 1048576, "maxTokens": 65536,
    "thinkingLevelMap": { "minimal": null },
    "compat": { "codeMode": "preferred" } }
  ```
- `docs/providers/google.md`: a Gemini 4 Hydrogen section with limits, inputs, thinking, caching and prices.
- `docs/tools/code-mode/configuration.md`: Hydrogen added to the Google preferred list.
- `extensions/google/manifest.test.ts`: the row count goes from 13 to 14, and the test now checks that Hydrogen follows Argon. No new test.

### Field choices

- **input**: `text`/`image`, the same as every Gemini row. The AI Studio static and live catalogs already add `video` at runtime (`buildGoogleStaticCatalogProvider` and the live projection), so `models list` shows `text+image+video`. The catalog has no `audio` modality. A manifest `document` row throws in `buildManifestCatalogModelInput`. Google's PDF and audio paths stay in media understanding (`nativeDocumentInputs: ["pdf"]`).
- **thinkingLevelMap** `{ minimal: null }`: same as Argon. Gemini 4 rejects MINIMAL (live contract recorded in `google-thinking-level.ts`). The offered ladder is low/medium/high. Google lists `xhigh` for Hydrogen, but `getGoogleThinkingLevel` has no XHIGH: `xhigh`/`max` clamp to HIGH. Offering xhigh would advertise a control that request construction does not honor, so that waits for a separate change with a dated live probe.
- **compat.codeMode `"preferred"`**: this keeps today's behavior and adds no new evaluation. On main, Hydrogen resolves through the Argon template and code mode engages (`codeModeEngaged: true` in the main-build turn below). Without the flag, the new row would silently turn code mode off for Hydrogen.
- **cost**: Google's paid-tier rates per 1M tokens. Input $1.50. Output $7.50, thinking included. Cached input $0.075 (implicit caching only; explicit caching is not supported). There is no cache-write price. Source: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing#gemini-4-hydrogen
- **Not changed**: `GEMINI_4_TEMPLATE_IDS`, the `gemini-4` alias, the default model and `recommended-models.json`. Hydrogen now has its own row, so it no longer needs the forward-compat template. Nothing shows Hydrogen as a template for another tier. #196988 changed only recommendations, and Carbon has no manifest row. That PR shows no rule that new models join recommendations, so recommendations stay as they are.

## Evidence

Vendor facts:
- Model page: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-4-hydrogen. Inputs are text, image, video, audio and PDF. Context is 1,048,576 tokens, shared by input and output. Max output is 65,536 by default. Thinking levels are low/medium/high/xhigh.
- `GET v1beta/models/gemini-4-hydrogen` with an AI Studio key: inputTokenLimit 1048576, outputTokenLimit 65536, thinking true. Methods: generateContent, countTokens, batchGenerateContent.
- Announcement: https://x.com/OfficialLoganK/status/2120940951292268640

Publisher (`node --import tsx scripts/publish-model-catalog.mts --pricing --out … --out-v2 … --out-v3 …`, exit 0):
- v1: `google/gemini-4-hydrogen` with contextWindow 1048576, maxTokens 65536, cost {input 1.5, output 7.5, cacheRead 0.075, cacheWrite 0}, thinkingLevelMap {minimal: null} and compat.codeMode preferred.
- v2 and v3: the same row, with pricing `{input 1.5, output 7.5, cacheRead 0.075, status known}`. models.dev published Hydrogen during this work: the first run took pricing from the manifest (`source: "manifest"`), and the rerun on this head took it from `modelsDev` at identical rates.

`node scripts/catalog-compare-released.mts --check --candidate <bundle>`:
- v1: 2026.11.3 (latest), 2026.9.37 (extended-stable) and 2026.11.5-beta.2 each read the bundle with 1251/1251 rows (exit 0).
- v2: the same three releases, 1251/1251 rows each (exit 0).
- v3: no released reader yet, so skipped (exit 0).
- `--filter google/gemini-4-hydrogen` report: on each release, the row changes from absent to listed. No other row changes.

Real end-to-end turn. Each checkout was built through pueue. Each Gateway ran under `env -i` with only PATH, a temp HOME, TMPDIR, OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR and `GEMINI_API_KEY`. The key reached the process over a pipe, never argv or a file. Each run used loopback only, its own port and a random token. The harness refused to start if any channel was configured. Afterward, every port was closed and no Gateway process remained. A log scan found no key material.

| | this branch | main (5dab86f) |
|---|---|---|
| reply | `pong` | `pong` |
| resolved / response model | google/gemini-4-hydrogen / gemini-4-hydrogen | google/gemini-4-hydrogen / gemini-4-hydrogen |
| usage | 16,189 in / 140 out | 16,157 in / 136 out |
| recorded cost | **$0.0253335** (input $0.0242835 + output $0.00105) | **$0**, `missingCostEntries: 1` (unpriced) |
| code mode engaged | true | true |
| `models list` | Gemini 4 Hydrogen, text+image+video, 1,048,576 | same (from live listing) |

The branch cost matches Hydrogen's rates exactly: 16,189 × $1.50/M + 140 × $7.50/M = $0.0253335.

Tests: `extensions/google/{manifest,provider-catalog,provider-models}.test.ts`, `src/agents/code-mode.config.test.ts`, `src/plugins/contracts/provider-catalog-deprecation.contract.test.ts` and `src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts` pass.

## Not verified

- No live run on Vertex.
- No turn with video, audio or PDF input.
- xhigh is not offered (see above).
- The `codeMode: "preferred"` flag preserves the current fallback behavior and has no separate evaluation.

prs.title: refactor(plugins): migrate binding and approval reads to async owners
prs.body:
Related: #192609 ([cleanup tracker](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/192609))

## What Problem This Solves

Bundled Codex binding guards and Telegram approval routing still use deprecated synchronous persistence adapters.

## User Impact

Bundled callers use the existing async surfaces while retaining host-owned binding inspection across awaited policy checks. Public synchronous compatibility remains through 2026-12-31, with removal in the first January 2027 stable release. Package delivery and live Gateway/Telegram effects remain unverified.

## Why This Change Was Made

Codex validates binding ownership before execution and disposes its prepared inspection lease on every exit. Telegram uses the existing async capability factory and nativeAsync routing surface. The existing SDK inspection entrypoint exports `prepareConversationBindingInspections`; no new state store or authority is added.

Two regressions cover policy changing during preparation and binding changing during the final policy check. The documented allocation covers 34 net counted test/helper lines without weakening either regression, assertions, counting rules or the shared ceiling.

## Evidence

- **Fresh candidate `49fc5d791fe6ab5858e92ff512e565220cbb1959`: 119 tests across five files/three shards passed**, covering Codex detach/binding/native-thread behavior and Telegram approval routing. The actual test process used the pinned Bun1.4.4 build on Darwin arm64; Node26.13.0 was the launcher. A fresh physical frozen install passed with pnpm12.15.0, and installed dependency data matches the frozen lockfile.
- Four files / 89 passing tests at prior head `a947576959161bd6c802a05cceeef7227f6a469c`, following a successful frozen install. These tests were not rerun or relabeled.
- Signed head `74f43f0a7b365b26b097bba0dfc3127ec7dc9875` adds only the allocation; runtime code, test bodies and dependency inputs are unchanged. Independent review and native gates/publication passed in `github_pending` mode.
- The earlier [SDK declaration/API comparison](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41791742723/job/126446888648) passed with only the intended prepared-inspection export; it remains prior-head proof, and fresh declaration/API coverage is not claimed.
- [Ordinary CI 43182040526](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43182040526), attempt 1: 44 successful, 2 failed, 26 skipped jobs. Ratchets and security-fast passed. The [raw-transcript permission case](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43182040526/job/131060881384) received an earlier physical-owner validation error; the aggregate gate also failed. The actual producer checkout and tested merge were independently verified. Its environmental trigger remains unknown; deterministic baseline reproduction is not claimed.

## Current Integration and Qualification

Signed candidate `49fc5d791fe6ab5858e92ff512e565220cbb1959` integrates selected baseline `0ac0df32c16506c2db7291793d36076cc94992a5` while retaining incoming `74f43f0a7b365b26b097bba0dfc3127ec7dc9875`. Native baseline preparation succeeded without manual resolutions. Independent source review accepted the ten-file delta: both race assertions remain intact, final ownership checks precede effects, and prepared inspections dispose on exit.

The baseline retains the real upstream fixture repair from [PR #197699](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/197699), [0518869](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/0518869e94ee4ffe1b668e65b3aaeb7d9af90f35): retire scoped database validation before fixture-directory removal. Its teardown regression and the prior raw-transcript permission case both explicitly passed in the fresh five-file run.

Fresh product installation, all 119 tests, scoped formatting, extension/core lint, the test-line ratchet and the baseline diff check passed. The ratchet reports +34 net lines, allowance400 and allocation credit34; source and frozen dependency inputs stayed unchanged. Initial native publication succeeded in `github_pending` mode at this exact candidate, without replacing hosted ancestry. [Fresh ordinary CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43274274745), attempt 1, passed at the exact reviewed head: 48 successful jobs, 27 skipped. [Workflow Sanity](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43274274614) also passed. Completed native hosted proof selected those successful runs; publication reseal and the single immediate corrected-head recovery both passed. The PR merged as [f05b22c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/f05b22c661320f167bf603f53a0e668d85325dd2). Auto-merge was not rearmed.

Historical inherited-failure admission was ineligible because a reached shared helper had a changed whole blob; equal reached functions could not replace whole-object equality. The current merge used fresh passing proof and normal native admission. No admin exception was submitted. The retired earlier intent remains in native outcome history.

Earlier [manual CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41791742723) and [ordinary CI 43178470759](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43178470759) remain failed. That older run's allocation overage and separate native-hook JSON assertion remain historical failures; the current candidate was qualified independently. No release or live-effect qualification is claimed.

## Native closeout

The immediate recovery recorded the merged squash in [the native comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/192623#issuecomment-6832613780), preserving the retired outcome in history. Reconciliation passed after the task shell left the native checkout. The current native GC command exited successfully but reported `No merged/closed PR worktrees removed.` The reason it selected nothing is unknown. The checkout, registration, preparation branches, workflow binding and required tooling remain retained; native completion was not submitted. This bookkeeping follow-up does not change the completed source landing.

prs.title: fix(mcp): mcp login prints an unusable sign-in link when the client ID is a JWT
prs.body:
Closes #197356

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw mcp login` prints a sign-in link that cannot be opened when the MCP provider issues a JWT as the client ID. ClickUp's hosted MCP server does this.

## User Impact

User impact: operators can sign in to OAuth MCP servers such as ClickUp from the link `openclaw mcp login` prints, and tools that read that link from the command's output get a working one.

Before, the middle of `client_id` was replaced with `…`, and the provider answered `401 invalid_client`. No error was shown by OpenClaw.

One behavior to know: the link line is now written to stdout as plain text in every console style. With `logging.consoleStyle: "json"`, that one line is no longer a JSON log line.

## Why This Change Was Made

The login printed the authorization URL through the console logger, which masks token-shaped text. A JWT client ID matches that mask. The URL holds no secret (client ID, PKCE challenge, state, redirect, scope), and it is printed for a person to open, so it now goes straight to stdout the way other commands write output that must reach the caller unchanged. Everything else the command prints is unchanged.

## Evidence

Head `cdadc1b492bc54a49ed127fb2a4070f97b966851`, rebased on `main` at `de6dc6249746de070d49c0ed521f39addd63cbb6`. The live output, tests and checks below were rerun at this head.

Since the first revision (`ec60bef41a9`): the source change is the same; the new test was shortened from +29 to +7 test lines after the test-lines ratchet failed in CI, and the branch was rebased.

**Live, real CLI path.** `openclaw mcp set` then `openclaw mcp login` run from source (`src/entry.ts`) in a fresh home against `https://mcp.clickup.com/mcp`, with real discovery and dynamic client registration. `state` and `code_challenge` are replaced below; nothing else is edited.

Before (`src/cli/mcp-cli-oauth.ts` as on `main`):

```
Open this URL to authorize "clickup":
https://mcp.clickup.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=mcp-client-eyJhbG…Nu1I&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Foauth%2Fcallback&state=<state>&scope=read+write&resource=https%3A%2F%2Fmcp.clickup.com%2Fmcp
After approval, run openclaw mcp login clickup --code <code>.
```

After (this branch):

```
Open this URL to authorize "clickup":
https://mcp.clickup.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=mcp-client-eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjEifQ.eyJ0b2tlblR5cGUiOiJqd3RfY2xpZW50X2lkIiwidXJpX2hhc2hlcyI6WyJlZWxHRHBqekpOTU9yZ0FJLW5JWTlBIl0sImlzcyI6ImNsaWNrdXAtbWNwLXNlcnZlciIsImlhdCI6MTc5NDQ5NzEzOH0.nYKl0LbVhLkKQUA4ZmxciuCZOEW-BBSu62tTdZfHeMg&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Foauth%2Fcallback&state=<state>&scope=read+write&resource=https%3A%2F%2Fmcp.clickup.com%2Fmcp
After approval, run openclaw mcp login clickup --code <code>.
```

The masked link sent to ClickUp's authorize endpoint returns `401 {"error":"invalid_client","error_description":"Invalid client_id"}`. The client ID shown is a throwaway registration for a callback at `example.com`.

**Tests.** `pnpm test src/cli/mcp-cli.login-loopback.test.ts src/cli/mcp-cli.oauth.test.ts src/cli/mcp-cli.oauth-integration.test.ts src/cli/mcp-cli.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 56 passed in 4 files (Node 24.22.2, Linux arm64). An existing loopback test now gives the login a JWT-shaped client ID, asserts that `redactSensitiveText` would change that URL, and asserts the URL is written whole. `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet`: `Test lines OK. Net test lines: +7; allowance: 400; allocation credit: 0.`

**Checks.** `pnpm check:changed` (Node 24.22.2, Linux arm64 container): 32 of 34 steps pass, including format, lint, `typecheck core`, `typecheck core tests`, the tsgo graph boundary, import cycles and plugin boundaries. The two that fail do so identically on unmodified `main` at `de6dc624974` in the same container, and neither touches a file in this PR:

- `dead export scan`: `src/config/sessions/session-accessor.pending-inputs.ts: bindSessionPendingInputMentionInvitation` and `src/config/sessions/session-pending-input-source.ts: readPendingInputSource` are reported unused.
- `SQLite worker ratchet`: the tool stops with `An error was suppressed during disposal` and outcome `failure` (a tool error), not `rejected` (a finding). This PR adds no SQLite call.

Format and lint of the changed files pass inside `check:changed`.

**Local review.** Autoreview (`openclaw/agent-skills` at 16121cf, helper `source-sha256:edb41e63c868269e193951a1fd9abe02494cff54885d541b2d5f20e1fc0f9700`), `--mode branch --base origin/main --max-priority P2`, run on this patch before the rebase (base `0e966cc6e0927ddc539d79f6937a8a7dc51e9b82`, head `d225043955abe3cb06a5a3c8b588866a1fd8b007`; `git patch-id --stable` equals this head's, `72d7d11e6851`): `scoped-clean`, no P0–P2 findings, one pass. Engine `claude` (`claude-fable-5`); the Codex CLI was not available for this work. The reviewer listed three things it could not confirm from the bundle; each was checked by hand: `writeStdout` appends the newline (`src/runtime.ts`); no other test reads the authorization URL from the log spy (the four `mcp login` CLI test files above are the ones that run this path, and all pass); and `mcp login` has no mode that routes logs to stderr for machine-readable stdout (`routeLogsToStderr` is used by JSON output, ACP, completion and doctor only).

**Not covered.** No macOS or Windows run. No completed sign-in against ClickUp: the run stops at the printed link, which is the changed behavior. The full test suite is left to CI.

prs.title: fix(agents): bound Proxy SSE by frame, not cumulative bytes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Proxy SSE streams that emit many small complete events fail once the *cumulative* decoded byte total crosses 16 MiB, even when no single frame is oversized. A long healthy stream is cut off mid-run.

## User Impact

Long Proxy SSE streams can finish normally. An oversized *pending* (unterminated) frame is still rejected before the buffer grows past 16 MiB. Aggregate traffic across many complete frames may exceed 16 MiB.

## Why This Change Was Made

The previous guard counted cumulative stream bytes. This change accounts one pending/complete SSE frame at a time (sibling of the Mistral frame-budget fix): completed newline-terminated frames release the budget; an oversized pending frame is rejected before decode/alloc.

Also: replaced `while (!terminalEventSeen)` with an explicit `for (;;)` break so oxlint `no-unmodified-loop-condition` is satisfied (the flag is updated inside `accountChunk`). Removed the low-value mocked-reader long-stream case; the real HTTP transport test covers the same contract.

## Evidence

- Changed: `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts`, `src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts`
- Exact head: `679e66e776b` on upstream/main `b2b07665c2b`

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Real `streamProxy` against loopback `/api/stream` via native fetch. ~20 MiB of small complete frames succeeds; an oversized pending frame is rejected.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `streamProxy` → native `fetch` → `response.body.getReader()` → per-frame byte budget → decode/process SSE line.
- **Boundary crossed:** Real Node HTTP server + native fetch (not a mocked reader).
- **Same command on base (RED) and head (GREEN):**

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts -t "accepts over 16 MiB of complete small SSE frames over real HTTP|caps an oversized pending" --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence before fix (current main `proxy.ts`):**

```text
 × |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > accepts over 16 MiB of complete small SSE frames over real HTTP 329ms
 × |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > caps an oversized pending SSE frame over real HTTP before decoding 4830ms
⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Tests 2 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯
AssertionError: expected 'Proxy SSE stream exceeded 16777216 by…' to be undefined
AssertionError: expected { role: 'assistant', …(8) } to match object { stopReason: 'error', …(1) }
      Tests  2 failed | 23 skipped (25)
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > flushes a final SSE frame without a trailing newline 243ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > caps unterminated pending SSE bytes before a frame delimiter arrives 183ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy > does not cancel a naturally drained response ending with a terminal frame 6ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > closes a hanging native SSE body after terminal success without applying later frames 38ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > closes a hanging native SSE body after terminal error without applying later frames 17ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > closes a hanging native SSE body after malformed event without applying later frames 9ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > accepts over 16 MiB of complete small SSE frames over real HTTP 285ms
 ✓ |agents-support| src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts > streamProxy loopback /api/stream > caps an oversized pending SSE frame over real HTTP before decoding 166ms
      Tests  8 passed | 17 skipped (25)
```

- **Independent readback:** success case asserts the streamed assistant content completed; oversized case asserts `stopReason: "error"` with the frame-limit message (not cumulative stream exceeded).
- **Normal-input control:** existing terminal success/error/malformed hanging-body cases still pass.
- **What was not tested:** Production cloud Proxy provider; multi-GB streams; mid-frame UTF-8 split across TCP packets beyond the existing decoder coverage.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix

prs.title: fix(agents): let healthy proxy streams exceed 16 MiB
prs.body:
<!--
Optional linked context:
Add a visible `Closes #<issue-number>` or `Related: #<issue-number>` line
below this comment.

Required PR title:
type: user-facing description
Use a parenthesized scope only when it adds clarity:
fix(auth): login redirect loops when session cookie is expired

Types: feat, fix, improve, refactor, docs, chore.
For fixes, describe the user-visible symptom and trigger:
fix: task list fails to load when user has no environments
Avoid implementation details such as:
fix: add null check to task query

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.
-->

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes healthy proxied model responses failing after 16 MiB of cumulative SSE traffic, even when every event line is small.

## User Impact

Long proxied responses can finish. Each outstanding event line remains capped at 16 MiB, oversized lines still cancel the response, and stalled reads and error bodies retain their existing limits. Accumulated assistant output can exceed 16 MiB.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing reader now charges raw bytes to the outstanding newline-delimited line before decoding, releasing that budget after each completed line. This keeps the current line parsing and reader cleanup while removing the lifetime traffic cap. No configuration or protocol change is needed.

## Evidence

- Real loopback HTTP through `streamProxy` and native fetch: 18 MiB of small valid text deltas completes; an oversized pending line fails and closes the upstream socket. Both regressions fail on baseline `9ca7932563ff3a8d2d3eca37e50d6ea7b031a527` and pass with this change.

prs.title: fix(signal): view-once attachments are downloaded and passed to the agent
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Signal view-once photos and videos are downloaded and handed to the agent like ordinary attachments when a view-once message is received.

## User Impact

User impact: media a sender marked view-once is no longer fetched, saved to the inbound media store, or passed into the agent's context. The agent sees `[signal view-once media not shown]` instead. Ordinary attachments behave as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Signal receive handler did not look at `dataMessage.viewOnce` before calling the attachment fetcher, and the fetcher saves the downloaded bytes for downstream use. The handler now skips the fetch when the flag is strictly `true` and emits the notice. A missing, `false` or `null` flag keeps the existing attachment path.

The unavailable-media text moved into the existing Signal media-text module so the already oversized event handler does not grow.

This covers OpenClaw's fetch decision and the context sent to the model. signal-cli's own attachment storage is outside the change.

## Evidence

Run with Node 24.22.2 and pnpm 12.15.0. No live Signal account or model provider was used; attachment transport is mocked and identifiers are synthetic.

- The new regression (`extensions/signal/src/monitor/event-handler.view-once.test.ts`) drives the real `createSignalEventHandler` and inbound runner. On `main` it fails 2 of 5 cases (the view-once attachment is fetched); on this branch all 5 pass, including three ordinary-media controls.
- A second, separately written test through the same entry point covers direct, edited, group and captioned view-once messages plus `ignoreAttachments`: 5 failed / 4 passed on `main`, 9 passed on this branch.
- Existing handler and media-text suites together with the new test: 36 passed across three files.
- `pnpm build` and `pnpm check:test-types` passed. Targeted type-aware lint, formatting, line-growth and test-budget checks passed. The per-change test allocation is 78 lines.

Gap: `pnpm check --base origin/main` passed its preflights and typechecks, then hit Tlon and Crabbox test line-limit errors that reproduce on an untouched `main` checkout. The remaining core lint shard was stopped after eleven minutes without diagnostics, so the full repository check is not claimed green locally.

### Running Gateway (local signal-cli stand-in)

The real Gateway was built from each revision and started with the Signal plugin enabled in its documented external daemon mode. The far end was a local stand-in for the signal-cli daemon, not signal-cli or the Signal service: JSON-RPC over HTTP plus the SSE receive stream, on loopback. A second local stand-in answered the model request with a fixed reply. Gateway transport, ingress, media storage, agent dispatch, transcript persistence and reply delivery ran unmodified. No real account or provider credential was used.

- Base: `b382a29a688a`. Head: `730cfcd13971`. Node 24.22.2, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm build`, then `pnpm openclaw gateway run --bind loopback --verbose`.
- The same scenario ran on both: a captionless view-once image, wait for the reply, then an ordinary image. Both attachments are the same synthetic 16x16 PNG (79 bytes).
- Observations come from the stand-in's request log, file events and snapshots of the inbound media store, the captured model request, and the Gateway's persisted transcript.

| Revision | Received | Attachment fetches | New inbound files | Persisted media paths | Images in the model request | Reply delivered |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Base | view-once | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Head | view-once | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Base | ordinary | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Head | ordinary | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

On head the persisted user content for the view-once message is exactly `[signal view-once media not shown]`; the retained media fact carries only the content type and kind, with no path or URL. The Gateway's own pre-prompt diagnostics report `promptImages=1` for the base view-once message, `promptImages=0` for head, and `promptImages=1` for the ordinary control on both.

Limits: this is the running product against local stand-ins. It does not establish the live Signal service's wire contract, account or device behaviour, or real-model behaviour. The no-write observation covers the inbound media store from injection through reply delivery plus one second; it is not a syscall audit.

prs.title: fix(telegram): span the album quiet window over ~1 s member gaps
prs.body:
Fixes #188353

## What Problem This Solves 📌

Telegram albums where the transport delivers members about 1 s apart are split into one agent turn per photo, so the bot answers each photo without seeing the rest of the album and the replies contradict each other. This raises the default album quiet window from 500 ms to 1500 ms so a starved sibling still joins its album's single turn.

- Problem: `MEDIA_GROUP_TIMEOUT_MS` (500 ms) is shorter than the observed ~1.04 s inter-member delivery gap, so the lone first member flushes before its sibling arrives and the sibling starts a new collection/turn.
- Solution: default the album quiet window to 1500 ms (within the reporter's suggested 1500–2000 ms range), still bounded by the existing 20 s `MEDIA_GROUP_MAX_HOLD_MS` deadline and the existing backlog-hold logic.
- What changed: the default window constant in `extensions/telegram/src/bot-updates.ts`; a durable-ingress regression for a ~1.04 s delayed sibling; the coalescing fixture gained an opt-in `useProductionAlbumWindow` flag (test-only).
- What did NOT change: no config option is reintroduced (`mediaGroupFlushMs` stays retired), the backlog-hold and hold-deadline semantics are untouched, and `testTimings.mediaGroupFlushMs` still overrides the window for tests.

## Why This Change Was Made

The quiet window is the only knob that governs whether a not-yet-delivered sibling joins the buffered album; the retired config option and shared-queue semantics were intentionally left alone (per the ClawSweeper review on the issue).

- Best fix: a focused default-window correction — every existing coalescing guarantee (member quiet resets, backlog holds, ordering, 20 s bound) keeps working; only the production default duration moves.
- Alternative: a lone-member grace extension would avoid +1 s latency on albums whose members arrive together, but it adds a second timing regime to `settleMediaGroup`; the flat window keeps one rule and matches the reporter's proposal.
- Risk / non-goals: every album now dispatches up to ~1 s later when its members arrive inside one window (accepted in the issue discussion); gaps larger than 1.5 s still split and would need the gateway-level batching tracked in #39343.

## User Impact

Albums sent through Telegram are answered as one turn even when Telegram/polling delivers the photos about a second apart, instead of producing contradictory half-context replies. Albums whose members arrive together simply dispatch about a second later than before.

## Evidence 📌

Observed result first — the shipped album handler was driven with the production default window (no `testTimings` override) and a sibling arriving ~1.04 s after the first member:

| Window | Album collections queued on the conversation lane | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `500` (base) | **2** | first member flushed alone at ~0.5 s; sibling started a second collection → album split |
| `1500` (fix) | **1** | sibling joined the buffered album → one turn, both photos downloaded |

```
$ node scripts/test-projects.mts extensions/telegram/src/bot.create-telegram-bot.channel-post-media.test.ts \
    # temporary production-window scenario, red at 500 / green at 1500
GREEN EXIT=0
 ✓ keeps a starved ~1.04 s sibling in one album turn (production window) 6229ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
```

The committed regression (`keeps an album together when a starved sibling arrives about 1 s later`) asserts the same behavior through the durable-ingress pipeline (durable queue → drain → grammY → album buffer) with the production window; it fails on the base window and passes with the fix. Adjacent suites on the changed area stay green:

```
$ node scripts/test-projects.mts extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-drain.test.ts \
    extensions/telegram/src/polling-session.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-spool.test.ts
Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  54 passed (54)
```

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `grep`/`git diff` to locate the album buffer in `bot-handlers.inbound-media.ts` and implemented the window change plus the delayed-sibling regression. The implementer understands the code: each member re-arms the album's quiet timer and `settleMediaGroup` flushes when the window elapses without a pending sibling. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix(process): keep literal semicolons in Windows command directories
prs.body:
Fixes #194337

## What Problem This Solves

Windows command resolution reports `spawn ... ENOENT` for an existing executable when the working directory name contains a literal semicolon (legal in Windows directory names) and the command uses a relative PATH directory or an explicit extensionless path. In plain terms: a project folder named `project;literal` breaks every command lookup inside it, because the resolver treats the folder name as a PATH separator.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveWindowsCommandFromCwdOrPath` prepared cwd-relative PATH entries correctly but then handed them back to the executable resolver as a semicolon-delimited string, which re-split them on the literal semicolon inside the directory name. The same re-split hit the explicit-path branch through `path.dirname(candidate)`. The resolver already accepts prepared directory arrays and uses array entries as-is, so both call sites now pass arrays; parsing of the `PATH` environment variable itself is unchanged.

## User Impact

Commands resolve and run inside Windows directories whose names contain semicolons, for both bare-name PATH lookups and explicit extensionless relative paths. Normal resolution (absolute entries, extensions, PATHEXT probing) is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Regression: `windows-command.test.ts > "resolves commands under a working directory whose name contains a semicolon"` — with a mocked win32 platform, a `project;literal/bin/fixture.exe` fixture resolves both via bare name with relative `PATH=bin` and via `./bin/fixture`, returning the fixture path. Red check: reverting the two call sites reproduces `spawn ... ENOENT` for the same scenario (1 failed → 10/10 green after restore).
- Existing resolution matrix unchanged: `windows-command.test.ts` 10 passed / 14 win32-only skipped, `windows-command-line.test.ts` 11 passed.

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used source inspection and the repository test harness to analyze issue #194337, locate the string re-split in windows-command.ts, and switch both call sites to prepared directory arrays. The implementer understands the code: only cwd-derived directory values were affected; PATH env parsing still splits on the delimiter. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix(browser): report crashed tabs explicitly instead of a generic timeout
prs.body:
Closes #194667

## What Problem This Solves

When a tab's renderer process dies (kernel OOM kill or crash), the managed browser keeps running, but every action on that tab reports misleading failures: `snapshot` hangs ~20 s and fails with the generic transient hint ("the browser is currently unavailable"), `screenshot`/`navigate` fail with raw Playwright text ("Target crashed"), and `tabs` still lists the dead tab as a normal entry. An agent retries the dead tab, then tells the user the whole browser is down — when only one tab died.

Plain language: the browser did not go down; one tab's rendering process was killed. The tool had no way to tell the two apart, so it gave a wrong diagnosis. Now every action on a dead tab says exactly that: the tab crashed, open the URL in a new tab — and `tabs` marks the dead tab.

## Why This Change Was Made

The browser tool had no notion of a crashed renderer. Playwright emits a `crash` event on the Page object, but nothing listened, so crash-shaped failures fell through to the generic timeout classifier. The fix records crashed pages (a page-scoped `WeakSet` wired into the existing per-page state bootstrap), refuses a known-crashed target during resolution before any action runs, translates mid-action "Target crashed" failures at the shared `awaitActionWithAbort` boundary, and marks crashed entries in tab listings.

Per review, three adjustments: `close` remains available for crashed targets (target resolution takes an `allowCrashed` admission flag, so the cleanup operation keeps its ownership checks); crash facts learned on the Playwright side (`getPageForTargetId` refusal and Playwright target enumeration) flow into a target-keyed registry that raw `/json/list` listings also consume, and the CLI renders the marker; the crash test fixture keeps a correctly typed emitter, with action-boundary regressions replacing translator-only tests.

## User Impact

Agents see one explicit error for every action on a crashed tab — fast, without the "browser is unavailable" retry hint — and can recover by opening the URL in a new tab. Tab listings (JSON and CLI output) distinguish a dead tab from a live one, and closing a crashed tab still works.

## Evidence

Real runtime runs on the main tree this change is based on (every changed file byte-compared as `main`/head + exactly this delta before push):

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `pw-session-crashed-target.test.ts`: crash-event marking; "Target crashed" translation incl. non-Error form; no false translation for locator timeout or genuine close; action-boundary: crashed rejection → explicit error, timeout and close-shaped failures unchanged | 5/5 green |
| Red checks: crash listener removed → marking test fails; action-boundary wiring reverted → boundary test fails (earlier round); fixture-typing round rerun green | confirmed |
| Adjacent `pw-session.connections.test.ts` (incl. connection scoping with the new admission flag), `pw-session-navigation-fence.test.ts` | 44/44 green |
| `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.extensions.json`: zero errors under `extensions/browser` | verified |

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used grep and git diff to analyze issue #194667, locate the missing crash handling in the browser tool's session layer, and implement the fix. The implementer understands the code: Playwright's per-page `crash` event marks the dead page, target resolution refuses it (close opts out via `allowCrashed`), and the shared action boundary translates "Target crashed" failures. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix(models): surface manual-selection permission in the full CLI inventory
prs.body:
Closes #194738

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw models list --all --json` reports a policy-blocked but authenticated model as `available: true` with no field distinguishing manual-selection permission from runtime readiness. An agent selecting a reviewer from this inventory then hits the native `sessions_spawn` policy rejection. The policy rejection is correct; the missing policy visibility is the bug.

Plain language: the model catalog told the agent "this model is ready to use", but the permission layer separately forbids picking it — and the catalog never said so. Now the catalog row says it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The projection already exists: `models-list-result.ts` renders `manualSelectionAllowed` for clients that opt in, gated by the `model-selection-policy` client capability, and the protocol schema documents the field as "Scoped manual-choice permission; separate from runtime readiness". The CLI never opted in, so the full inventory omitted it. The CLI now advertises the capability on the gateway path, passes the internal `includeManualSelection` flag on the local-reader path, and carries the projected field through to each JSON row. Models are not removed from the full inventory and admission is unchanged.

## User Impact

`models list --all --json` rows for policy-blocked models now show `manualSelectionAllowed: false` (and `true` for allowed ones), so inventory consumers can filter before attempting `sessions_spawn`. When the projection is unavailable (older gateway, or the field is not projected), rows omit the field exactly as before.

## Evidence

Real runtime runs on the latest main tree this change is based on (files byte-compared as `main` + exactly this delta):

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `list.prepared-catalog.test.ts` new test: gateway result carrying `manualSelectionAllowed: false` surfaces on the `--all --json` row, and the CLI gateway call advertises the `model-selection-policy` cap | green (16/16) |
| Red check: reverting the capability advertisement and the row passthrough makes exactly the new test fail (caps missing, field absent) | confirmed |
| Adjacent suites `list.refresh-secrets.test.ts`, `load-config.test.ts` | 7/7 green |
| `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.core.json`: zero errors in changed files | verified |

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used grep to trace the existing `manualSelectionAllowed` projection through the gateway capability gate and the CLI row mapping, then wired the existing mechanism into the CLI. The implementer understands the code: no new policy logic is introduced; the CLI simply joins the existing opt-in projection. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix(doctor): stop false Telegram first-time setup warning
prs.body:
Closes #124705

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw doctor` reports `channels.telegram` as being in first-time setup mode when a multi-account Telegram setup already configures `groups` for every active account.

## User Impact

Configured multi-account Telegram users no longer receive this parent-scope false positive. Accounts that actually lack group configuration still warn at their own scope, and configurations that rely on an implicit default account keep the first-time guidance.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor inspects configuration without starting channels, so the live channel registry can be empty. Account-id resolution now falls back to Doctor's config-driven read-only plugin loader for bundled and configured external channels, and forwards the active Doctor environment.

The Telegram parent container is not itself an account. Telegram's extra warning hook now suppresses first-time guidance only when an explicit default account exists, at least one child account is active, and every active child configures `groups`. With an implicit default account, the container remains the only scope that can carry the guidance, so the warning is preserved.

## Evidence

- Focused Doctor and Telegram tests pass: 3 Vitest shards, 5 test files, including new coverage for config-driven account discovery and the parent/child warning cases.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` pass.
- Changed-file `oxlint --type-aware --deny-warnings` and `oxfmt --check` pass.
- `git diff --check`, `pnpm check:assertion-safety`, `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet`, and `pnpm check:test-mock-exports` pass.
- Shipped CLI proof: `pnpm openclaw doctor --non-interactive` was run from this head with isolated `HOME`/state/config/workspace and `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS=1`. The issue's reported two-account config no longer prints `Telegram is in first-time setup mode`; four retained-guidance controls still do (missing child groups, single account with no `accounts` block, top-level-token implicit default, and environment-token implicit default). These are synthetic diagnostic configs only; no live Telegram credential or message delivery is claimed.

```text
reported two-account config                  first-time warning: absent
child account missing groups                 first-time warning: retained
single account, no groups                    first-time warning: retained
top-level token, implicit default            first-time warning: retained
env token, implicit default                  first-time warning: retained
```

- Latest-stable config upgrade: published `openclaw@2026.10.5` normalized the issue config, then the same isolated state was run through this head's shipped `doctor --fix`. Stable printed the reported false positive; head completed without it and wrote no config change.

```text
stable 2026.10.5: channels.telegram: Telegram is in first-time setup mode. ...
head 8165969:     no first-time setup warning; Doctor complete
config SHA-256 (stable-after == head-after): 67870af688ef809509cc6c99e98ebf125f3b2c67baa88871b71c072ec32d67f3
Telegram subtree SHA-256 (stable-after == head-after): f6f69a5a2dbaa6334bde89d13a46d9da62640ecd9c7d4974f5195936729fe20b
preserved: defaultAccount=default, groupPolicy=allowlist, groupAllowFrom=["11111111"], accounts=default+second with groups
```

The branch identifies itself as `2026.10.4 (8165969)`, older than npm `latest` `2026.10.5`; the run therefore demonstrates compatibility from a real latest-stable config/state into this candidate, not a version-number increase.

- Base-fail/head-pass: the new test blocks were applied to a detached worktree at merge base `1507c89eaa51d713a97b4135d72afb976856a485` without changing production source. Base failed the reported-config suppression test (`1 failed | 45 passed`) and read-only account-discovery test (`1 failed | 14 passed`); this head passed `46/46` Telegram tests and `15/15` channel-capability tests.

Not verified: full repository CI will run after the PR is updated. Local `pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet` is blocked by unrelated existing UI baseline failures. No live Telegram Test Server userbot run is claimed because this environment has no Telegram credentials; Doctor does not send messages in the evidence above.

AI assistance: implementation and validation were completed with Codex; the submitter reviewed the final diff and results.
